📜 The Evolution That Led to eBPF & Cilium

From iptables to programmable kernel networking

2000s
iptables Era

Sequential rule matching. Works for basic firewalling but doesn't scale.

❌ O(n) linear
2014
eBPF Born

Linux 3.18 merges eBPF. Programmable kernel. Verifier guarantees safety.

🟡 O(1) hash
2017
Cilium Launched

First eBPF-based CNI. Identity-based networking replaces iptables.

✅ eBPF CNI
2023
CNCF Graduated

Enterprise maturity. Hubble, WireGuard, Cluster Mesh — all eBPF.

🚀 Enterprise
Today
eBPF Everywhere

Meta, Google, Netflix power networking, security & observability.

🌍 Standard

🐝 What is Cilium?

Cilium is an open-source CNI plugin powered by eBPF that provides networking, security, and observability for Kubernetes. Unlike traditional CNIs (Calico, Flannel) that use iptables, Cilium runs eBPF programs directly in the Linux kernel — making it 587x faster at scale. It replaces your CNI, kube-proxy, service mesh sidecar, and network policy engine — all with one eBPF-powered agent per node.

⚡
eBPF Powered

Runs in the Linux kernel at native speed. No sidecars, no proxies, no overhead.

🛡️
Identity-Based Security

Policies based on pod labels, not fragile IP addresses. Survives pod restarts.

🔭
Hubble Observability

Built-in flow logs, service map, and latency metrics — no extra tools needed.

🌍
Multi-Cluster

Cluster Mesh connects pods across clusters — direct pod-to-pod, encrypted.

📋 Detailed Implementation Commands

Phase 1: Deploy — Get anihpj Running on Cilium
# Step 1: Install Cilium (if not already installed)
cilium install --version 1.16.5 \
  --set kubeProxyReplacement=true \
  --set hubble.enabled=true \
  --set hubble.ui.enabled=true

# Step 2: Verify Cilium is healthy
cilium status --wait
cilium connectivity test

# Step 3: Deploy anihpj application
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl apply -f anihpj-service.yaml -n anihpj

# Step 4: Verify pods are managed by Cilium
kubectl get cep -n anihpj
cilium endpoint list
Phase 2: Secure — Network Policies for Defense in Depth
# Step 1: Create L3/L4 baseline policy (default deny + explicit allows)
kubectl apply -f anihpj-cnp-baseline.yaml -n anihpj

# Step 2: Add L7 HTTP rules (protect /admin, allow GET /api)
kubectl apply -f anihpj-cnp-l7.yaml -n anihpj

# Step 3: Test policies in audit mode first
# Add enableAudit: true to policy, observe with Hubble:
hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict AUDIT

# Step 4: Enable Host Firewall for node protection
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.5 \
  --namespace kube-system --reuse-values \
  --set hostFirewall.enabled=true
kubectl apply -f host-firewall-policy.yaml
Phase 3: Observe — Full Visibility with Hubble + Prometheus
# Step 1: Port-forward Hubble UI
cilium hubble ui
# Open https://localhost:12000

# Step 2: Observe flows for anihpj namespace
hubble observe -n anihpj
hubble observe -n anihpj --verdict DROPPED
hubble observe -n anihpj --http-method POST --http-path /api

# Step 3: Deploy Prometheus + Grafana
helm install prometheus prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  --namespace monitoring --create-namespace

# Step 4: Import Cilium dashboards into Grafana
# Dashboards: Cilium Overview, Hubble DNS, Hubble HTTP, Hubble TCP
Phase 4: Optimize — KPR + Bandwidth + BBR
# Step 1: Enable KPR Strict mode (requires kernel 5.10+)
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.5 \
  --namespace kube-system --reuse-values \
  --set kubeProxyReplacement=true \
  --set kubeProxyReplacementHealthzBindAddr="0.0.0.0:10256"

# Step 2: Enable Bandwidth Manager + BBR
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.5 \
  --namespace kube-system --reuse-values \
  --set bandwidthManager.enabled=true \
  --set bandwidthManager.bbr=true

# Step 3: Add bandwidth annotations to anihpj pods
kubectl annotate pod anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj \
  kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth=50M

# Step 4: Verify
cilium status | grep -E "KubeProxyReplacement|BandwidthManager"
cilium bpf bandwidth list
Phase 5: Harden — Encryption + Threat Model
# Step 1: Enable WireGuard encryption
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.5 \
  --namespace kube-system --reuse-values \
  --set encryption.enabled=true \
  --set encryption.type=wireguard

# Step 2: Verify encryption
cilium encrypt status
# Should show "OK" with WireGuard keys for each peer

# Step 3: Apply Threat Model hardening checklist
# - Ensure RBAC is scoped
# - Enable K8s audit logging
# - Deploy Tetragon for runtime security
# - Enable TLS for Hubble Relay/UI
Phase 6: Scale — Cluster Mesh for Multi-Region
# Step 1: Enable Cluster Mesh on both clusters
cilium clustermesh enable --context cluster1
cilium clustermesh enable --context cluster2

# Step 2: Connect clusters
cilium clustermesh connect --context cluster1 --destination-context cluster2

# Step 3: Verify mesh
cilium clustermesh status --context cluster1
# Should show both clusters connected

# Step 4: Create global service for anihpj
kubectl apply -f anihpj-global-service.yaml
# anihpj pods in cluster1 can now reach anihpj pods in cluster2!

⚠️ Common Study Mistakes to AVOID

❌ Reading without doing: CCA is a practical exam. Run every command yourself.
❌ Skipping diagrams: Architecture questions are 30% of the exam. Diagrams encode relationships.
❌ Memorizing YAML without understanding: The exam tests WHY, not just WHAT.
❌ Ignoring Hubble: Observability is 18% — study Hubble CLI flags thoroughly.
❌ Not timing yourself: The exam is 90 minutes. Practice under time pressure.
❌ Skipping appendices: Appendix E (Exam Cram) and Appendix A (CLI Cheatsheet) are gold.

📚 Part 1: Foundation — Kubernetes Networking Basics Chapters 1-2

Chapter 1: Why Kubernetes Networking is Hard (And Why You Need Cilium)

Before diving into eBPF and Cilium, let's understand why Kubernetes networking is challenging in the first place — what problems exist, why traditional solutions fall short, and where Cilium fits in. We'll use our anihpj/jobpost Django app to make every concept concrete.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2 hours 📖 Conceptual 🎯 Foundation

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ How pods communicate on the same node and across nodes
  • ✅ What the Kubernetes Network Model requires (4 immutable rules)
  • ✅ What a CNI plugin is and what it does
  • ✅ Why traditional networking (iptables) doesn't scale
  • ✅ Where Cilium fits in the Kubernetes stack
  • ✅ Real networking problems anihpj faces and how Cilium solves them
  • ✅ Key networking terminology refresher (IP, CIDR, DNS, ports, etc.)
🎓 CCA Relevance
Architecture & Concepts 30% Foundation ALL DOMAINS
Understanding "Why" Matters on the CCA

The CCA exam tests your understanding of why Cilium uses eBPF instead of iptables. Key concepts to internalize from this chapter:

  • Kubernetes Network Model — The 4 rules that every CNI must implement. Cilium implements them via eBPF.
  • CNI Interface — How kubelet invokes CNI plugins. Cilium's CNI is a thin binary that delegates to the Cilium Agent.
  • iptables Limitations — Sequential O(n) rule matching vs eBPF O(1) hash lookups. This is the core argument for Cilium.
  • Stack Consolidation — Cilium replaces 4 separate tools (CNI, kube-proxy, service mesh, network policy engine) with ONE eBPF-powered agent.

1.1 The "Hello World" of K8s Networking

Imagine you've deployed anihpj (Django backend on port 8000) and PostgreSQL (database on port 5432) as two separate pods. They need to communicate. How does that actually work?

📖 The Kubernetes Network Model — 4 Fundamental Rules

Rule 1: Every Pod gets its OWN unique IP address — no NAT, no port mapping. Like every house has its own street address.

Rule 2: Pods on any node can communicate with ALL pods on ALL nodes WITHOUT NAT. Like being able to call any extension in any building.

Rule 3: Agents on a node (kubelet, daemons) can communicate with ALL pods on that node. Like the building manager can reach every desk.

Rule 4: Pods see their OWN IP as what other pods see — no "inside vs outside" confusion.

💡 These 4 rules define the "flat network" model. CNI plugins implement these rules differently. Cilium implements them with eBPF — the fastest way!

Pod-to-Pod on the SAME Node

Two pods on the same worker node communicate through a Linux bridge — just like two computers plugged into the same network switch. The Linux bridge (cbr0/cni0) acts as a virtual L2 switch connecting all pod veth interfaces.

Same-Node Communication — Linux Bridge
                          WORKER NODE
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                      │
  │  ┌──────────────┐              ┌──────────────┐     │
  │  │   Pod A       │              │   Pod B       │     │
  │  │   10.0.0.1    │              │   10.0.0.2    │     │
  │  │   (anihpj)    │              │   (postgres)  │     │
  │  └──────┬────────┘              └──────┬────────┘     │
  │         │ veth0                        │ veth1         │
  │         └──────────┬───────────────────┘               │
  │                    │                                   │
  │             ┌──────┴──────┐                            │
  │             │ Linux Bridge │  ← cbr0 / cni0            │
  │             │  (L2 Switch) │                            │
  │             └──────────────┘                            │
  │                                                      │
  │  ✅ Pod A → Pod B: Direct L2 bridge forwarding       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Pod-to-Pod Across DIFFERENT Nodes

When pods are on different nodes, the CNI must encapsulate the packet and tunnel it across the physical network. Traditional CNIs use VXLAN tunnels with ~50 bytes of overhead:

Cross-Node Communication — VXLAN Tunnel
  ┌──────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────────┐
  │    NODE 1         │              │     NODE 2            │
  │  ┌──────────┐    │              │    ┌──────────┐       │
  │  │  Pod A    │    │    VXLAN     │    │  Pod C    │       │
  │  │ 10.0.0.1  │    │   TUNNEL     │    │ 10.1.0.1  │       │
  │  │ (anihpj)  │    │              │    │ (redis)   │       │
  │  └─────┬─────┘    │              │    └─────┬─────┘       │
  │        └──────────┼──────────────┼──────────┘             │
  │                   │              │                         │
  │  ❌ VXLAN: Extra 50-byte header per packet (overhead!)    │
  │  ✅ Cilium eBPF: Direct kernel routing — NO encapsulation │
  └──────────────────┘              └──────────────────────┘

🚢 The Kubernetes Shipping Port — How Cilium Fits the Analogy

Kubernetes (Greek for "helmsman") maps beautifully onto a modern shipping port. If you understand how a port operates, you understand Kubernetes — and where Cilium adds its eBPF superpowers:

Port RoleKubernetes EquivalentCilium's eBPF Enhancement
🏗️ Port Authority HQControl Plane (API Server, etcd, Scheduler)Cilium watches API for pods/services/policies
📋 Shipping ManifestYAML Manifests (Deployment, Service)CiliumNetworkPolicy YAML — identity-based rules
🏷️ Cargo LabelPod Labels (app=anihpj, tier=backend)Cilium Identity — label hash → numeric ID stored in eBPF
🚢 Container ShipPod (group of containers)Cilium networks every pod via eBPF at kernel level
📦 Shipping ContainerDocker Container (isolated process)eBPF programs inspect every packet to/from container
🛣️ Road NetworkCNI / Pod Network (how pods communicate)eBPF replaces slow iptables roads with hash-map highways

🔒 Security GateRBAC / mTLSWireGuard transparent encryption — zero code changes
📹 Security CamerasMonitoring (Prometheus)Hubble — identity-aware flow logs (who talked to whom)
🗺️ Port MapService Discovery (CoreDNS)Cilium eBPF replaces kube-proxy — O(1) service lookup

💡 The key insight: Cilium gives the port authority (control plane) direct, kernel-level visibility and control over every container ship (pod) and its cargo (packets) — something traditional CNIs can't do because they rely on slow, sequential iptables rules at the userspace/kernel boundary.

1.2 The CNI (Container Network Interface) Explained

Think of CNI as the "network driver" for Kubernetes. Just like USB defines how devices connect, CNI defines how pods get network connectivity:

📖 CNI is a SPECIFICATION, not software

CNI defines 4 operations that a plugin must implement:

ADD: "Give this container a network!" → Allocates IP, creates veth pair, sets routes

DEL: "Remove this container's network!" → Releases IP, removes veth, cleans up

CHECK: "Is this container's network healthy?" → Verifies connectivity

VERSION: "What CNI spec version do you support?"

💡 CNI plugins are BINARIES on the node filesystem. kubelet executes them directly — no daemon needed!

CNI Flow — kubelet → CRI → CNI Plugin
  ① kubelet watches API Server → "New pod assigned: anihpj-abc123"
       │
       ▼
  ② kubelet calls CRI (Container Runtime) → "Start container: anihpj:v2"
       │
       ▼
  ③ containerd creates container (NO network yet! 😱)
       │
       ▼
  ④ kubelet calls CNI: /opt/cni/bin/cilium-cni ADD <config>
       ├── 4a. Allocate IP address (from Pod CIDR)
       ├── 4b. Create veth pair (pod ↔ host)
       ├── 4c. Assign IP to pod interface
       ├── 4d. Set up routes (default gw, pod routes)
       └── 4e. Apply NetworkPolicy (eBPF programs in kernel!)
       │
       ▼
  ⑤ Pod READY — has IP, can communicate! ✅

CNI Plugin Comparison

Calicoiptables / BGP❌❌❌
WeaveVXLAN overlay❌✅❌
Cilium ☸️eBPF kernel✅✅✅ Hubble

1.3 Where Cilium Fits in the Kubernetes Stack

Cilium replaces your old CNI (Calico/Flannel/Weave). But it goes much further — it also replaces kube-proxy, service mesh sidecars, and network policy engines. One Cilium agent per node = 4 separate tools consolidated into 1.

1.4 Real-World Networking Problems anihpj Faces — Before vs After Cilium

Let's look at 3 real problems our anihpj/jobpost application faces — and how Cilium elegantly solves each one:

🔴 PROBLEM 1: "Someone is brute-forcing the Django /admin login"

Without Cilium: Block IP ranges at the WAF/nginx — fragile, IPs change daily.

🟢 Cilium Solution: L7 NetworkPolicy

Block POST /admin from external CIDRs at the KERNEL level — fast, permanent, no code changes!

🔴 PROBLEM 2: "Which of our 20 Django pods is slow?"

Without Cilium: kubectl top pods only shows CPU/RAM — no network visibility. Flying blind!

🟢 Cilium Solution: Hubble UI

See latency PER pod, PER endpoint. Pod X slow on /jobs/? Pinpoint in seconds!

🔴 PROBLEM 3: "Encrypt database traffic for compliance (HIPAA/PCI-DSS)"

Without Cilium: Reconfigure Django for TLS, configure PostgreSQL for SSL, manage certificates — weeks of work.

🟢 Cilium Solution: Transparent Encryption

cilium install --set encryption.enabled=true --set encryption.type=wireguard — DONE. ZERO code changes!

💡 CCA Exam Tip: OSI Model Layers

The CCA exam expects you to know which OSI layers Cilium operates at:

L7 (Application): HTTP/gRPC/Kafka/DNS policies — "Block POST /admin"

L4 (Transport): TCP/UDP port policies — "Allow port 5432 only"

L3 (Network): IP/CIDR-based rules — "Deny 192.168.0.0/16"

Traditional CNIs only work at L3-L4. Cilium works at L3, L4, AND L7 — it actually understands your application protocols!

⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 1

❌ MISTAKE 1: Thinking "pods automatically have network security" → TRUTH: By default, ALL pods can talk to ALL pods! No isolation. FIX: You MUST create NetworkPolicies (Chapter 7).

❌ MISTAKE 2: Confusing CNI with CRI → TRUTH: CNI handles networking. CRI handles container lifecycle. They're completely different interfaces.

❌ MISTAKE 3: Thinking all CNIs are the same → TRUTH: Calico uses iptables (O(n)). Cilium uses eBPF (O(1)). Massive performance difference at scale.

│  │ Cilium   │ eBPF         │ O(1) hash lookup, identity-based, L7-aware   │  │

│                                                                              │

🌐 The 4 Rules of the Kubernetes Network Model — What Every CNI Must Implement
RuleDescriptionHow Cilium Implements It
1. Pods communicate without NATEvery pod has a unique, routable IP. Pod A sees Pod B's real IP — no source NAT.eBPF programs route directly between pod IPs using identity-based forwarding.
2. Nodes communicate with all pods without NATkubelet and node processes can reach any pod directly by its IP.Cilium manages node routes via eBPF; host endpoint policies control node→pod access.
3. Pod sees its own IP as others see itNo container-level NAT. The IP inside the container matches the IP outside.Cilium assigns IPs from node-local CIDRs; pod interface gets direct IP.
4. All containers in a pod share network namespaceSame IP, same ports, communicate via localhost.Cilium programs eBPF at the POD level (veth interface), not per-container.
🔬 How kubelet Calls the CNI Binary — The Exact Flow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CNI INVOCATION FLOW (kubelet → Cilium CNI → Cilium Agent)                    │
│                                                                              │
│  1. kubelet creates container via CRI (containerd)                           │
│  2. kubelet reads CNI config: /etc/cni/net.d/05-cilium.conf                  │
│  3. kubelet EXECUTES: /opt/cni/bin/cilium-cni (stateless binary!)            │
│  4. Passes JSON via stdin:                                                    │
│     {                                                                         │
│       "cniVersion": "0.4.0",                                                   │
│       "name": "cilium",                                                        │
│       "containerID": "abc123...",                                              │
│       "netns": "/var/run/netns/cni-xxx",                                      │
│       "args": "K8S_POD_NAMESPACE=anihpj;K8S_POD_NAME=web-xxx"                │
│     }                                                                         │
│  5. cilium-cni binary → Unix socket → Cilium Agent (DaemonSet pod)           │
│  6. Cilium Agent: creates endpoint, allocates IP, programs eBPF              │
│  7. Returns result JSON via stdout: {interfaces:[{name:"eth0",ip:"10.0.1.5"}]}│
│  8. kubelet updates pod status: PodIP=10.0.1.5 → pod enters Running          │
│                                                                              │
│  KEY: CNI binary is STATELESS. Real work done by Cilium Agent via socket.    │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CCA Insight: The CCA exam tests CNI fundamentals heavily. Remember: CNI handles networking (pod IP assignment, routing). CRI handles container lifecycle. They are COMPLETELY separate interfaces. Without a CNI, pods stay in ContainerCreating forever. Cilium replaces BOTH the CNI plugin AND kube-proxy — it handles pod networking AND Service load balancing through eBPF.

📝 Chapter 1 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
Without a CNI plugin installed, what is the state of a newly created pod?
Show Answer
Answer

The pod gets stuck in ContainerCreating state. The container runtime creates the container, but kubelet cannot complete networking setup without a CNI plugin. The pod will remain in ContainerCreating indefinitely until a CNI is installed.

Explanation

On the CCA exam, understanding the CNI's role in pod lifecycle is critical. The CNI is invoked by kubelet AFTER the container is created by the CRI. Without a CNI, the container exists but has no network — so the pod never reaches Running state. Cilium's CNI is a thin binary that delegates to the Cilium Agent, which programs eBPF maps for networking.

Q2
Name 3 separate tools that Cilium replaces in a traditional Kubernetes stack.
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium replaces: 1) CNI plugin (Calico/Flannel for pod networking), 2) kube-proxy (service load balancing with iptables), 3) Service Mesh sidecar (Istio/Linkerd proxy), and 4) NetworkPolicy engine. All consolidated into ONE eBPF-powered agent per node.

Explanation

This "stack consolidation" is Cilium's key value proposition. Instead of running 4 separate DaemonSets/Deployments, you run 1. This reduces operational complexity, resource overhead, and troubleshooting surface area. The CCA exam frequently asks about Cilium's role as a unified networking, security, and observability layer.

Q3
Why is iptables-based networking slower than eBPF-based networking at scale?
Show Answer
Answer

iptables does linear rule matching (O(n)). Each packet walks through ALL rules sequentially. With 5,000 services, that's 5,000+ rule checks per new connection. eBPF uses hash table lookups (O(1)) — one lookup finds the result, regardless of how many rules exist.

Explanation

This is the fundamental architectural reason Cilium exists. At scale (1,000+ services), iptables becomes unusable — 500ms+ per new connection, 30+ seconds for rule updates, 80% CPU usage. Cilium's eBPF handles the same workload in microseconds with 5% CPU. The CCA exam expects you to articulate this performance difference.

Q4
What are the 4 rules of the Kubernetes Network Model?
Show Answer
Answer

Rule 1: Every pod gets its own unique IP address (no NAT, no port mapping). Rule 2: All pods on all nodes can communicate without NAT. Rule 3: Node agents (kubelet) can reach all pods on their node. Rule 4: Pods see their own IP as what other pods see (no inside/outside confusion).

Explanation

These 4 rules define the "flat network" model that every CNI plugin must implement. Cilium implements these using eBPF programs at the TC hook point — the most efficient way. Traditional CNIs implement them with VXLAN tunnels and iptables rules.

Q5
How does kubelet invoke the CNI plugin? What information does it pass?
Show Answer
Answer

kubelet executes the CNI binary directly (e.g., /opt/cni/bin/cilium-cni), passing configuration as JSON via stdin. No daemon, no gRPC — just a simple binary execution. The JSON config includes container ID, network namespace path, and CNI configuration.

Explanation

This is a common CCA exam question. CNI plugins are stateless binaries — each invocation is independent. For Cilium, the CNI binary is thin: it communicates with the Cilium Agent (which runs as a DaemonSet pod) via a Unix socket to program the actual eBPF networking.

Q6
What happens when an anihpj pod (10.0.0.55) needs to talk to a PostgreSQL pod (10.0.1.99) on a different node — in VXLAN vs Cilium eBPF?
Show Answer
Answer

VXLAN: Packet is encapsulated with extra 50-byte VXLAN header, wrapped in a UDP packet, sent across the physical network, then decapsulated at the destination. Cilium eBPF: Cilium routes directly at the kernel level using eBPF programs — no encapsulation needed (in direct routing mode), lower latency, higher throughput.

Explanation

Cilium supports both tunnel mode (VXLAN/Geneve) and direct routing mode. In direct routing mode, Cilium programs the kernel routing table via eBPF so pod traffic takes the shortest path with no encapsulation overhead. This is one reason Cilium achieves near line-rate performance.

Q7
What is the difference between an overlay network and an underlay network in Kubernetes?
Show Answer
Answer

Overlay: A virtual network built on top of the physical network using encapsulation (VXLAN, Geneve). Pod IPs are hidden inside tunneled packets. Works anywhere but has overhead. Underlay: Uses the physical network's routing tables directly (BGP, static routes). Faster but requires the physical network to know pod CIDRs.

Explanation

Cilium is unique in supporting BOTH modes. In cloud environments, overlay (VXLAN) is common because you don't control the physical network. In bare metal/data center, direct routing (underlay) with BGP gives maximum performance. The CCA exam may ask which mode to use in different scenarios.

Q8
Why can't two containers in the same pod both listen on port 8000?
Show Answer
Answer

All containers in a pod share the SAME network namespace — same IP address, same port space. Port 8000 can only be bound once per IP address. If two containers try to bind port 8000, the second one fails with "address already in use". Use different ports for different containers in the same pod.

Explanation

This is a direct consequence of the pause container pattern (Chapter 2.2). Since all containers join the pause container's network namespace, they share everything: IP, interfaces, routing table, and port space. The upside: they can communicate via localhost (127.0.0.1) at memory speed with zero network overhead.

Q9
What happens to pod-to-pod communication when you migrate from Calico/Flannel to Cilium? Does traffic interrupt?
Show Answer
Answer

During migration, drain one node at a time. Pods on drained nodes reschedule to Cilium-managed nodes. Traffic between pods on different CNIs may not work because each CNI manages its own network. For zero-downtime, use Cilium's CNI chaining mode where Cilium coexists with the existing CNI during transition.

Explanation

CCA exam may ask about CNI migration. The safe approach: (1) Install Cilium in CNI chaining mode, (2) Cordon and drain one node, (3) Verify pod connectivity on Cilium nodes, (4) Repeat for all nodes, (5) Remove old CNI. Cilium's eBPF programs take over once the old CNI stops assigning IPs.

Q10
How does Cilium provide both L3/L4 AND L7 filtering in a single platform without sidecar proxies per pod?
Show Answer
Answer

L3/L4 (IP+port) filtering runs entirely in eBPF at kernel speed — no proxy. For L7 (HTTP method/path/headers), Cilium's eBPF redirects matching traffic to a per-NODE Envoy proxy (not per-pod) for application-layer inspection. Most traffic only hits L3/L4 eBPF — Envoy is only invoked for L7 rules, keeping overhead minimal.

Explanation

CCA key distinction: L3/L4 = eBPF only (fastest). L7 = eBPF redirects to per-node Envoy. Compare this to Istio which runs a sidecar Envoy per pod (~200MB RAM each). Cilium's approach gives you L7 filtering with zero per-pod memory overhead and only one Envoy instance per node shared by all pods.

Chapter 2: Containers, Pods, and the Network Namespace — The Foundation of Pod Networking

To understand Cilium's networking magic, you must first understand how Linux containers and pods actually get their network connectivity. This chapter demystifies network namespaces, the pause container pattern, IPAM, service discovery, and kube-proxy.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2 hours 📖 Conceptual + Technical 🎯 Foundation

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What Linux namespaces are and how they isolate containers
  • ✅ How containers in the same pod share a network namespace
  • ✅ The "pause container" pattern — the secret behind pod networking
  • ✅ How pods get their IP addresses (IPAM basics)
  • ✅ How Kubernetes Service discovery works (DNS, ClusterIP, Endpoints)
  • ✅ How kube-proxy works — and why Cilium replaces it entirely
  • ✅ How Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement achieves O(1) lookups
🎓 CCA Relevance
Architecture & Concepts 30%
Pod Networking Fundamentals are Critical for CCA

The CCA exam tests your understanding of how Cilium enhances pod networking. You must understand:

  • Network Namespaces — Why they exist and how pods share them. This is why CNI only networks the pause container.
  • kube-proxy Replacement — Cilium's eBPF LB replaces iptables-based kube-proxy. Know the performance difference: O(n) vs O(1).
  • Service Discovery — CoreDNS resolution flow and how Cilium handles service load balancing without iptables.

2.1 What Happens When You Run "docker run anihpj"?

Behind every container is the Linux kernel providing isolation through namespaces and resource limits through cgroups. Each container gets its own virtual network stack:

📖 Linux Network Namespace

A network namespace is like giving each container its own PRIVATE NETWORK ROOM. Inside that room:

• It sees its own network cards (interfaces: lo, eth0)

• It has its own routing table ("how to reach the internet")

• It has its own firewall rules (iptables/nftables)

• It has its own IP addresses (no conflict with host or other containers!)

But it CAN'T see what's in OTHER rooms — unless connected via bridges/veth pairs. Namespaces are why containers can all use port 8000 without conflicting!

Container Isolation — Linux Namespaces
  HOST LINUX SYSTEM
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    KERNEL (shared by all containers)      │
  │                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐   │
  │  │  Container A │  │  Container B  │  │  Container C │   │
  │  │  (anihpj)    │  │  (postgres)   │  │  (nginx)     │   │
  │  │              │  │               │  │              │   │
  │  │ Own NET NS   │  │ Own NET NS    │  │ Own NET NS   │   │
  │  │ Own PID NS   │  │ Own PID NS    │  │ Own PID NS   │   │
  │  │ Own MNT NS   │  │ Own MNT NS    │  │ Own MNT NS   │   │
  │  │              │  │               │  │              │   │
  │  │ IP: 10.0.0.1 │  │ IP: 10.0.0.2  │  │ IP: 10.0.0.3 │   │
  │  │ Port 8000 ✅ │  │ Port 5432 ✅  │  │ Port 80 ✅   │   │
  │  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 Each container thinks it has its OWN network stack!
     But they share the same kernel — magic of namespaces.

2.2 The Pause Container Pattern — The Secret Behind Pod Networking

A Pod is NOT a container — it's a GROUP of containers sharing resources. The key shared resource is the NETWORK NAMESPACE. But how is it shared? Enter the pause container.

Pod Network Namespace — The Pause Container Pattern
  POD: anihpj-web (One Pod, Three Containers)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                          │
  │  ① PAUSE CONTAINER (created FIRST, PID 1)                │
  │     ┌────────────────────────────────────┐               │
  │     │  Creates & HOLDS the Network NS     │               │
  │     │  • IP Address: 10.0.0.55            │               │
  │     │  • Network interfaces: eth0, lo     │               │
  │     │  • Routing table, iptables rules    │               │
  │     │  • Just sleeps forever (pause() syscall)            │
  │     └───────────┬────────────────────────┘               │
  │                 │ "Join my network namespace!"            │
  │     ┌───────────┼───────────┐                            │
  │     ▼           ▼           ▼                            │
  │  ② DJANGO      ③ NGINX      ④ LOG SHIPPER                │
  │  Container     Container    Container                     │
  │  :8000         :80          (any port)                   │
  │                                                          │
  │  ✅ All 3 share: 10.0.0.55 (same IP!)                    │
  │  ✅ Can communicate via localhost (127.0.0.1)             │
  │  ✅ Django → Nginx = curl localhost:80 ← SAME MACHINE!   │
  │  ⚠️  Can't both listen on port 8000 (shared port space!) │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 Why the Pause Container Exists

❌ If you network the first app container directly and it crashes → network namespace destroyed → ALL containers lose connectivity!

✅ The pause container does NOTHING except sleep. It never crashes. It holds the network namespace stable. It's a tiny 700KB static binary that literally just calls pause().

This is why CNI only needs to network the PAUSE container — all other containers automatically inherit its network namespace!

2.3 How Pods Get Their IP Addresses — IPAM

IPAM (IP Address Management) is how Kubernetes divides the Pod CIDR range across nodes, and how each CNI allocates IPs to individual pods.

IPAM Allocation — Pod CIDR Division
  CLUSTER POD CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16 (65,536 total IPs)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                          │
  │  NODE 1: 10.0.0.0/24          NODE 2: 10.0.1.0/24      │
  │  (256 IPs)                    (256 IPs)                  │
  │  ┌────────────────┐           ┌────────────────┐        │
  │  │10.0.0.1: Pod A │           │10.0.1.1: Pod E │        │
  │  │10.0.0.2: Pod B │           │10.0.1.2: Pod F │        │
  │  │10.0.0.3: Pod C │           │10.0.1.3: Pod G │        │
  │  │10.0.0.4: FREE  │           │10.0.1.4: Pod H │        │
  │  │...              │           │...              │        │
  │  └────────────────┘           └────────────────┘        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 New pod scheduled to Node 1 → gets 10.0.0.4 (next free)
     Cilium tracks this via CiliumNode CRD (not host-local file)

2.4 Service Discovery — How anihpj Finds PostgreSQL

Services provide stable networking: a fixed ClusterIP and DNS name that doesn't change even when pods restart. CoreDNS resolves service names to ClusterIPs, then kube-proxy (or Cilium) load-balances to actual pod IPs.

Service Discovery — DNS + Load Balancing
  STEP 1: DNS RESOLUTION
  anihpj Pod (10.0.0.55)              CoreDNS (10.96.0.10)
       │                                      │
       │ ① "What IP is postgres.anihpj.svc?" │
       │─────────────────────────────────────▶│
       │                                      │ ② Look up Service
       │ ③ Response: "10.100.50.10"          │
       │◀─────────────────────────────────────│

  STEP 2: LOAD BALANCING
  anihpj → 10.100.50.10:5432
                │
                ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  postgres Service → Endpoints:      │
  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐         │
  │  │ Pod A    │ │ Pod B    │  ...    │
  │  │10.0.0.99│ │10.0.1.88│         │
  │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘         │
  │  kube-proxy/Cilium picks ONE pod   │
  │  and rewrites: 10.100.50.10 → IP  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

2.5 kube-proxy Modes — and Why Cilium Replaces It

kube-proxy is responsible for implementing Kubernetes Services. It runs on every node and creates network rules to route traffic to pods. But its default iptables mode doesn't scale:

kube-proxy Performance Comparison

MetriciptablesIPVSCilium eBPF
Rule LookupO(n) linearO(1) hashO(1) hash
10 Services~1ms<0.5ms~0.01ms
1000 Services~100ms~5ms~0.02ms
5000 Services~500ms+~25ms~0.05ms ⚡
CPU at 5K Svc80%40%5% ⚡
Rule Update30+ sec500msINSTANT

Observability❌❌✅ Hubble
iptables Rule Explosion — Why It Gets Slow
  IPTABLES (5,000+ rules per node!)        CILIUM eBPF
  ┌────────────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐
  │ For EACH new connection:        │       │ Hash Table:       │
  │                                 │       │ key(10.100.50.10  │
  │ Rule 1: match 10.100.50.10? ❌│       │   :5432) →        │
  │ Rule 2: match 10.100.60.20? ❌│       │   [ep1, ep2, ep3] │
  │ ...                             │       │   → Pick one →   │
  │ Rule 5000: match...?  ✅       │       │   → DONE! ⚡     │
  │                                 │       │                   │
  │ ⏱️ Walks ALL 5000 rules! 🐌    │       │ ⏱️ ONE lookup!    │
  └────────────────────────────────┘       └──────────────────┘
⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 2

❌ MISTAKE 1: Thinking each container in a pod has its own IP → TRUTH: All containers share ONE IP. Use different PORTS.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Deleting the pause container manually → TRUTH: This destroys the network namespace for ALL containers in the pod!

❌ MISTAKE 3: Confusing Service ClusterIP with Pod IP → TRUTH: ClusterIP is VIRTUAL — no interface has this IP. It only exists in iptables/eBPF rules.

│  COMPLETE SERVICE RESOLUTION FLOW (Cilium eBPF)                                │
│                                                                              │
│  Pod anihpj → Service postgres-svc:5432                                       │
│                                                                              │
│  1. DNS: anihpj queries CoreDNS for "postgres-svc" → returns 10.100.50.10    │
│  2. Pod sends TCP SYN to 10.100.50.10:5432 (ClusterIP — VIRTUAL!)            │
│  3. Packet hits TC egress hook → Cilium eBPF intercepts                      │
│  4. eBPF lookup: Service IP 10.100.50.10:5432 → backend list [10.0.1.7, ...]│
│  5. Maglev consistent hash: select backend → 10.0.1.7:5432                   │
│  6. eBPF rewrites: dstIP 10.100.50.10 → 10.0.1.7 (DNAT)                     │
│  7. eBPF CT: records mapping for reply packets (reverse DNAT)                │
│  8. Packet forwarded via overlay/direct routing to postgres pod              │
│                                                                              │
│  ALL IN KERNEL: No userspace proxy, no iptables, no context switches.        │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CCA Insight: The pause container is fundamental to pod networking. It's created FIRST by kubelet. All other containers join its network namespace (via `setns()`). This is why all containers in a pod share one IP. Cilium's eBPF programs operate at the pod level — they see the pod's veth interface, not individual containers. Deleting the pause container = destroying the pod's entire network namespace. For Service traffic: Cilium replaces kube-proxy entirely — eBPF handles the DNAT directly in the kernel at the TC hook, with Maglev hashing for optimal load distribution.

📝 Chapter 2 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
Why do containers in a pod share a network namespace? What are the benefits and drawbacks?
Show Answer
Answer

Benefits: Containers in the same pod can communicate via localhost (127.0.0.1) at memory speed with zero network overhead. They share the same IP, simplifying service discovery. Drawback: Shared port space — no two containers can bind the same port number. They must coordinate port usage.

Explanation

Pod networking uses the pause container pattern: the pause container creates and holds the network namespace, and all other containers join it via --net=container:<pause-id>. This is why sidecar patterns (logging, proxies, etc.) work so well — they share the pod's network namespace and can communicate with the main container via localhost.

Q2
What is the "pause container" and why is it critical for pod networking?
Show Answer
Answer

The pause container holds the network namespace (Option B). It's a tiny (~700KB) static binary that does nothing except call the pause() syscall and sleep forever. It exists because if you networked the first app container directly and it crashed, ALL containers would lose network connectivity.

Explanation

The pause container is PID 1 in every pod. The CNI only networks this container. All other containers join its namespace. This architecture ensures the network namespace survives individual container crashes. On the CCA exam: you should know that Cilium manages the pause container's networking via eBPF — not iptables.

Q3
How does CoreDNS resolve postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local to an IP address? Walk through the complete resolution process.
Show Answer
Answer

1) anihpj pod sends DNS query to CoreDNS (at the cluster DNS IP, usually 10.96.0.10). 2) CoreDNS watches the Kubernetes API for Services and maintains an internal DNS records database. 3) CoreDNS looks up "postgres" Service in "anihpj" namespace. 4) Returns the Service's ClusterIP (e.g., 10.100.50.10). 5) kube-proxy or Cilium eBPF then load-balances to actual pod IPs.

Explanation

DNS resolution is the CRITICAL first step in pod-to-service communication. If DNS fails (CoreDNS pod down, network policy blocking port 53, etc.), pods cannot find any services. Cilium can enforce DNS-based NetworkPolicies (toFQDNs rules), so understanding this flow is essential for the CCA exam.

Q4
Why does iptables performance degrade significantly with more Services?
Show Answer
Answer

iptables rules are matched sequentially (O(n) chain traversal) — Option B. Every new connection walks through ALL iptables rules in the KUBE-SERVICES chain. With 5,000 services, that's 5,000+ rule evaluations per new connection. iptables has no indexing or hashing — it's a linked list walk.

Explanation

This is why the Cilium project was created. At 10,000 services, iptables processes only ~8,000 packets/second. Cilium eBPF handles ~4,700,000 packets/second — a 587x improvement. The CCA exam expects you to quantify this performance gap and explain the architectural reason (chain walk vs hash lookup).

Q5
What does Cilium's kube-proxy replacement do differently from iptables-based kube-proxy? Explain at the architectural level.
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium replaces iptables chain traversal (O(n)) with eBPF hash map lookups (O(1)). Instead of walking thousands of iptables rules, Cilium does a single hash table lookup to find the destination pod. The eBPF programs are JIT-compiled to native x86/ARM machine code running in kernel space — no userspace/kernel context switches.

Explanation

Key architectural differences: 1) Hash maps instead of linked-list chains. 2) JIT-compiled native code (not interpreted netfilter rules). 3) Connection tracking in eBPF maps (not kernel conntrack table). 4) Maglev consistent hashing for even load distribution. 5) Built-in observability via Hubble. Enable with: --set kubeProxyReplacement=true.

Q6
If pod A (10.0.0.55) needs to talk to Service S (ClusterIP 10.100.50.10) which has 3 endpoints, walk through every step.
Show Answer
Answer

Step 1: Pod A does DNS lookup → CoreDNS returns 10.100.50.10. Step 2: Pod A sends TCP SYN to 10.100.50.10:port. Step 3: Kernel routes to the service IP — eBPF program intercepts at TC hook. Step 4: eBPF hash lookup: 10.100.50.10:port → [endpoint1, endpoint2, endpoint3]. Step 5: Maglev hash selects endpoint2 (10.0.1.88). Step 6: DNAT rewrites destination: 10.100.50.10 → 10.0.1.88. Step 7: Packet delivered to endpoint2.

Explanation

With iptables kube-proxy, Step 4 would walk 5,000+ rules sequentially. With Cilium eBPF, it's a single O(1) hash lookup. Maglev hashing ensures connections from the same client consistently go to the same backend (connection affinity), which is important for stateful applications.

Q7
What's the difference between a Service's ClusterIP and its Endpoints? Why does this separation exist?
Show Answer
Answer

ClusterIP: A VIRTUAL IP address — it exists only in iptables/eBPF rules, NOT on any network interface. It never changes for the lifetime of the Service. Endpoints: The REAL pod IPs that actually receive traffic. These change whenever pods restart or scale. This separation provides stable service identity despite dynamic pod IPs.

Explanation

This decoupling is fundamental to Kubernetes. If you tried to connect directly to pod IPs, your application would break every time a pod restarts (new IP). The Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name. Cilium enhances this by replacing iptables-based DNAT with eBPF-based load balancing — much faster, with built-in observability via Hubble.

Q8
What happens if you manually kill the pause container process with kill -9?
Show Answer
Answer

The network namespace is destroyed immediately. ALL containers in the pod lose network connectivity instantly — their network interfaces disappear, IP addresses are released, and all connections drop. Kubernetes detects the pod failure and restarts it (new pause container, new IP, new network namespace).

Explanation

This is why you should NEVER manually interact with pause containers. They are the foundation of pod networking. Killing one is like unplugging the network switch for all containers in that pod. Kubernetes handles this gracefully (restarts the pod), but you'll have brief downtime. Cilium handles the re-networking of the new pause container via its CNI plugin.

Q9
How does Kubernetes Service discovery work with CoreDNS and ClusterIP? Walk through a pod resolving postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local.
Show Answer
Answer

Pod queries CoreDNS for postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local → CoreDNS returns the ClusterIP (e.g., 10.96.100.50) → Pod connects to 10.96.100.50:5432 → kube-proxy (or Cilium's KPR via eBPF) DNATs the connection to a real backend pod IP → Backend pod responds. With Cilium, the DNAT step uses eBPF hash maps instead of iptables.

Explanation

CCA domain: Architecture (30%). The DNS resolution chain: pod → /etc/resolv.conf (nameserver = CoreDNS ClusterIP) → CoreDNS pod → returns Service ClusterIP → socket-level eBPF redirect to backend. Every pod's resolv.conf is auto-configured by kubelet. Cilium's eBPF programs handle the ClusterIP→backend translation at the socket layer, before TCP handshake.

Q10
In a pod with 3 containers, one crashes. What happens to the other 2 containers' network connectivity?
Show Answer
Answer

Nothing — they continue normally. The other 2 containers still run in the same network namespace (pause container still alive). They keep their IP, interfaces, and connections. Only the crashed container's application process stops. Kubernetes may restart the crashed container, which rejoins the same network namespace.

Explanation

This highlights a key advantage of the pause container pattern: the network namespace survives individual container failures. Only killing the pause container destroys the namespace. This is why Cilium's endpoint identity persists — the pod's identity stays the same even as individual containers restart, so network policies remain valid.

⚡ Part 2: eBPF Deep Dive — The Engine Behind Cilium Chapters 3-4

Chapter 3: What is eBPF? — The Technology That Makes Cilium Possible

eBPF is the secret engine inside Cilium. It's what makes Cilium 587x faster than iptables. This chapter demystifies eBPF — what it is, how it works, why it's safe, and why it's revolutionizing Linux networking. We'll use our anihpj/jobpost Django app to make every concept concrete.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 📖 Conceptual + Technical 🎯 CCA Core

eBPF is the Foundation of the CCA Exam

The CCA exam heavily tests your eBPF understanding. You must know:

  • Why eBPF is faster than iptables: O(1) hash lookups vs O(n) chain traversal. Quantify it: 587x faster at 10,000 services.
  • The Verifier's Role: eBPF programs are SAFE because the verifier proves they terminate, have bounded memory access, and can't crash the kernel.

  • eBPF Maps: The communication bridge between kernel eBPF programs and userspace Cilium Agent.

3.1 eBPF Explained Simply — "A Safe Sandbox Inside the Linux Kernel"

The best way to understand eBPF is through an analogy: eBPF is like JavaScript for the Linux kernel. Just as JavaScript runs safely inside your browser sandbox without crashing your operating system, eBPF programs run safely inside the Linux kernel with ZERO risk of crashing it.

The "e" in eBPF stands for "extended" — it evolved from classic BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter), which tcpdump has used since 1992 for packet filtering. The key insight: You can CHANGE how the kernel behaves — without changing kernel source code, loading kernel modules, or rebooting!

📖 Key Term: eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter)

eBPF allows you to run SANDBOXED programs in the Linux kernel WITHOUT:

❌ Changing kernel source code

❌ Loading kernel modules (no kernel crashes!)

❌ Rebooting the system

✅ Programs are VERIFIED before running (no infinite loops, bounded memory)

✅ Programs are JIT-compiled to native x86/ARM machine code

✅ Programs access data via eBPF Maps (key-value store shared with userspace)

✅ Programs attach to events: network packets, syscalls, tracepoints, kprobes

💡 eBPF turns Linux into a PROGRAMMABLE operating system. Cilium is the biggest production user of eBPF.

3.2 A Brief History: From BPF to eBPF — The Journey

Understanding where eBPF came from helps you appreciate why it's so revolutionary. What started as a simple packet filter in 1992 has evolved into the most powerful kernel technology of the modern era:

📦
1992
BPF Born

Berkeley Packet Filter — tcpdump's packet capture engine. Filter only, no programmability.

🔴 Filter Only
🐧
1997
Linux BPF Port

Linux kernel gets BPF for socket filtering. Still limited — can only inspect, not act.

🔴 Limited
⚡
2011
JIT Compilation

Just-In-Time compilation makes BPF 3-4× faster by converting to native CPU instructions.

🟡 Faster
🚀
2014
eBPF — Linux 3.18

Extended BPF with Maps, Verifier, and 10 hook points. The era of programmable kernel begins!

✅ Programmable
🐝
2017
Cilium v1.0!

First eBPF-based CNI plugin. Replaces iptables, kube-proxy, and service mesh — all in the kernel.

✅ eBPF CNI
🏆
2023
CNCF Graduated

Cilium reaches enterprise maturity. Hubble, WireGuard, Cluster Mesh — all powered by eBPF.

🚀 Enterprise

Today, eBPF is used by Meta (network load balancing at 100Gbps+), Google (GKE's Dataplane V2), Netflix (performance monitoring at 400Gbps), and Cloudflare (DDoS mitigation at the edge). It's not just for networking — eBPF powers security monitoring, performance profiling, Kubernetes pod security, and even observability without agents or sidecars.

💡 Why the Verifier Matters (CCA Exam Key Point)

The eBPF verifier is what makes eBPF safe for production use. It mathematically proves that your program: (1) always terminates (no infinite loops), (2) never accesses memory out of bounds, (3) never dereferences NULL pointers, and (4) executes at most 1 million instructions. If ANY check fails, the program is REJECTED — the kernel refuses to load it. This is why eBPF can't crash your kernel, unlike traditional kernel modules.

🔄 eBPF Lifecycle — Layman's Terms (for anihpj)

① Write: You write a small C program that says "if port is 5432, drop the packet." ② Compile: clang turns it into eBPF bytecode. ③ Verify: The kernel's safety checker proves this program won't crash anything. ④ JIT: Bytecode is converted to native CPU instructions (x86/ARM). ⑤ Attach: You hook it to the TC (Traffic Control) layer. ⑥ Execute: Now EVERY packet passing through TC runs your program at native speed — for anihpj, every Django request and PostgreSQL query is checked in ~5 microseconds. ⑦ Communicate: Results (drop/allow, byte counts) are written to eBPF Maps — userspace (Cilium Agent, Hubble) reads them.

3.5 eBPF Maps — The "Database" Inside the Kernel

Maps are the ONLY way for eBPF programs to persist data and the ONLY way for userspace to communicate with eBPF programs:

Map TypeCilium Stores...Real Analogy
BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASHPod IP → Identity (10.0.0.55→12345)Phone book: name→number
BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASHConnection tracking (auto-evicts old)Recent calls list
BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAYPolicy rules indexed by identityRulebook by ID number
BPF_MAP_TYPE_LPM_TRIECIDR → Identity (10.0.0.0/16→cluster)Zip code → region map
BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUFHubble flow events → userspaceLive event stream

💡 Maps are created by userspace (Cilium Agent), written by eBPF programs (kernel), and read by userspace (Cilium Agent / Hubble). This two-way communication is the foundation of Cilium's real-time policy updates and observability.

3.6 Why eBPF is Faster Than iptables — The Architectural Difference

This is the single most important concept for the CCA exam. iptables and eBPF are fundamentally different in how they process network rules:

iptables (O(n) Chain Walk) vs eBPF (O(1) Hash Lookup)
  IPTABLES — Sequential Chain Walk              eBPF — Hash Table Lookup
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐              ┌──────────────┐
  │ For EACH new packet:          │              │ Hash(key) →   │
  │                               │              │ bucket →      │
  │ Rule 1: dest 10.0.0.55?  ❌  │              │ value         │
  │ Rule 2: dest 10.0.0.99?  ❌  │              │              │
  │ Rule 3: dest 10.0.1.10?  ❌  │              │ ONE lookup!   │
  │ ...                           │              │ Independent   │
  │ Rule 5000: dest 10.0.5.5? ✅ │              │ of table size │
  │                               │              └──────────────┘
  │ ⏱️ ~500ms for 5000 rules      │              ⏱️ ~0.001ms
  └──────────────────────────────┘

Real Benchmarks (from Cilium Project)

Service Countiptables (pps)eBPF (pps)Speedup
14,500,0005,200,0001.15x
1003,200,0005,100,0001.59x
1,0001,100,0004,900,0004.45x
5,000120,0004,800,00040x ⚡
10,0008,0004,700,000587x ⚡

💡 With 10,000 services, iptables processes only 8,000 packets/second. eBPF handles 4,700,000 packets/second — a 587x improvement. This is why Cilium was created.

🔑 CCA Exam — Before/After eBPF in One Sentence

Before eBPF (iptables): Each new connection walks 5,000+ sequential rules → 500ms latency → 80% CPU → unusable at scale.

After eBPF (Cilium): One hash table lookup → 5μs latency → 5% CPU → handles 4.7M packets/sec.

For anihpj specifically: When a user visits /jobs/, the iptables chain walks rules for ALL 5,000 services before finding the anihpj rule. With Cilium eBPF, it does ONE hash lookup: "10.100.50.10:8000? → Forward to anihpj pod 10.0.0.55." That's the difference between O(n) and O(1).

3.7 eBPF in Action — How Cilium Secures anihpj Traffic

Let's see how eBPF programs actually protect anihpj/jobpost:

eBPF Packet Processing for anihpj — Real Flow
  EXTERNAL USER → curl https://anihpj.com/jobs/

  ① PACKET ARRIVES at Node interface
       │
  ② eBPF TC HOOK: Identity lookup (src→ID:100, dst→ID:12345)
       │
  ③ eBPF POLICY CHECK: Allow ID:100→ID:12345:8000? GET /jobs/? → YES ✅
       │
  ④ PACKET DELIVERED to anihpj pod → Django responds with job JSON
       │
  ⑤ HUBBLE EXPORT: {src:ingress, dst:anihpj, verdict:FORWARDED}

  ⏱️ Steps ②-③ complete in ~5 MICROSECONDS (all kernel-space!)
💡 What if someone tries POST /admin from outside?

At Step ③, the eBPF L7 check sees method:POST, path:/admin/ from external IP. Policy says: "POST /admin/ only from internal CIDR 10.0.0.0/8." eBPF returns DROP. Hubble logs: verdict:DROPPED, reason:Policy denied. Total time: ~2μs. Zero impact on legitimate traffic.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 3

❌ MISTAKE 1: Thinking eBPF is a kernel module → TRUTH: eBPF programs are verified and sandboxed. They CANNOT crash the kernel.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Confusing XDP and TC hooks → TRUTH: XDP is at the NIC driver (earliest, no pod context). TC is where Cilium operates (has full pod/identity context).

❌ MISTAKE 3: Thinking eBPF maps are regular Linux files → TRUTH: Maps are in-kernel key-value stores accessible only via bpf() syscalls.

🔧 Under the Hood — How eBPF Actually Works Inside the Linux Kernel: Verifier, JIT Compilation, Hook Points, Maps, and Why It's Faster Than iptables
🗺️ eBPF Lifecycle — From C Code to Kernel Execution

│  eBPF PROGRAM LIFECYCLE                                                        │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 1: WRITE (userspace)                                                    │
│  C code → Clang/LLVM → eBPF bytecode (.o ELF file)                           │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 2: LOAD (userspace → kernel via bpf() syscall)                          │
│  bpftool prog load my_prog.o /sys/fs/bpf/my_prog                              │

│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Verifier checks:                                                      │   │
│  │ 1. No infinite loops (must terminate, checks all paths)               │   │

│  │ 3. Valid stack usage (max 512 bytes)                                  │   │
│  │ 4. Maximum 1 million instructions                                     │   │
│  │ 5. All helper functions allowed for this program type                 │   │
│  │ → FAILS any check → program REJECTED, never executes                  │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │

│                                                                              │
│  STEP 5: ATTACH (kernel — bind to hook point)                                │
│  Program attached to: XDP → TC Ingress → TC Egress → Socket → kprobe         │
│  Cilium primarily uses TC (Traffic Control) hooks                             │
│                                                                              │
│  HOOK POINT COMPARISON:                                                        │
│  ┌──────────┬──────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │ XDP      │ NIC driver level  │ Earliest, fastest, NO pod context      │    │
│  │ TC       │ After XDP          │ Has pod identity → Cilium uses this!  │    │
│  │ Socket   │ Per-socket         │ Application-level filtering           │    │
│  │ kprobe   │ Any kernel func    │ Observability, tracing                │    │
│  └──────────┴──────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
│  WHY eBPF IS O(1) vs iptables O(n):                                          │
│  iptables: linked list of rules → walk sequentially until match              │
│  eBPF:     hash table → key(IP:port) → direct lookup → O(1)                 │
│  10,000 services: iptables = 10,000+ checks; eBPF = 1 hash lookup            │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CCA Insight: The eBPF verifier is THE key concept for CCA. It's what makes eBPF safe for production — unlike kernel modules that can crash the system. The verifier mathematically proves program safety before execution. Cilium uses TC hooks (not XDP) because TC has full pod context (identity, labels, policy). XDP is too early — no pod identity info available. This is a guaranteed CCA exam concept.

📝 Chapter 3 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What is the eBPF verifier and what 5 things does it check?
Show Answer
Answer

The verifier checks: 1) No infinite loops (must terminate), 2) No out-of-bounds memory access, 3) Valid pointers (no NULL dereferences), 4) Maximum 1 million instructions, 5) All code paths reachable. The verifier mathematically proves these properties by simulating all possible execution paths.

Explanation

The verifier is what makes eBPF safe for production. Without it, eBPF programs could crash the kernel like traditional kernel modules. The CCA exam expects you to explain WHY eBPF is safer than kernel modules — the verifier is the answer.

Q2
Name 5 eBPF hook points from earliest to latest in the network stack. Which one does Cilium primarily use?
Show Answer
Answer

1) XDP (NIC driver — earliest, before SKB allocation), 2) TC Ingress (after XDP, before kernel stack), 3) TC Egress (outbound), 4) Socket hooks (per-socket), 5) kprobe/tracepoint (any kernel function). Cilium primarily uses TC hooks because they have full pod context (identity, labels, policy).

Explanation

Cilium specifically uses TC (Traffic Control) hooks, not XDP, because XDP is too early in the pipeline — it doesn't have access to pod identity information stored in eBPF maps. TC hooks have the right balance of speed and context.

Q3
How do eBPF programs communicate with userspace? Name 3 map types used by Cilium.
Show Answer
Answer

eBPF programs communicate with userspace exclusively through eBPF Maps — shared key-value data structures in kernel memory accessible via bpf() syscalls. Cilium uses: 1) BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASH (pod IP → identity), 2) BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASH (connection tracking), 3) BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF (Hubble flow events).

Q4
Why is an eBPF hash lookup O(1) while iptables is O(n)?
Show Answer
Answer

iptables stores rules as a linked list (chain) — each packet must walk through rules sequentially until a match is found. eBPF uses a hash table — the key (e.g., IP:port) is hashed to directly find the matching rule in constant time, regardless of how many rules exist.

Explanation

This is the core architectural difference. At 10,000 services, iptables does 10,000+ sequential checks per new connection. eBPF does ONE hash lookup. This is why Cilium exists — iptables literally cannot handle modern Kubernetes scale.

Q5
What does JIT compilation do for eBPF programs and why does it matter?
Show Answer
Answer

JIT (Just-In-Time) compilation converts eBPF bytecode into native x86/ARM machine instructions that run directly on the CPU. Without JIT, eBPF bytecode would be interpreted instruction-by-instruction (much slower). JIT compilation gives eBPF near-native performance.

Q6
Why can't you have an infinite loop in an eBPF program?
Show Answer
Answer

The eBPF verifier mathematically proves program termination by checking that all code paths are acyclic (no backward jumps that could create loops). It also enforces a maximum of 1 million instructions. Infinite loops in kernel space would hang the entire system — so the verifier prevents them entirely.

Q7
At which hook point does Cilium primarily attach its eBPF programs and why not XDP?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium uses TC (Traffic Control) hooks. XDP is too early — it runs before the kernel allocates the SKB, so it has no access to pod identity, labels, or policy information stored in eBPF maps. TC hooks provide the right balance: very fast (near line rate) with full pod context.

Q8
What happens if the eBPF verifier rejects your program?
Show Answer
Answer

The kernel refuses to load the program. The bpf() syscall returns an error with a verifier log explaining what failed. The program is never executed — preventing any potential kernel crash. Developers must fix the issue and recompile. This is a safety feature, not a bug.

Q9
How does Cilium use eBPF maps for connection tracking and why is this better than conntrack?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium uses BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASH maps for connection tracking — each connection (5-tuple: srcIP, srcPort, dstIP, dstPort, protocol) maps to its state. This is faster than Linux conntrack because: (1) it's in eBPF memory (no syscall), (2) LRU eviction is automatic, (3) per-endpoint maps avoid global lock contention. Linux conntrack has a global table with a global lock — a bottleneck at scale.

Explanation

CCA Architecture domain (30%). Connection tracking is how Cilium knows if a packet belongs to an existing flow (fast path) or needs policy evaluation (slow path). eBPF maps make this O(1) with no global locks. The CCA exam may ask about the eBPF datapath steps — connection tracking is step 4 after policy enforcement.

Q10
Why is eBPF considered safer than traditional kernel modules for networking customization?
Show Answer
Answer

Traditional kernel modules run with FULL kernel privileges — a bug can crash the entire system (kernel panic). eBPF programs: (1) Are verified before loading (no unsafe code), (2) Run in a sandbox with limited access, (3) Have guaranteed termination (no infinite loops), (4) Can't access arbitrary memory, (5) Are independent — one program crashing doesn't affect others. This is why cloud providers allow eBPF but not custom kernel modules.

Explanation

This is the elevator pitch for eBPF. The CCA exam will test your understanding of WHY eBPF exists and WHY it's production-safe. The verifier + sandbox combination makes eBPF programmable kernel space without the risk of kernel space programming.

  └─────────────────────────┘           └─────────────────────────┘

4.2 The Cilium Agent Deep Dive — What Happens at Startup?

The Cilium Agent is the brain on each node. Here's its 9-step startup sequence:

Cilium Agent Startup — 9 Steps
  Cilium Agent Pod Starts
       │
       ▼
  ① Read ConfigMap (cilium-config)
       │
       ▼
  ② Detect Kernel eBPF Support (CONFIG_BPF=y?)
       │
       ▼
  ③ Compile & Load eBPF Programs → Verifier → JIT
       │
       ▼
  ④ Connect to K8s API Server, watch Pods/Services/Policies
       │
       ▼
  ⑤ Sync Existing Pods → Allocate identities → Program eBPF Maps
       │
       ▼
  ⑥ Start Hubble Flow Export (Ring Buffer → Relay)
       │
       ▼
  ⑦ Start Health Checking (cilium status reports)
       │
       ▼
  ⑧ Agent READY! Continuously reconciling...

4.3 Cilium CRDs — How Cilium Extends Kubernetes

Cilium registers 9 Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) to store its state in the Kubernetes API:

CRDScopePurpose
CiliumNetworkPolicy (CNP)NamespaceL3/L4/L7 network policies
CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy (CCNP)ClusterCluster-wide policies across all namespaces
CiliumNodeClusterPer-node IPAM allocation state
CiliumIdentityClusterLabel set → Numeric Identity (e.g., {app:anihpj}→12345)
CiliumEndpoint (CEP)NamespacePer-pod Cilium state (ID, IP, policies)
CiliumBGPPeeringPolicyClusterBGP peer configuration
CiliumEgressGatewayPolicyClusterEgress gateway rules

4.4 Identity-Based Networking — Cilium's Secret Sauce

Traditional networking uses IP addresses for rules: "Allow 10.0.0.55 → 10.0.0.99:5432." But pod IPs change on restart! Cilium solves this with identity-based networking:

Identity-Based Policy — Labels → Numeric ID → eBPF Maps
  STEP 1: LABELS → IDENTITY (Cilium Operator)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Pod: anihpj-abc123           Pod: postgres-xyz789    │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐    │
  │  │ app: anihpj      │  hash   │ app: postgres    │    │
  │  │ component: django │────────▶│ component: db    │    │
  │  │ env: production  │         │ env: production  │    │
  │  └──────────────────┘         └──────────────────┘    │
  │           │                            │               │
  │           ▼                            ▼               │
  │    IDENTITY: 12345              IDENTITY: 67890        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  STEP 2: IDENTITY → eBPF MAPS (Cilium Agent)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  eBPF Map: IP_TO_IDENTITY                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┐              │
  │  │ 10.0.0.55 → 12345│ 10.0.0.99 → 67890│              │
  │  └──────────────────┴──────────────────┘              │
  │                                                        │
  │  eBPF Map: POLICY_RULES                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ ALLOW: Identity 12345 → Identity 67890 :5432    │ │
  │  │ DENY:  All others → Identity 67890              │ │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 Pod restarts → new IP (10.0.0.77) → same labels → same ID (12345)
     → policies still work! No YAML changes needed!

💡 Identity in Practice — 3 Real-World Scenarios

🔄
Scenario 1 — Pod Restart
Identity survives IP changes
anihpj pod crashes and restarts with new IP 10.0.0.77. Labels {app:anihpj, component:django} unchanged → same Identity 12345 → ALL policies still work.
✅ Zero YAML changes needed.
📈
Scenario 2 — Scale Up
Identity scales with labels
Deploy 5 more anihpj pods. Each gets a unique IP but ALL share Identity 12345 (same labels). Policy "Allow ID:12345→ID:67890" instantly applies to all 5 new pods.
✅ No policy updates needed.
🎯
Scenario 3 — Canary Deploy
Identity enables traffic splitting
Deploy anihpj v2 with label {version:v2}. Cilium assigns new Identity 12346. Policy splits traffic: 90% → ID 12345, 10% → ID 12346.
✅ Identity-based canary — no sidecar!

4.5 Cilium's eBPF Datapath — What Happens to EVERY Packet

This is the "hot path" — executed for every single packet. The eBPF programs are JIT-compiled to native code:

eBPF Datapath — 6-Step Pipeline
  📨 PACKET ARRIVES
       │
       ▼
  ① PRE-FILTER — Is this for a Cilium-managed endpoint?
       │ YES
       ▼
  ② IDENTITY LOOKUP — Hash(src IP)→SrcID, Hash(dst IP)→DstID
       │
       ▼
  ③ POLICY ENFORCEMENT — Allow SrcID→DstID:Port?
       │                    L7 check: HTTP method? path?
       ├── NO ──▶ DROP 🔴 (Hubble: POLICY_DENIED)
       │ YES
       ▼
  ④ CONNECTION TRACKING — Established flow? Fast-path forward!
       │                    New flow? Create CT entry.
       ▼
  ⑤ FORWARD/DELIVER — To destination pod, apply LB, encrypt
       │
       ▼
  ⑥ HUBBLE EXPORT — Send flow event via Ring Buffer

  ⏱️ Steps ①-⑥ complete in MICROSECONDS (JIT-native code!)

4.6 How Cilium Routes Cross-Node Traffic

Cilium supports two modes for cross-node communication:

ModeMethodProsCons
Tunnel (VXLAN/Geneve)Encapsulate pod traffic in UDPWorks on ANY network~50 bytes overhead
Direct RoutingDirect L3 routing, no encapsulationFASTEST — no overheadRequires network to know pod CIDRs

💡 Cilium auto-detects the best mode. In cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure), tunnel mode is common. In bare metal/data centers with BGP, direct routing gives maximum performance.

4.7 How Everything Connects — eBPF + Cilium + anihpj in One Flow

Let's trace a complete request through the entire Cilium stack — from the moment a user visits /jobs/ to the database response. Every step below happens in microseconds thanks to eBPF:

🌐
User Request curl /jobs/
▸
🔀
Ingress nginx :443
▸
⚡
eBPF Datapath Policy + LB
▸
🐍
Django Pod anihpj:8000
▸
🗄️
PostgreSQL :5432
STAGE 1
🔀 Ingress Controller Receives HTTPS Request
curl https://anihpj.com/jobs/?skill=Python → nginx pod receives request
Cilium Identity: ID=100 (label: app=ingress, tier=frontend)
TLS terminated at ingress → forwards to Django backend service
▼
STAGE 2
⚡ Cilium eBPF Datapath — 6 Microsecond Checks
① Pre-filter: dst=10.0.0.55 (anihpj pod) → YES, Cilium-managed endpoint
② Identity Lookup: src IP → ID=100 | dst IP (10.0.0.55) → ID=12345
③ Policy Check: Allow ID=100 → ID=12345:8000? ✅ | L7: GET /jobs/ → allowed ✅
④ Connection Tracking: New flow → create CT entry (5-tuple hash)
⑤ Forward: Packet delivered to pod veth interface
⑥ Hubble: {ingress→anihpj, GET /jobs/, FORWARDED, 2ms}
▼
STAGE 3
🐍 Django Pod Processes Request — Needs PostgreSQL
JobPost.objects.filter(skills__name='Python')
Django ORM needs database → DNS query: postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
Cilium Identity: ID=12345 (label: app=anihpj, tier=backend)
▼
STAGE 4
⚡ Cilium eBPF Datapath — Service LB + Cross-Node Routing
① DNS Resolution: CoreDNS → postgres.anihpj.svc → 10.100.50.10 (ClusterIP)
② eBPF Service LB: Maglev hash selects endpoint → 10.0.1.99 (postgres pod on Node 2)
③ Identity: src ID=12345 | dst ID=67890
④ Policy Check: Allow ID=12345 → ID=67890:5432? ✅
⑤ WireGuard: Encrypt packet (if encryption enabled) 🔒
⑥ Cross-Node: Tunnel or direct route to Node 2
⑦ Hubble: {anihpj→postgres, 5432, FORWARDED, encrypted}
▼
STAGE 5
🗄️ PostgreSQL Processes Query — Response Flows Back
PostgreSQL pod (ID=67890) on Node 2 receives query
Returns job listings → response flows back through eBPF in reverse
✅ User sees job listings matching "Python" skill
🔑 Key Insight — Why Cilium Wins

Cilium's eBPF programs process EVERY packet in this flow — at kernel-native speed. All decisions (allow/deny, load balance, encrypt, observe) happen in microseconds without leaving the kernel. No context switches to userspace. No proxy processes. No iptables rule walking. Just pure eBPF hash lookups — O(1) complexity regardless of how many policies or services you have.

💡 CCA Exam Mind Map — Cilium's 5 Superpowers

Every CCA exam question maps to one of these 5 capabilities. Memorize them and you'll instantly know which domain any question falls into:

🌐
1. NETWORKING

eBPF replaces CNI + kube-proxy — pod IPs, cross-node routing, service load balancing. One agent per node does it all.

🛡️
2. SECURITY

Identity-based NetworkPolicies at L3/L4/L7 — DNS, HTTP, gRPC, Kafka aware. Zero-trust by default.

🔭
3. OBSERVABILITY

Hubble flow logs, service map, metrics — all from eBPF. Zero overhead, zero agents.

🔀
4. SERVICE MESH

Sidecar-less mTLS, canary deployments, traffic splitting — in the kernel. No Envoy sidecars needed.

🔒
5. ENCRYPTION

WireGuard transparent encryption — one flag, zero code changes. All pod traffic encrypted.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 4

❌ MISTAKE 1: Thinking Cilium Agent is a Deployment → TRUTH: It's a DaemonSet — ONE per node! Check with kubectl get ds -n kube-system cilium.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Confusing CiliumIdentity with K8s ServiceAccount → TRUTH: Identity is for networking (labels→numeric ID). ServiceAccount is for RBAC (API access).

❌ MISTAKE 3: Deleting Cilium CRDs without understanding dependencies → TRUTH: Deleting CiliumNode or CiliumIdentity CRDs can BREAK networking! Use cilium uninstall.
