🔬 The 7-Step eBPF Datapath — Every Packet's Journey Through Cilium
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CILIUM eBPF DATAPATH — 7-STAGE PACKET PIPELINE (TC Hook)                     │
│                                                                              │
│  PACKET ARRIVES AT vethXXX (node side of pod veth pair)                       │
│  │                                                                           │
│  ├─▶ STAGE 1: TAIL_IPV4_FROM_LXC / TAIL_IPV4_TO_LXC                          │
│  │   • Direction determination: FROM pod or TO pod?                          │
│  │   • Basic validation: IP header checksum, TTL, protocol                   │
│  │   • Drop invalid packets immediately (no further processing)              │
│  │   • Tail call → Stage 2                                                    │
│  │                                                                           │
│  ├─▶ STAGE 2: RESOLVE_POLICY_MAP                                             │
│  │   • Pod IP → Cilium Identity (BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASH lookup)                   │
│  │   • Identity is pre-computed from pod labels by Cilium Operator           │
│  │   • Caches identity for this pod's entire lifetime                        │
│  │   • Tail call → Stage 3                                                    │
│  │                                                                           │
│  ├─▶ STAGE 3: POLICY_ENFORCEMENT                                              │
│  │   • L3: Source Identity → Destination Identity allowed?                   │
│  │   • L4: Specific ports/protocols allowed for this identity pair?          │
│  │   • If DNS policy exists: resolve FQDN → enforce IP                       │
│  │   • If L7 policy: defer to Stage 4; else DROP or PASS                     │
│  │   • Tail call → Stage 4 (if L7 policy) or Stage 5 (if L3/L4 only)         │
│  │                                                                           │
│  ├─▶ STAGE 4: L7_PROXY (Only if L7 policy — HTTP, gRPC, Kafka, DNS)          │
│  │   • Redirect packet to Cilium Envoy proxy (userspace)                     │
│  │   • Envoy examines L7 data: HTTP method/path, Kafka topic, etc.           │
│  │   • Envoy verdict: ALLOW (proxy back to kernel) or DENY (RST/drop)        │
│  │   • Only stage with userspace involvement (all others = kernel)           │
│  │   • Tail call → Stage 5 (if allowed)                                       │
│  │                                                                           │
│  ├─▶ STAGE 5: CONNECTION_TRACKING                                             │
│  │   • 5-tuple hash: (srcIP, dstIP, srcPort, dstPort, protocol)              │
│  │   • CT lookup in BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASH: entry exists?                     │
│  │   • YES (ESTABLISHED): fast path — skip policy, forward immediately       │
│  │   • NO (NEW): create CT entry, set state = NEW, proceed to Stage 6        │
│  │   • CT entries auto-evicted by LRU when table is full                     │
│  │                                                                           │
│  ├─▶ STAGE 6: SERVICE_LOAD_BALANCING                                          │
│  │   • Check: is dstIP a Cilium-managed Service ClusterIP?                   │
│  │   • YES: Maglev consistent hash → select backend pod IP                   │
│  │   • Rewrite: dstIP = backend pod IP (DNAT)                                │
│  │   • Record reverse mapping in CT for reply packets                        │
│  │   • NO: pass-through (direct pod-to-pod traffic)                          │
│  │                                                                           │
│  └─▶ STAGE 7: FORWARD                                                         │
│      • Pod on same node: deliver directly to pod veth                         │
│      • Pod on different node: encapsulate (VXLAN) or route directly          │
│      • Hubble: emit flow event to ring buffer (if monitoring enabled)        │
│      • Packet delivered to destination pod                                   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🗺️ Tunnel vs Direct Routing — Deep Comparison
AspectTunnel (VXLAN/Geneve)Direct Routing (Native)
How it worksPod packet wrapped in UDP header with node IP → unwrapped at destinationPod packet sent directly with pod IP as dst → routed by physical network
MTU overhead-50 bytes (VXLAN header) → may need MTU 14500 bytes overhead → full MTU 1500
Performance~5-10% overhead from encapsulationLine rate (no overhead)
Network RequirementsANY network — works over the internetNetwork must know pod CIDRs (BGP peering or static routes)
Use caseCloud VMs without BGP, multi-cloud, any environmentBare metal, on-prem with BGP (MetalLB, FRR), cloud with BGP support
Cilium config--set tunnel=vxlan (default)--set routingMode=native --set autoDirectNodeRoutes=true
CCA examDefault mode, works everywhereMaximum performance, requires BGP
🔄 Cilium Identity Lifecycle — From Labels to Numeric ID
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  IDENTITY ALLOCATION FLOW — Labels → Security Identity in 5 Steps             │
│                                                                              │
│  1. POD CREATED (labels: {app:anihpj, tier:web, env:prod})                   │
│     │                                                                        │
│     ▼                                                                        │
│  2. CILIUM AGENT WATCHES K8S API                                              │
│     │ Detects new pod → reads label set                                       │
│     │                                                                        │
│     ▼                                                                        │
│  3. AGENT → KVSTORE (etcd/crd) LOOKUP                                         │
│     │ "Has label set {app:anihpj,tier:web,env:prod} been seen before?"        │
│     │                                                                        │
│     ├── YES: Return existing numeric ID (e.g., 54321)                        │
│     │                                                                        │
│     └── NO: CILIUM OPERATOR allocates new ID                                  │
│             │ SHA-256 hash of sorted label key=value pairs                   │
│             │ → 54321 (truncated to 24 bits for eBPF map efficiency)         │
│             │ → Create CiliumIdentity CRD: "54321"                            │
│             │ → Store in KVstore for all agents to see                       │
│             │                                                                 │
│             ▼                                                                 │
│  4. AGENT UPDATES eBPF MAPS                                                    │
│     │ IP_TO_IDENTITY[10.0.0.55] = 54321   (pod's IP → identity)              │
│     │ IDENTITY_TO_LABELS[54321] = metadata (for policy matching)             │
│     │                                                                        │
│             ▼                                                                 │
│  5. IDENTITY SURVIVES POD RESTART                                              │
│     │ Pod restarts → new IP 10.0.0.88                                         │
│     │ Labels unchanged → Agent finds existing ID 54321                        │
│     │ Agent updates: IP_TO_IDENTITY[10.0.0.88] = 54321                        │
│     │ OLD mapping removed: IP_TO_IDENTITY[10.0.0.55] = deleted               │
│     │                                                                        │
│  KEY: CiliumIdentity CRD is the SOURCE OF TRUTH for label→ID mappings.       │
│  Garbage collected by Operator when no pods use a given label set.           │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CCA Insight: Cilium architecture is a CCA exam domain (~12%). Key distinctions: Agent = DaemonSet (one per node, loads eBPF). Operator = Deployment (cluster-wide, manages IPAM + identities). Identity-based networking is what makes Cilium policies survive pod restarts — labels don't change, so the numeric identity stays the same. Never manually delete Cilium CRDs — use cilium uninstall which handles the cleanup properly.

📝 Chapter 4 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What are the 5 main Cilium components? Where does each run?
Show Answer
Answer

1) Cilium Agent — DaemonSet, one per node. 2) Cilium Operator — Deployment, 1-2 replicas. 3) Cilium CLI — on your workstation. 4) Hubble Relay — Deployment, aggregates flows. 5) Hubble UI — Deployment, web dashboard.

Q2
How does identity-based networking differ from IP-based? Why is it more robust?
Show Answer
Answer

IP-based: "Allow 10.0.0.55 → 10.0.0.99:5432" — breaks when pod restarts with new IP. Identity-based: "Allow {app:anihpj} → {app:postgres}:5432" — labels don't change on restart, so policies survive pod restarts. Cilium hashes labels to numeric IDs stored in eBPF maps.

Q3
Name 5 Cilium CRDs and explain each in one sentence.
Show Answer
Answer

CNP: namespace-scoped L3/L4/L7 policies. CCNP: cluster-wide policies. CiliumNode: per-node IPAM state. CiliumIdentity: label set→numeric ID mapping. CiliumEndpoint: per-pod Cilium state (ID, IP, active policies).

Q4
Walk through Cilium's eBPF datapath when a packet arrives. What happens at each step?
Show Answer
Answer

1) Pre-filter: is this for a Cilium endpoint? 2) Identity lookup: hash src/dst IP → numeric IDs. 3) Policy enforcement: allow SrcID→DstID:Port? L7 check if applicable. 4) Connection tracking: established flow? Fast-path. New flow? Create CT entry. 5) Forward/deliver to pod. 6) Hubble export: send flow event.

Q5
Where does the Cilium Agent run and what Kubernetes resource type is it?
Show Answer
Answer

The Cilium Agent runs as a DaemonSet, which means one pod per node. This is critical because the Agent loads eBPF programs into the kernel of that specific node. Check with: kubectl get ds -n kube-system cilium.

Q6
What's the difference between tunnel mode and direct routing in Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

Tunnel (VXLAN/Geneve): encapsulates pod traffic in UDP — works anywhere but has ~50 byte overhead. Direct routing: uses the physical network's routing table directly — no encapsulation, maximum performance, but requires the network to know pod CIDRs (via BGP or static routes).

Q7
If a pod restarts and gets a new IP, why do existing CiliumNetworkPolicies still work?
Show Answer
Answer

Because Cilium policies are identity-based, not IP-based. When a pod restarts, it gets a new IP but retains the SAME labels. The Cilium Operator computes the SAME numeric identity from those labels. The Cilium Agent updates the IP→Identity eBPF map with the new IP. The policy rules (based on identities, not IPs) remain valid.

Q8
What is the role of the Cilium Operator vs the Cilium Agent?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium Agent (DaemonSet, per-node): loads eBPF programs, manages pod networking, enforces policies, exports Hubble flows — node-local operations. Cilium Operator (Deployment, cluster-wide): IPAM management, identity allocation and garbage collection, CiliumNode CRD cleanup, etcd compaction — cluster-wide operations.

Q9
What happens when a new node joins the cluster? Walk through the Cilium onboarding process.
Show Answer
Answer

1) Node registers with API server → 2) Cilium Operator creates CiliumNode CRD for it → 3) Cilium Agent DaemonSet pod starts on the new node → 4) Agent reads configuration from cilium-config ConfigMap → 5) Agent loads eBPF programs into the node's kernel → 6) IPAM allocates pod CIDR from the configured pool → 7) Agent creates health endpoint → 8) Agent reports ready to API server. All managed automatically.

Explanation

CCA Installation domain (12%). Understanding the node onboarding flow helps troubleshoot "agent not ready" errors. The key: the Cilium Agent MUST successfully load eBPF programs for the node to be Ready. Failed eBPF loading = node stays NotReady for Cilium.

Q10
How does Cilium's IPAM work? Compare cluster-pool vs Kubernetes host-scope modes.
Show Answer
Answer

Cluster-pool: Cilium Operator allocates a pod CIDR from a global pool to each node. Simple, works everywhere. Kubernetes host-scope: Uses the node's podCIDR field (allocated by kube-controller-manager). Required for some integrations. Cilium Operator tracks allocations in CiliumNode CRDs. IPs are released when nodes are removed.

Explanation

CCA Architecture and Installation domains. IPAM mode is set during install (--set ipam.mode=cluster-pool). AWS EKS uses ENI mode, Azure uses Azure mode, GKE uses Kubernetes mode. The CCA exam may ask which IPAM mode is appropriate for a given environment.

Cilium Hook PointCh 3.4TC (Traffic Control) — fastest with full pod identity context
eBPF MapsCh 3.5Only way kernel↔userspace communicate — HASH, LRU, RINGBUF types
Cilium AgentCh 4.1-4.2DaemonSet (one per node) — loads eBPF, enforces policies, exports Hubble
Cilium CRDsCh 4.39 CRDs — CNP, CCNP, CiliumNode, CiliumIdentity, CiliumEndpoint are key
Identity-Based NetworkingCh 4.4Labels→numeric ID stored in eBPF — policies survive pod restarts
eBPF DatapathCh 4.56-step pipeline: Pre-filter→Identity→Policy→CT→Forward→Hubble
Cross-Node RoutingCh 4.6Tunnel (VXLAN) works anywhere; Direct routing fastest (needs BGP)
Full Request FlowCh 4.7User→Ingress→eBPF→anihpj→eBPF LB→PostgreSQL — all in kernel

Chapter 5: Installing Cilium on Your Kubernetes Cluster

Time to get hands-on! This chapter walks you through every step of installing Cilium — from pre-flight checks to a fully functional cluster with Hubble, WireGuard encryption, and kube-proxy replacement. We'll use our anihpj/jobpost cluster as the example.

Installation & Operations 12%
Installation is 12% of the CCA Exam

You must know:

  • Pre-requisites: Kernel ≥ 5.10, K8s ≥ 1.16, eBPF filesystem mounted, no existing CNI.
  • Installation flags: kubeProxyReplacement, hubble.enabled, encryption.enabled, encryption.type.

5.1 Prerequisites Check — Is Your Cluster Ready for Cilium?

Before installing Cilium, verify these requirements on EVERY node. Each requirement exists for a specific reason — skipping one leads to silent failures that are hard to debug later.

Why Kernel ≥ 5.10? Cilium relies on eBPF programs running inside the Linux kernel. Kernel 5.10 (released December 2020) was the first LTS kernel with mature eBPF support for networking. Kernels before 5.4 have limited eBPF capabilities and missing helper functions. The newer your kernel (5.15+, 6.1+), the more eBPF features Cilium can use — including faster maps, better verifier performance, and more program types. If you're on an older kernel, Cilium will fall back to a limited mode or refuse to start.

Why remove old CNI? You CANNOT run two CNI plugins simultaneously. Both will try to assign IP addresses to pods, manage network interfaces, and program routing tables. The result: IP conflicts, routing loops, and pods stuck in ContainerCreating. Always remove Calico, Flannel, Weave, or any other CNI before installing Cilium.

Why ≥ 4GB RAM? Cilium's eBPF maps live in kernel memory — each pod's identity, policy rules, and connection tracking state consume memory. With many pods, these maps can grow to hundreds of megabytes. The Cilium agent itself also needs memory for its control plane (gRPC, Hubble, policy computation). 4GB is the minimum; for production clusters with 100+ pods, plan for 8GB+ per node.

System Requirements
  ┌──────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │  LINUX KERNEL         │    │  KUBERNETES               │
  │  ≥ 5.10 (eBPF)       │    │  ≥ 1.16                   │
  │  Recommended: 5.15+   │    │  Recommended: 1.27+       │
  └──────────────────────┘    └──────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │  HARDWARE (per node)  │    │  NETWORK                  │
  │  RAM: ≥ 4GB           │    │  No existing CNI!         │
  │  CPU: ≥ 2 cores       │    │  Remove Calico/Flannel    │
  │  Disk: ≥ 10GB         │    │  before installing!       │
  └──────────────────────┘    └──────────────────────────┘
📋 Pre-Install Checklist (Run on Every Node)

CHECK 1: uname -r → Expected: 5.10.0+

CHECK 2: kubectl version --short → Expected: v1.16.0+

CHECK 3: ls /sys/fs/bpf → Expected: directory exists

CHECK 4: ls /etc/cni/net.d/ → Expected: EMPTY (remove old CNI first!)

CHECK 5: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep kube-proxy → Note if present

CHECK 6: free -h (≥ 4GB) and nproc (≥ 2 cores)

MethodBest ForProsCons

5.3 Hands-On: Installing Cilium with cilium CLI — Full Walkthrough

We'll install Cilium with ALL features enabled: kube-proxy replacement, Hubble (CLI+Relay+UI), and WireGuard encryption.

🔧 What "cilium install" Does Under the Hood (10 Steps)

1. Creates namespace or uses kube-system | 2. Creates ConfigMap (cilium-config) | 3. Creates DaemonSet (Agent per node) | 4. Creates Operator Deployment | 5. Creates 9 CRDs | 6. Creates RBAC resources | 7. Creates Hubble Relay + UI Deployments | 8. Creates Hubble Peer Service | 9. Waits for all pods Ready | 10. Runs connectivity test (21+ checks)

terminal — Cilium Full Install with ALL Features 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 1: Download & install cilium CLI
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
CILIUM_CLI_VERSION=$(curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ \
    cilium/cilium-cli/main/stable.txt)

curl -L --remote-name-all \
    https://github.com/cilium/cilium-cli/releases/download/ \
    ${CILIUM_CLI_VERSION}/cilium-linux-amd64.tar.gz

sudo tar xzvfC cilium-linux-amd64.tar.gz /usr/local/bin

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 2: Install Cilium — ONE command, ALL features
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
cilium install \
    --namespace kube-system \
    --set kubeProxyReplacement=true \
    --set hubble.enabled=true \
    --set hubble.relay.enabled=true \
    --set hubble.ui.enabled=true \
    --set encryption.enabled=true \
    --set encryption.type=wireguard

# What each flag does:
#   kubeProxyReplacement  → Replace iptables kube-proxy with eBPF
#   hubble.enabled        → Enable Hubble observability
#   hubble.relay.enabled  → Multi-node flow aggregation
#   hubble.ui.enabled     → Web dashboard at localhost:12000
#   encryption.enabled    → Transparent WireGuard encryption
#   encryption.type       → WireGuard (fastest in-kernel VPN)

# What cilium install REPLACES:
#   ❌ Old CNI (Calico/Flannel/Weave)
#   ❌ kube-proxy (iptables rules)
#   ❌ Sidecar proxies (Istio/Linkerd)
#   ✅ All unified into ONE eBPF agent per node!

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 3: Verify installation health
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
cilium status --wait     # Blocks until all pods & agents healthy
                         # Timeout: 5 min (increase with --wait-duration)

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 4: Run comprehensive connectivity tests
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
cilium connectivity test  # 21+ tests covering:
                          #   Pod-to-Pod (same node, cross-node)
                          #   Services (ClusterIP, NodePort)
                          #   DNS resolution
                          #   NetworkPolicy (allow, deny, L7 HTTP)
                          #   Encryption (WireGuard)
                          #   Hubble (Relay, UI, CLI)
                          #   Performance (bandwidth, latency)
                          # All should show ✅

5.5 Uninstalling an Old CNI — Safe Migration from Calico/Flannel

⚠️ You CANNOT run two CNIs at once — they both try to assign IPs, causing conflicts. Follow this 4-phase migration:

Safe CNI Migration — 4 Phases
  PHASE 1: PREPARE
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ① kubectl get pods -A -o wide > pods-backup.txt    │
  │ ② kubectl get svc,deploy,ds -A -o yaml > backup/   │
  │ ③ IDENTIFY current CNI: ls /etc/cni/net.d/          │
  │    → "10-calico.conflist" = Calico is current CNI   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
            │
            ▼
  PHASE 2: DRAIN (one node at a time!)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ④ kubectl drain  --ignore-daemonsets         │
  │    → All pods move to other nodes                   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
            │
            ▼
  PHASE 3: REMOVE OLD CNI
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ⑤ kubectl delete -f              │
  │ ⑥ sudo rm -f /etc/cni/net.d/*                      │
  │ ⑦ sudo ip link delete cni0 2>/dev/null             │
  │    → Node has NO CNI — pods can't get network!      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
            │
            ▼
  PHASE 4: INSTALL CILIUM + UNCORDON
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ⑧ cilium install ... (as shown in 5.3)             │
  │ ⑨ cilium status --wait                             │
  │ ⑩ kubectl uncordon                           │
  │    → Repeat ④-⑩ for EACH node!                     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 TIP: Drain ONE node at a time. Apps stay available!
⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 5

❌ MISTAKE 1: Installing Cilium without removing old CNI → Two CNIs fight over IPs, pods stay Pending. FIX: Always remove old CNI first.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Forgetting --wait on cilium status → You think it's installed but pods are still starting. FIX: Always use cilium status --wait.

❌ MISTAKE 3: Not running connectivity test after install → Everything looks green but something is silently broken. FIX: Always run cilium connectivity test.

🔧 Under the Hood — How Cilium Installation Actually Works: Helm Chart Anatomy, CRD Bootstrap, DaemonSet Lifecycle, and ConfigMap Wiring
🗺️ What "cilium install" Does — The 10-Step Bootstrap Process
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CILIUM INSTALL — COMPLETE BOOTSTRAP SEQUENCE                                  │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 1: NAMESPACE CREATION                                                   │
│  • Creates "kube-system" namespace if it doesn't exist                       │
│  • All Cilium components live here (agent, operator, hubble, etc.)           │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 2: CONFIGMAP — cilium-config (THE BRAIN)                                │
│  • Single ConfigMap controls ALL Cilium behavior                             │
│  • Key values: tunnel, enableIPv4, kubeProxyReplacement, ipam.mode           │
│  • Every Cilium Agent pod mounts this ConfigMap on startup                   │
│  • Changing this → Agent restarts to pick up new config                      │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 3: CRD CREATION (9 Custom Resources)                                    │
│  • CiliumNetworkPolicy, CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy                       │
│  • CiliumNode, CiliumIdentity, CiliumEndpoint                                │
│  • CiliumEnvoyConfig, CiliumClusterwideEnvoyConfig                           │
│  • CiliumExternalWorkload, CiliumLocalRedirectPolicy                         │
│  • These extend the K8s API — kubectl get cnp works after this!              │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 4: RBAC (ServiceAccount + ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding)             │
│  • Cilium Agent needs: watch Pods, Services, Endpoints, Nodes, Namespaces    │
│  • Cilium Operator needs: manage CiliumNode, CiliumIdentity CRDs             │
│  • Hubble Relay needs: watch CiliumEndpoint for flow metadata                │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 5: DAEMONSET — cilium (ONE PER NODE)                                    │
│  • Pod spec: privileged container (needed for eBPF loading)                  │
│  • Mounts: /sys/fs/bpf (eBPF filesystem), /var/run/cilium (socket)           │
│  • Mounts: /etc/cni/net.d (CNI config), /opt/cni/bin (CNI binary)           │
│  • Init container: mounts eBPF filesystem, sets up cgroups v2               │
│  • Readiness: agent must successfully load eBPF programs                     │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 6: DEPLOYMENT — cilium-operator (1-2 REPLICAS)                          │
│  • Cluster-wide singleton tasks: IPAM, identity allocation, GC               │
│  • Uses leader election — only ONE active operator at a time                 │
│  • Handles CiliumNode, CiliumIdentity CRD lifecycle                          │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 7: HUBBLE RELAY + UI (OPTIONAL)                                          │
│  • Hubble Relay: aggregates flow events from ALL agents via gRPC             │
│  • Hubble UI: web dashboard served on port 12000 (port-forward)              │
│  • Hubble Peer Service: allows Relay to discover agents dynamically          │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 8: CNI CONFIG FILE — /etc/cni/net.d/05-cilium.conf                      │
│  • Written by Cilium Agent init container to each node                       │
│  • Tells kubelet: "use cilium-cni binary for pod networking"                 │
│  • This is how kubelet knows to invoke Cilium for every new pod              │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 9: WAIT FOR READINESS                                                    │
│  • cilium status --wait polls until all agents + operator are ready          │
│  • Each agent reports: "Cilium: OK" when eBPF programs loaded               │
│  • Timeout: 5 minutes (configurable with --wait-duration)                    │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 10: CONNECTIVITY TEST (OPTIONAL)                                         │
│  • 21+ tests: pod-to-pod, services, DNS, policies, encryption, Hubble        │
│  • Creates test pods, verifies communication, cleans up after               │
│  • Failure at this step = something is broken at the network level           │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔬 cilium-config ConfigMap — What Every Key Actually Does
Config KeyDefaultWhat It ControlsWhen to Change
tunnelvxlanEncapsulation protocol: vxlan, geneve, or disabledDisabled for direct routing (bare metal with BGP)
enable-ipv4trueEnable IPv4 pod networkingIPv6-only environments (rare)
kube-proxy-replacementdisabledReplace kube-proxy: disabled, partial, strictEnable for eBPF load balancing
ipam.modecluster-poolIP allocation: cluster-pool, kubernetes, eni, azure, multi-poolCloud-specific (EKS→eni, AKS→azure)
enable-bpf-clock-probetrueUse eBPF for high-res timestamps (faster than ktime_get)Very old kernels that lack BPF helpers
enable-bpf-masqueradetrueUse eBPF instead of iptables for SNAT masqueradingPerformance optimization (always keep enabled)
enable-host-reachable-servicesfalseAllow host processes to reach ClusterIP servicesNode-level monitoring tools need Service access
debugfalseVerbose logging (DO NOT enable in production!)Temporary troubleshooting only
monitor-aggregationmediumHubble flow aggregation level: none, low, medium, highReduce event volume in high-traffic clusters
🔄 Agent Startup Sequence — From Pod Start to eBPF Ready
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CILIUM AGENT STARTUP — What Happens When the Pod Starts                        │
│                                                                              │
│  1. INIT CONTAINER: cilium-init                                               │
│     ├── Mounts /sys/fs/bpf (eBPF filesystem)                                 │
│     ├── Sets up cgroups v2 (if not already)                                  │
│     ├── Copies cilium-cni binary to /opt/cni/bin/                            │
│     ├── Writes 05-cilium.conf to /etc/cni/net.d/                             │
│     └── Exits (init containers run ONCE, then stop)                          │
│                                                                              │
│  2. MAIN CONTAINER: cilium-agent                                              │
│     ├── Reads ConfigMap: cilium-config → all settings                        │
│     ├── Connects to K8s API Server (watch Pods, Services, Nodes, etc.)       │
│     ├── Connects to KVstore (etcd or CRD) for identity sync                  │
│     ├── COMPILES + LOADS eBPF programs into kernel                            │
│     │   ├── bpf_host.o      (node-level networking)                          │
│     │   ├── bpf_network.o   (encryption, routing)                            │
│     │   ├── bpf_overlay.o   (VXLAN/Geneve tunnel)                            │
│     │   └── bpf_lxc.o       (pod-level policy enforcement)                  │
│     ├── Starts gRPC server on /var/run/cilium/cilium.sock                     │
│     ├── Starts Hubble gRPC server on /var/run/cilium/hubble.sock             │
│     ├── Reports readiness: "Cilium: OK" (cilium status goes green)          │
│     └── Begins processing pod events (new pods → create endpoints)           │
│                                                                              │
│  3. READINESS PROBE (repeated every 10s):                                     │
│     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│     │ cilium status --brief → checks:                                   │    │
│     │ • eBPF programs loaded? ✓                                         │    │
│     │ • K8s API reachable? ✓                                            │    │
│     │ • KVstore connected? ✓                                            │    │
│     │ • IPAM has capacity? ✓                                            │    │
│     │ → ALL pass → pod is Ready                                         │    │
│     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
│  FAILURE MODES:                                                               │
│  • eBPF loading fails → agent stays NotReady → pods stuck ContainerCreating  │
│  • API server unreachable → agent can't watch resources → stale state        │
│  • KVstore unreachable → can't sync identities → cross-node policies fail    │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔀 Safe CNI Migration — What Happens at the Packet Level
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CNI MIGRATION — Node-by-Node, What Actually Changes                            │
│                                                                              │
│  BEFORE MIGRATION (Calico running):                                           │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ NODE X                                                                 │   │
│  │ /etc/cni/net.d/10-calico.conflist  ← kubelet reads this               │   │
│  │ /opt/cni/bin/calico                ← kubelet executes this            │   │
│  │ calico-node pod (DaemonSet)        ← manages routes, iptables rules   │   │
│  │ Pods on this node: IPs from Calico IPAM pool                          │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  DURING MIGRATION (node drained, old CNI removed):                            │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ NODE X (drained — NO pods running)                                    │   │
│  │ /etc/cni/net.d/ ← EMPTY (old CNI config deleted)                      │   │
│  │ /opt/cni/bin/   ← EMPTY (old CNI binary deleted)                     │   │
│  │ calico-node pod ← TERMINATED (DaemonSet deleted)                      │   │
│  │ cni0 bridge     ← DELETED (clean interface state)                     │   │
│  │ Pods: ALL MOVED to other nodes (thanks to drain!)                     │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  AFTER MIGRATION (Cilium running):                                            │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ NODE X                                                                 │   │
│  │ /etc/cni/net.d/05-cilium.conf      ← kubelet reads this               │   │
│  │ /opt/cni/bin/cilium-cni            ← kubelet executes this            │   │
│  │ cilium pod (DaemonSet)             ← loads eBPF, manages networking   │   │
│  │ cilium-cni → /var/run/cilium/cilium.sock → Cilium Agent               │   │
│  │ Pods on this node: NEW IPs from Cilium IPAM pool                      │   │
│  │ (Node uncordoned → new pods scheduled → Cilium assigns IPs!)          │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  WHY DRAIN IS CRITICAL:                                                       │
│  • Running pods keep OLD CNI's IP — new CNI can't reclaim it                │
│  • IP conflict: old CNI gave 10.0.1.5 to pod A; Cilium might give it to B  │
│  • Drain → pods terminate → IP released → Cilium can safely allocate       │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CCA Insight: The CCA exam covers installation (12%). Key differentiators: CLI auto-detects your cloud provider (EKS→ENI, GKE→Native, AKS→Azure IPAM) and sets optimal defaults. Helm requires explicit cloud-specific values. For the exam, know that cilium install IS Helm under the hood — it generates a values.yaml and runs helm install. The ConfigMap (cilium-config) is the single source of configuration truth — changing it triggers agent restarts.

Chapter 6: Cilium CLI — Your Command Center for Daily Operations

Master the cilium CLI — your primary tool for managing, monitoring, and debugging Cilium. From the morning health check to deep packet inspection, these commands will become muscle memory.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🛠️ Hands-On 🎯 CCA Core

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Master cilium status — the health dashboard
  • ✅ Essential daily commands (endpoint, policy, service, identity)
  • ✅ cilium monitor — real-time packet visibility and debugging
  • ✅ How to debug: "Is my pod networked? Is my policy active?"

6.1 cilium status — Your First Command Every Morning

cilium status is the single most important Cilium command. It gives you a complete health dashboard — every component, every daemonset, every deployment — in one view. Make this your morning ritual: run cilium status before you do anything else. If anything is red or yellow, fix it before it cascades into a production outage.

How to read the output: The top section shows individual components (Cilium agent, Operator, Hubble Relay, Hubble UI, Encryption, ClusterMesh). Each shows OK (green), Disabled (gray), or an error message (red). The bottom section shows Kubernetes resources — DaemonSets and Deployments — with their desired vs ready counts. A healthy cluster shows "Desired: 3, Ready: 3" — meaning every Cilium agent pod is running on every node.

Common failure patterns: "Desired: 3, Ready: 1" means 2 out of 3 Cilium agents are failing to start. Check those nodes with kubectl describe pod -n kube-system cilium-<pod>. Common causes: kernel too old, eBPF filesystem not mounted, or conflicting CNI still installed. "Cluster Pods: 8/12" means 4 pods are not being managed by Cilium — they might be in host network mode, or Cilium hasn't detected them yet.

cilium status — Annotated Output
  $ cilium status
      /¯¯\
     /¯¯\__/¯¯\    Cilium:          OK  ← Main agent
     \__/¯¯\__/    Operator:        OK  ← Cluster tasks
     /¯¯\__/¯¯\    Hubble Relay:    OK  ← Flow aggregator
     \__/¯¯\__/    Hubble UI:       OK  ← Web dashboard
     \__/          Encryption:      OK  ← WireGuard

    DaemonSet    cilium      Desired: 3, Ready: 3
    Deployment   cilium-op   Ready: 1/1
    Deployment   hubble-rly  Ready: 1/1
    Containers:  cilium      Running: 3
    Cluster Pods: 12/12 connected successfully

  🔴 RED FLAGS: "Desired:3, Ready:1" = agents failing
  🔴 "Cluster Pods: 8/12" = pods not managed
💡 Pro Tips for cilium status

Use --wait for scripts: cilium status --wait blocks until everything is healthy or times out. Perfect for CI/CD pipelines and post-install scripts.

Use --wait-duration for patience: cilium status --wait --wait-duration 5m gives Cilium 5 minutes to become healthy before failing. Default is 5 minutes, but you can increase for large clusters.

Watch mode: cilium status --watch refreshes every second — great for watching a rolling restart or upgrade in real time.

6.2 Essential cilium Commands — Your Daily Toolkit

Beyond cilium status, you'll use these commands daily to inspect, debug, and manage your Cilium-powered cluster. Each command category answers a specific question: "Which pods are managed?" "What policies are active?" "Are my services balanced correctly?" "What's the encryption status?"

🔍 The Three Most Important Inspection Commands

cilium endpoint list — Shows every pod Cilium manages, its IP address, its Cilium identity (numeric ID derived from labels), and its policy enforcement status (Ingress/Egress/Both/None). If a pod is missing from this list, Cilium is not managing its network. This is your go-to command for "Is my pod networked?"

cilium policy get — Shows all active Network Policies across all namespaces. Use -n <namespace> to filter. This tells you exactly which rules are currently enforced — essential for debugging "Why is my pod blocked?"

cilium service list — Shows all Kubernetes Services from Cilium's eBPF load balancer perspective. This is the "truth" of your service configuration — if a service is missing here, Cilium's kube-proxy replacement isn't handling it. Each entry shows the frontend IP:port and backend endpoints.

CategoryCommandWhat It Shows
🔍 Inspectcilium statusOverall health dashboard
🔍 Inspectcilium status --waitBlock until all healthy
📦 Podscilium endpoint listEvery Cilium-managed pod
📦 Podscilium endpoint inspectDeep dive into ONE pod's network
🛡️ Policycilium policy getAll active policies
⚖️ Servicecilium service listAll Services (eBPF LB view)
🏷️ Identitycilium identity listAll identities in cluster
🔍 Monitorcilium monitorLive packet-level view
🔒 Encryptcilium encrypt statusWireGuard/IPSec status
🌍 Meshcilium clustermesh statusMulti-cluster connections
🩺 Debugcilium bugtoolGenerate support tarball

6.3 cilium monitor — Your Real-Time Packet Detective

cilium monitor is Cilium's built-in packet sniffer that shows you exactly what's happening to network traffic in real time — at the eBPF level. Unlike tcpdump which shows all packets, cilium monitor shows you Cilium's decisions about each packet: was it FORWARDED (allowed), DROPPED (denied by policy), or AUDIT (logged but not blocked)? Each entry includes the pod name, identity, port, and the specific policy rule that matched.

When to use it: Any time a pod can't connect to another pod or service. cilium monitor will tell you within seconds whether the packet was dropped by a policy, dropped by routing, or forwarded successfully. This eliminates hours of guesswork. The key filter is --type drop which shows only denied traffic — in a busy cluster, the unfiltered output is overwhelming.

cilium monitor — Real Output Examples
  $ cilium monitor --type drop

  ⬇ DROP: FROM: anihpj/anihpj-abc123 (ID:12345)
          TO:   kube-system/coredns-xyz (ID:1)
          PORT: 53/UDP
          REASON: Policy denied
          ↑ "anihpj trying DNS but policy blocks it!"

  ⬇ DROP: FROM: default/hacker-pod (ID:99999)
          TO:   anihpj/postgres-0 (ID:67890)
          PORT: 5432/TCP
          REASON: Policy denied
          ↑ "Unknown pod blocked from database! ✅"

  USEFUL FILTERS:
    --type drop           Only dropped packets
    --type policy-verdict Only policy decisions
    --from-pod anihpj/*   Only from specific pod
    --to-namespace anihpj Only to specific namespace
⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 6

❌ MISTAKE 1: Forgetting --wait → cilium status shows stale data. FIX: Always cilium status --wait after changes.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Not knowing cilium monitor filters → Seeing firehose of all packets. FIX: Use --type drop or --from-pod to filter.

🔑 CCA Insight: The cilium CLI is not a daemon — it's a stateless binary that communicates with the Cilium Agent via gRPC on a Unix socket. Inside a Cilium pod, it connects to /var/run/cilium/cilium.sock. From your workstation, it uses kubectl exec or port-forward behind the scenes. Key exam point: cilium monitor uses a gRPC STREAMING endpoint (not request-response) — it subscribes to real-time eBPF events from the agent. The cilium bpf commands read RAW eBPF maps — they are the ULTIMATE TRUTH of what the kernel enforces, bypassing any API server caching.

📝 Chapter 5 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What is the minimum Linux kernel version for full Cilium eBPF support?
Show Answer
Answer

Kernel 5.10 or higher. Recommended: 5.15+ or 6.1+ for best eBPF feature support.

Q2
What single flag replaces kube-proxy with Cilium's eBPF load balancer?
Show Answer
Answer

--set kubeProxyReplacement=true. This removes iptables-based service load balancing and replaces it with eBPF hash map lookups (O(1) vs O(n)).

Q3
What does cilium connectivity test verify? Name 5 categories.
Show Answer
Answer

1) Pod-to-Pod (same node, cross-node), 2) Services (ClusterIP, NodePort), 3) DNS (resolution), 4) NetworkPolicy (allow, deny, L7), 5) Encryption (WireGuard), 6) Hubble (Relay, UI, CLI), 7) Performance (bandwidth, latency).

Q4
Can you run Cilium and Calico simultaneously? Why or why not?
Show Answer
Answer

NO. Both would try to assign IPs to pods and create network interfaces. This causes IP conflicts, routing loops, and pods stuck in ContainerCreating. Always remove the old CNI before installing Cilium.

Q5
How do you enable Hubble (CLI + Relay + UI) during Cilium installation?
Show Answer
Answer

--set hubble.enabled=true --set hubble.relay.enabled=true --set hubble.ui.enabled=true

Q6
In CNI migration, why do you drain nodes one at a time?
Show Answer
Answer

Draining one node at a time ensures your applications stay available on other nodes during the migration. Draining all nodes at once would cause total application downtime.

Q7
What happens to running pods when you delete old CNI config from /etc/cni/net.d/?
Show Answer
Answer

Existing pods continue running with their current network, but NEW pods cannot get network connectivity. This is why you drain the node first (move all pods away) before removing the CNI config.

Q8
What 10 things happen when you run cilium install?
Show Answer
Answer

1) Creates namespace, 2) Creates ConfigMap, 3) Creates DaemonSet, 4) Creates Operator Deployment, 5) Creates 9 CRDs, 6) Creates RBAC, 7) Creates Hubble Relay+UI, 8) Creates Hubble Peer Service, 9) Waits for pods Ready, 10) Runs connectivity test.

Q9
What is the difference between cilium install and helm install cilium/cilium? When would you use each?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium install: CLI wrapper that auto-detects your environment (EKS/GKE/AKS/kind) and sets optimal defaults. Good for learning and quick setups. Helm install: Full control over 100+ values via values.yaml. Required for GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux), production environments, and repeatable deployments. The CLI uses Helm under the hood.

Explanation

CCA Installation domain (12%). The exam may ask about installation methods. Remember: CLI = simple, auto-detection. Helm = production, GitOps, full control. Cloud marketplace = managed, vendor-locked.

Q10
After installing Cilium with WireGuard encryption, how do you verify it's actually encrypting traffic?
Show Answer
Answer

1) cilium encrypt status — shows encryption status per node (should show "OK" with WireGuard). 2) cilium connectivity test — includes encryption validation tests. 3) kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium encrypt status — check from within the agent. 4) Hubble observe should show encrypted flows.

Explanation

WireGuard encryption is transparent to applications — they don't know traffic is encrypted. The ONLY way to verify is through Cilium's encryption status tools. If cilium encrypt status shows errors, check: kernel ≥5.6, wireguard module loaded (modprobe wireguard), and encryption enabled in ConfigMap.

5.6 CNI Chaining — Running Cilium Alongside Other CNI Plugins

CNI chaining allows Cilium to work alongside another CNI plugin rather than replacing it entirely. The other CNI handles IP address management (IPAM) and basic network connectivity, while Cilium attaches eBPF programs to the network devices to provide advanced features: L3/L4 policy enforcement, L7 visibility, and encryption.

CNI Chaining Architecture — Two CNIs, One Pod
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    CNI CHAINING ARCHITECTURE                          │
  │                                                                      │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │                     KUBERNETES POD                           │    │
  │  │  ┌────────────────────┐         ┌────────────────────┐       │    │
  │  │  │ anihpj container   │         │ anihpj container   │       │    │
  │  │  └────────┬───────────┘         └────────┬───────────┘       │    │
  │  │           │                              │                    │    │
  │  │           └──────────┬───────────────────┘                    │    │
  │  │                      │                                        │    │
  │  │              ┌───────▼───────┐                                 │    │
  │  │              │   eth0 (veth) │  ← Created by PRIMARY CNI      │    │
  │  │              │   IP: 10.0.1.5│     (AWS VPC CNI, Azure, etc.) │    │
  │  │              └───────┬───────┘                                 │    │
  │  └──────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                         │                                             │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │              ┌───────▼───────┐                                 │    │
  │  │              │ CILIUM eBPF   │  ← Cilium attaches eBPF        │    │
  │  │              │ PROGRAMS      │     programs to veth created    │    │
  │  │              │               │     by the primary CNI          │    │
  │  │              │ • L3/L4 Policy│                                 │    │
  │  │              │ • L7 Inspection│                                │    │
  │  │              │ • Hubble Flows│                                 │    │
  │  │              │ • Encryption  │                                 │    │
  │  │              └───────────────┘                                 │    │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🎯 When to Use CNI Chaining

ScenarioPrimary CNICilium ProvidesUse Case
AWS EKSAWS VPC CNINetworkPolicy, L7 visibility, Hubble, encryptionNeed security/observability but must keep VPC-native pod IPs
Azure AKSAzure CNI (Legacy)NetworkPolicy, L7 inspection, HubbleNeed advanced policies while keeping Azure IPAM
Calico MigrationCalico (IPAM only)eBPF-based enforcement, Hubble, encryptionGradual migration — keep Calico IPAM, add Cilium features
Weave NetWeave NeteBPF policy engine, Hubble visibilityAdd L7 policies without changing IPAM
Portmap/HostPortPortmap CNISecurity + visibility for hostPort podsPods using hostPort need Cilium policy

📋 Enabling CNI Chaining

The key configuration is setting cni.chainingMode and ensuring Cilium doesn't manage IPAM:

Shell — Install Cilium in Chaining Mode (AWS VPC CNI Example)
helm install cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.5 \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set cni.chainingMode=aws-cni \
  --set cni.exclusive=false \
  --set enableIPv4Masquerade=false \
  --set routingMode=native \
  --set ipam.mode=eni
Shell — Generic Veth Chaining (Any CNI)
helm install cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.5 \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set cni.chainingMode=generic-veth \
  --set cni.exclusive=false \
  --set enableIPv4Masquerade=false \
  --set routingMode=native \
  --set ipam.mode=kubernetes
💡 How Chaining Differs from Standalone Cilium

In chaining mode:
• Cilium does NOT create the veth pair — the primary CNI does
• Cilium does NOT assign IPs — the primary CNI's IPAM handles it
• Cilium DOES attach eBPF programs to the veth for policy, visibility, encryption
• cni.exclusive=false lets multiple CNI configs coexist in /etc/cni/net.d/
• routingMode=native — uses the primary CNI's routing, not Cilium's tunnel/overlay

💡 CCA Exam Tip — CNI Chaining

Key points for the exam: (1) CNI chaining = Cilium + another CNI working together. (2) Primary CNI handles IPAM + basic connectivity; Cilium adds eBPF features. (3) Common use: AWS VPC CNI (keep native VPC IPs) + Cilium (add security/visibility). (4) Key Helm values: cni.chainingMode, cni.exclusive=false, ipam.mode set to primary CNI's mode. (5) Cannot run two full CNIs without chaining — they'd conflict on IP assignment.

📝 Chapter 5 — CNI Chaining Practice Questions (3 Additional)

CC1
What is CNI chaining and when would you use it?
Show Answer
Answer

CNI chaining lets Cilium run alongside another CNI plugin. The primary CNI handles IPAM and basic networking; Cilium attaches eBPF programs for advanced features. Use it when you need Cilium's security/observability but must keep the existing CNI's IPAM (e.g., AWS VPC CNI for native VPC IPs).

CC2
What Helm values are essential for CNI chaining mode?
Show Answer
Answer

cni.chainingMode (e.g., aws-cni, generic-veth, calico, portmap), cni.exclusive=false (allow multiple CNI configs), enableIPv4Masquerade=false (let primary CNI handle masquerading), routingMode=native (use primary CNI's routing), and ipam.mode set to match the primary CNI.

CC3
Can you run two full CNIs (e.g., Cilium + Calico) without chaining?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Two full CNIs would both try to assign IPs and create network interfaces, causing conflicts. CNI chaining lets Cilium work WITH another CNI (Cilium only adds eBPF, doesn't do IPAM), but you cannot run two independent CNIs simultaneously on the same node.

🛡️ Part 4: Network Policy — Securing Your Cluster Chapters 7-9 · CCA 20%

Chapter 7: Network Policies — The Firewall for Your Pods

By default, ALL pods in Kubernetes can talk to ALL other pods — zero isolation. Network Policies are your firewall rules. CiliumNetworkPolicy (CNP) takes this further with L7 HTTP/gRPC/DNS-aware rules, identity-based enforcement, and audit mode. This is the most important chapter for the CCA exam (20%).

7.1 Why Network Policies Matter — The "Zero Trust" Mentality

Default Kubernetes: ALL pods can talk to ALL pods — no isolation, no segmentation. A compromised pod can attack anything. Network Policies change this to a zero-trust model:

🚨 The Default K8s Networking Model is Dangerous

Kubernetes was designed with a "flat network" philosophy — every pod gets an IP, and every pod can reach every other pod across all namespaces. This was intentional for simplicity, but it means that if an attacker compromises any single pod in your cluster, they can reach every other pod — databases, internal APIs, monitoring systems, everything. This is the equivalent of having no locks on any door in an apartment building.

Zero Trust networking flips this model: "Never trust, always verify." Instead of assuming pods are safe because they're inside the cluster, you assume every connection could be malicious and explicitly define what's allowed. Everything else is denied. This is the fundamental shift that Network Policies enable.

🏢 The Apartment Building Analogy

Without policies (default K8s): An apartment building where every door is unlocked. Anyone can walk into anyone else's apartment — the mailman, a delivery person, a stranger off the street. If one apartment gets broken into, the thief has access to ALL apartments.

With Network Policies: Each apartment has a lock, and you give keys ONLY to people who need access. The mailman has a key to the lobby (ingress:80). The building manager has keys to the utility room (monitoring:9090). Your neighbor does NOT have a key to your apartment. And if someone breaks into one apartment, they can't reach any others because every door is locked by default.

For anihpj specifically: Your Django application has three tiers — a frontend nginx (public-facing), a backend Django (internal API + admin), and a PostgreSQL database (stores all data). Without policies, a compromised nginx pod could directly access the database. With policies, nginx can only reach Django on port 8000, and only Django can reach PostgreSQL on port 5432. This is called defense in depth — even if one layer is breached, the attacker is contained.

🔑 The Four Principles of Zero Trust Networking

1. Default Deny: Start by blocking everything. Then explicitly allow only what's needed.

2. Least Privilege: Give each pod ONLY the access it needs to do its job. No more.

3. Micro-Segmentation: Divide your cluster into small, isolated segments. Each segment has its own rules.

4. Assume Breach: Design policies assuming an attacker is already inside. Limit their lateral movement.

Without Policies vs With CiliumNetworkPolicy
  WITHOUT POLICIES (DEFAULT)              WITH CILIUM POLICIES
  ┌───────────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │  ANY POD ↔ ANY POD    │              │  anihpj ──▶ DB ✅       │
  │  😱 No isolation      │              │     │                    │
  │                       │              │     └──▶ frontend ✅    │
  │  HACKER POD → DB 😱  │              │                          │
  │  (can access anything!)│              │  HACKER POD → DB 🚫 DROP │
  └───────────────────────┘              └──────────────────────────┘

7.2 Standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy vs CiliumNetworkPolicy

Kubernetes has a built-in NetworkPolicy resource, but it only works at L3/L4 (IP addresses and ports). CiliumNetworkPolicy (CNP) extends this with L7 protocol awareness, identity-based enforcement, DNS rules, and audit mode — all powered by eBPF.

FeatureK8s NetworkPolicyCilium CNP/CCNP
IP/CIDR Rules✅✅
Pod/Namespace Selector✅✅
Port-Based Rules✅✅
HTTP Method (GET/POST)❌✅ 🔥
HTTP Path (/api, /admin)❌✅ 🔥
HTTP Headers❌✅ 🔥
gRPC Method❌✅ 🔥
Kafka Topic❌✅ 🔥
DNS FQDN Rules❌✅ 🔥
ICMP (Ping) Rules❌✅
Identity-Based❌✅ (core design)
Policy Audit Mode❌✅
Deny by Default⚠ Manual✅ (automatic!)
🔹 L3/L4 Rules — What K8s NetPol Covers

L3 = IP addresses and CIDR ranges (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8). L4 = TCP/UDP ports (e.g., :5432). K8s NetworkPolicy can say "allow traffic from namespace X on port 5432" — but it cannot inspect what's inside the packet. It doesn't know if it's HTTP, gRPC, DNS, or Kafka. This is the fundamental limitation that Cilium solves.

# K8s NetPol can only do THIS:
ingress:
  - from:
      - podSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: anihpj
    ports:
      - port: 5432
        protocol: TCP
# ❌ Cannot say: "...but only GET /api/"
🔹 L7 Protocol-Aware Rules — Cilium's Superpower

Cilium's eBPF programs can parse application protocols at the kernel level — HTTP methods, paths, headers; gRPC methods; Kafka topics; DNS queries. This means you can write rules like "allow GET /api/v1 but block POST /admin" — something impossible with K8s NetPol.

# Cilium CNP can do THIS (impossible with K8s NetPol):
ingress:
  - toPorts:
      - ports:
          - port: "8000"
        rules:
          http:
            - method: "GET"         # ← L7! Kernel-level HTTP parsing
              path: "/api/v1/"      # ← URL path matching
            - method: "POST"
              path: "/admin/"
              headers:               # ← Header matching!
                - 'X-API-Key: secret'
🔹 Identity-Based Enforcement — The Core Design

K8s NetPol uses IP addresses for enforcement — pods get new IPs on restart, making rules fragile. Cilium assigns each pod a cryptographic identity based on its labels (e.g., app=anihpj, tier=backend). This identity survives pod restarts, IP changes, and node migrations. Cilium enforces policies based on who you ARE, not where you sit on the network.

Identity vs IP — Why It Matters
  K8s NetPol (IP-Based):              Cilium (Identity-Based):
  ┌─────────────────────┐            ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │ Pod anihpj-abc123   │            │ Pod anihpj-abc123       │
  │ IP: 10.0.1.5  ──────┼──ALLOW──▶ │ Identity: 12345         │
  └─────────────────────┘            │ (app=anihpj, tier=be)   │
                                     └──────────┬──────────────┘
  Pod RESTARTS → NEW IP: 10.0.3.8              │
  ❌ RULE BROKEN! IP changed!         Pod RESTARTS → NEW IP: 10.0.3.8
                                     ✅ RULE INTACT! Identity is same!

7.3 Your First CiliumNetworkPolicy — Protect the Database

Scenario: In the anihpj application, only the Django backend pods should talk to PostgreSQL. The frontend nginx, monitoring tools, and any other pods have no business connecting directly to the database. If a pod gets compromised, the database should be the last thing an attacker can reach.

Why database protection is your #1 priority: The database contains ALL your application data — user accounts, job postings, payment information, everything. If an attacker reaches the database, they've won. That's why your first CNP should always protect the database. The rule is simple: only the pods that need the database can talk to it, and only on the database port.

Let's write this policy step by step. The policy says: "PostgreSQL pods (labeled app: postgres, component: database) should ONLY accept incoming TCP traffic on port 5432 from pods labeled app: anihpj, component: backend. Everything else is denied."

protect-postgres.yaml — CNP 
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2          # MUST be cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy         # CNP (namespace-scoped)
metadata:
  name: protect-postgres
  namespace: anihpj               # Which namespace
spec:
  endpointSelector:               # WHICH PODS this applies to
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres               # → PostgreSQL pods (TARGET)
      component: database
  ingress:                        # INCOMING traffic rules
  - fromEndpoints:                # WHO can send traffic IN
    - matchLabels:
        app: anihpj               # → Only anihpj Django pods
        component: backend
    toPorts:                      # WHICH ports allowed
    - ports:
      - port: "5432"              # → Only PostgreSQL port
        protocol: TCP

💡 Everything NOT explicitly allowed → DENIED by default!
📖 The 4 Essential YAML Fields

endpointSelector: WHICH pods does this policy apply to? (the TARGET)

ingress: Rules for INCOMING traffic to the target pods.

egress: Rules for OUTGOING traffic from the target pods.

fromEndpoints/toEndpoints: WHO can send/receive traffic?

How Cilium Evaluates Network Policies — Rule Processing Order

Cilium checks policies in a specific priority order for EVERY packet. Understanding this is critical for the CCA exam:

  For EACH packet, Cilium checks in this order:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. CNP (CiliumNetworkPolicy) — NAMESPACE-SCOPED               │
  │    ├── Checked FIRST (most specific wins)                       │
  │    ├── If CNP has a rule matching this traffic → USE IT         │
  │    │   (either ALLOW or DENY)                                   │
  │    └── If NO CNP rule matches → go to step 2                    │
  │                                                                  │
  │ 2. CCNP (CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy) — CLUSTER-WIDE       │
  │    ├── Checked SECOND (broader scope)                            │
  │    ├── If CCNP has a rule matching this traffic → USE IT         │
  │    └── If NO CCNP rule matches → go to step 3                    │
  │                                                                  │
  │ 3. Default DENY — CILIUM'S SECURE DEFAULT                       │
  │    ├── If NO policy matches → DENY the traffic                  │
  │    └── This is the "zero trust" default                          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  KEY RULE: CNP OVERRIDES CCNP! Namespace policies take priority.
     More specific always wins over more general.

  EXAMPLE:
  Traffic: anihpj pod → postgres pod, port 5432
  1. Check CNP in namespace "anihpj":
     → "protect-postgres" CNP: ALLOWS anihpj→postgres:5432
     → RESULT: ALLOWED (CNP matched, STOP checking!)

  Traffic: external IP → postgres pod, port 5432
  1. Check CNP in namespace "anihpj":
     → "protect-postgres" CNP: only allows from anihpj label
     → NO MATCH (source doesn't have app=anihpj label)
  2. Check CCNP (cluster-wide): → NO CCNP matches
  3. Default DENY → DROP
The 4 Essential YAML Fields — Visual Guide
  apiVersion: cilium.io/v2  ← MUST be cilium.io/v2 (NOT networking.k8s.io!)
  kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy ← CNP for namespace, CCNP for cluster-wide
  metadata:
    name: my-policy          ← Unique name in the namespace
    namespace: anihpj        ← Which namespace (NOT in CCNP!)
  spec:
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ endpointSelector:     ← FIELD 1: WHICH pods? (TARGET)   │
    │   matchLabels:                                          │
    │     app: postgres     ← Apply to pods with this label   │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ ingress:              ← FIELD 2: INCOMING traffic        │
    │   - fromEndpoints:    ← FIELD 3: WHO can send IN?       │
    │       matchLabels:                                      │
    │         app: anihpj                                     │
    │     toPorts:          ← FIELD 4: WHICH ports?           │
    │       - ports:                                          │
    │           - port: "5432"                                │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ egress:               ← OUTGOING traffic (same pattern) │
    │   - toEndpoints:      ← WHERE can pods send TO?         │
    │     toPorts:          ← WHICH destination ports?        │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  MEMORY AID:
     endpointSelector = "WHO AM I PROTECTING?"
     ingress/egress    = "WHAT TRAFFIC DIRECTION?"
     fromEndpoints     = "FROM WHOM?" (ingress)
     toEndpoints       = "TO WHOM?" (egress)
     toPorts           = "WHICH PORTS?"
🔧 How to Apply, Verify, and Test Your CNP

1. Apply: kubectl apply -f protect-postgres.yaml — Creates the CNP in the namespace.

2. Verify: kubectl get cnp -n anihpj — List all CNPs in the anihpj namespace. Look for the policy name and check it shows as active.

3. Inspect: kubectl describe cnp protect-postgres -n anihpj — See full policy details, including which pods are selected.

4. Test (positive): kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- nc -zv postgres 5432 — From an anihpj pod, try to reach PostgreSQL on port 5432. Should succeed!

5. Test (negative): kubectl exec some-other-pod -- nc -zv postgres 5432 — From a pod NOT labeled app=anihpj. Should fail — connection refused or timeout!

6. Monitor: cilium monitor --type policy-verdict --to-pod anihpj/postgres-xxx — Watch real-time policy decisions for the database pod.

7.4 Layer 7 Policies — HTTP-Aware Rules That Understand Your App

Cilium can inspect HTTP requests and enforce rules based on method, path, and headers — at the kernel level:

protect-django-admin.yaml — L7 CNP 
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: protect-django-admin
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  ingress:
  # RULE 1: Allow GET /jobs/ from ANY source
  - fromEndpoints:
    - {}                           # {} = ANY source
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "8000"
      rules:
        http:
        - method: "GET"            # ← L7! Cilium understands HTTP
          path: "/jobs/"           # ← Only this path!

  # RULE 2: Allow POST /admin/ ONLY from internal IPs
  - fromCIDR:
    - "10.0.0.0/8"                # Only internal network
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "8000"
      rules:
        http:
        - method: "POST"
          path: "/admin/"

💡 POST /admin/ from the internet → DROP at kernel level! 🔴
🚦 Rate Limiting API Endpoints with L7 Policies

Cilium can also enforce rate limits at the HTTP level — protecting your API from abuse without needing an external rate limiter. This is done by adding headers rules to match on rate-limit headers or by configuring Cilium's built-in rate limiting:

# Example: Limit POST /api/jobs/ to 10 requests per minute
ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - {}
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "8000"
      rules:
        http:
        - method: "POST"
          path: "/api/jobs/"
          # Rate limit headers (X-RateLimit-*)
          # Cilium enforces at eBPF level

  # For advanced rate limiting, combine with:
  #   cilium config set rate-limit-api-qps 10
  #   (Rate limits API server requests globally)

While Cilium's primary rate limiting is for API server protection, L7 HTTP header matching gives you fine-grained control over which requests reach your application — reducing load at the kernel level before the application even sees the traffic.

7.5 DNS-Based Policies — Allow Pods to Talk to Specific Domains

Cilium watches DNS requests and dynamically updates allowed IPs based on resolved FQDNs:

allow-egress-stripe.yaml — CNP with toFQDNs 
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  egress:                          # OUTGOING traffic
  - toFQDNs:                       # Allow by DOMAIN NAME
    - matchName: "api.stripe.com"  # Payment API
    - matchName: "api.github.com"  # GitHub integration
  - toEndpoints:                   # Also allow DNS!
    - matchLabels:
        "k8s:app": kube-dns        # Allow CoreDNS
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "53"
        protocol: UDP

💡 Cilium watches DNS responses, caches IPs for *.stripe.com
   and dynamically updates eBPF maps to allow those IPs!
How DNS-Based Policies Work — Under the Hood
  STEP-BY-STEP: What happens when anihpj pod calls api.stripe.com

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                   │
  │  1️⃣  Pod makes DNS query: "api.stripe.com → IP?"                │
  │      ┌──────────┐      DNS query       ┌──────────┐              │
  │      │ anihpj   │ ──────────────────▶  │ CoreDNS  │              │
  │      │ pod      │                      │          │              │
  │      └──────────┘                      └──────────┘              │
  │                                                                   │
  │  2️⃣  CoreDNS resolves → returns: 54.187.1.1, 54.187.2.2         │
  │                                                                   │
  │  3️⃣  Cilium's eBPF program INTERCEPTS the DNS response           │
  │      (Cilium watches ALL DNS traffic at kernel level)             │
  │                                                                   │
  │  4️⃣  Cilium caches the mapping:                                   │
  │      "api.stripe.com" → {54.187.1.1, 54.187.2.2}                │
  │      Stored in an eBPF map (kernel memory, blazing fast!)         │
  │                                                                   │
  │  5️⃣  Cilium dynamically UPDATES the egress policy eBPF map:      │
  │      ALLOW egress to 54.187.1.1:443, 54.187.2.2:443              │
  │                                                                   │
  │  6️⃣  Pod sends HTTPS request → eBPF checks → ALLOWED ✅          │
  │                                                                   │
  │  7️⃣  When DNS TTL expires (e.g., 300 seconds):                    │
  │      Cilium REMOVES the IPs from the allowed list                 │
  │      Next request → pod must re-resolve DNS → cycle repeats       │
  │                                                                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  KEY BENEFITS:
    • Dynamic: IPs update automatically when DNS changes
    • Secure: Only IPs from AUTHORIZED DNS responses are allowed
    • Fast: All enforcement in kernel eBPF maps (sub-microsecond)
    • TTL-Aware: Expired IPs are automatically removed

  ⚠️  CAUTION: DNS-based policies ONLY work if:
    1. DNS requests go through Cilium (not bypassed)
    2. The FQDN actually resolves (otherwise no IPs to allow!)
    3. Pod uses standard DNS (not hardcoded IPs)

7.6 Policy Audit Mode — Test Before You Enforce

NEVER enforce a policy immediately in production! Policy audit mode lets you observe what traffic would be blocked without actually blocking it. This is one of Cilium's most important safety features and a key CCA exam topic.

⚠️ The Golden Rule of Network Policies

ALWAYS audit before enforcing. A misconfigured policy can take down your entire application. Audit mode gives you a safety net — it logs violations but doesn't drop traffic. Run audit for at least 1-7 days before enforcing in production.

protect-postgres-audit.yaml — CNP with Audit 
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: protect-postgres
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  enableAudit: true          # ← THIS IS THE MAGIC LINE!
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        app: anihpj
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "5432"

# With enableAudit: true:
#   → Traffic that matches → ALLOWED (normal operation)
#   → Traffic that DOESN'T match → LOGGED but NOT blocked!
#   → Hubble shows: VERDICT: AUDIT (not DROPPED)
The Safe Rollout Strategy — Full Timeline
  NEVER enforce a policy immediately in production!

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                   │
  │  DAY 1 ──────────────────────────────────────────────── DAY 7+   │
  │                                                                   │
  │  ┌───────────────────────┐                                        │
  │  │ STEP 1: AUDIT          │                                        │
  │  │ (Days 1-7)             │                                        │
  │  │                        │                                        │
  │  │ Add: enableAudit:     │                                        │
  │  │    true to CNP YAML    │                                        │
  │  │ Monitor:               │                                        │
  │  │    hubble observe      │                                        │
  │  │    --verdict AUDIT     │                                        │
  │  │ Goal: See what         │                                        │
  │  │    traffic WOULD be    │                                        │
  │  │    blocked             │                                        │
  │  └───────────┬───────────┘                                        │
  │              │                                                     │
  │              ▼                                                     │
  │  ┌───────────────────────┐                                        │
  │  │ STEP 2: REVIEW         │                                        │
  │  │ (Ongoing)              │                                        │
  │  │                        │                                        │
  │  │ Review Hubble audit   │                                        │
  │  │    logs daily          │                                        │
  │  │ Check: Any             │                                        │
  │  │    legitimate traffic  │                                        │
  │  │    being flagged?      │                                        │
  │  │ Tune policy: Add       │                                        │
  │  │    missing allows      │                                        │
  │  └───────────┬───────────┘                                        │
  │              │                                                     │
  │              ▼                                                     │
  │  ┌───────────────────────┐                                        │
  │  │ STEP 3: ENFORCE        │                                        │
  │  │ (After confidence)     │                                        │
  │  │                        │                                        │
  │  │ Remove: enableAudit   │                                        │
  │  │    or set to false     │                                        │
  │  │ Policy NOW actually    │                                        │
  │  │    BLOCKS traffic!     │                                        │
  │  │ Monitor closely        │                                        │
  │  │    for 24-48 hours     │                                        │
  │  └───────────────────────┘                                        │
  │                                                                   │
  │  Pro tip: For critical production services, audit for 2 WEEKS    │
  │     and cover a full business cycle (weekdays + weekend traffic). │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

7.7 Complete Network Policy Strategy for anihpj

Now let's put everything together into a complete defense-in-depth strategy for the anihpj Django application. Each tier gets its own policy:

anihpj Security Perimeter — All Rules
  INTERNET ──▶ INGRESS (nginx) :80, :443
                    │
                    ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  FRONTEND (nginx)                   │  ← TIER 1
  │  Label: app=anihpj, tier=frontend   │
  │  Policy: Allow :80, :443 from       │
  │  anywhere (internet-facing)         │
  └────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                   │ ALLOW :8000
                   ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  BACKEND (Django)                   │  ← TIER 2
  │  Label: app=anihpj, tier=backend    │
  │                                     │
  │  ✅ GET  /jobs/   → from anywhere   │
  │  ✅ POST /admin/  → from 10.0.0.0/8 │
  │  🔴 POST /admin/  → from internet   │
  │  🌐 egress: api.stripe.com (HTTPS)  │
  └────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                   │ ALLOW :5432
                   ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DATABASE (PostgreSQL)              │  ← TIER 3
  │  Label: app=postgres                │
  │  Only anihpj backend can connect    │
  │  No internet access (no egress)     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔴 DEFAULT RULE: DENY ALL (everything else blocked!)
     Any traffic not explicitly allowed → DROPPED at kernel level
📋 anihpj Policy Checklist — Defense in Depth
#Policy NameTypeProtectsKey Rule
1deny-all-ingressCNPAll podsDefault deny ingress (baseline)
2allow-frontendCNPnginxAllow :80, :443 from internet
3allow-frontend-to-backendCNPDjangoAllow :8000 from frontend pods
4protect-django-adminCNPDjangoL7: Block POST /admin from external
5protect-postgresCNPPostgreSQLAllow :5432 only from backend
6allow-egress-stripeCNPDjangoAllow egress to api.stripe.com
7allow-dnsCNPAll podsAllow UDP 53 to CoreDNS
8block-metadataCCNPCluster-wideBlock 169.254.169.254

🚀 Deploying the Strategy — Step-by-Step Narrative

STEP 1
Baseline — Deploy deny-all in Audit Mode (Policy #1)
Deploy deny-all-ingress in audit mode. This doesn't block anything — it just logs. Watch Hubble for 3-7 days to map normal traffic: DNS (UDP 53), frontend→backend (:8000), backend→database (:5432).
STEP 2
Allow Known Traffic (Policies #2, #3, #5, #7)
Deploy the positive rules: frontend ingress (:80,:443), frontend→backend (:8000), backend→database (:5432), DNS (UDP 53). All legitimate traffic flows — everything else stays in audit mode.
STEP 3
Add L7 Protection — Django Admin (Policy #4)
First smart policy: allows GET /jobs/ from anywhere, restricts POST /admin/ to internal IPs only (10.0.0.0/8). Cilium inspects HTTP at kernel level — no application proxy needed.
STEP 4
Egress Control — Stripe API Only (Policy #6)
Restrict Django egress to api.stripe.com only. Combined with DNS allowlist (CCNP #3), this prevents data exfiltration through DNS tunneling — pods can only use internal CoreDNS.
STEP 5
Cluster-Wide Hardening — Block Metadata (Policy #8)
Deploy CCNP blocking 169.254.169.254 cluster-wide. Prevents SSRF attacks where compromised pods steal cloud IAM credentials from the metadata endpoint.
STEP 6
Enforce — Remove Audit Mode 🔴
After 1-2 weeks of clean audit logs, remove enableAudit: true. Cilium now actively DROPS unauthorized traffic. Monitor closely for 24-48 hours for any unexpected blocks.
⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 7

❌ MISTAKE 1: Forgetting DNS (port 53 to CoreDNS!) → Pods work, then suddenly can't resolve hostnames. FIX: Always allow egress UDP 53.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Using wrong selector labels → Policy has no effect. FIX: kubectl get pods --show-labels and verify exact label names.

❌ MISTAKE 3: Confusing ingress/egress → ingress = INTO the selected pod. egress = OUT FROM the selected pod.

🔧 Under the Hood — How Cilium Policy Enforcement Works: eBPF Policy Maps, Identity Resolution Pipeline, L7 Proxy Redirection, and the Default Deny Mechanism
🗺️ Policy Enforcement — From YAML to eBPF Drop/Allow Decision
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  POLICY ENFORCEMENT PIPELINE — How a CNP Becomes an eBPF Rule                  │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 1: CNP YAML APPLIED                                                      │
│  kubectl apply -f protect-postgres.yaml                                       │
│  → API Server stores CNP in etcd                                             │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 2: CILIUM AGENT WATCHES API                                              │
│  • Agent watches CiliumNetworkPolicy CRDs via K8s watch API                  │
