│  • Detects new/modified/deleted CNP → triggers policy recomputation          │
│  • Uses Cilium's internal "policy repository"                                │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 3: LABEL → IDENTITY RESOLUTION                                           │
│  • Agent reads endpointSelector: matchLabels → finds matching pods           │
│  • For each matching pod: looks up its Cilium Identity (numeric ID)          │
│  • ID_TO_IDENTITY[10.0.0.55] = 12345  (from eBPF map)                       │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 4: POLICY RULE COMPILATION                                               │
│  • fromEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {app:anihpj}}] → Rule: "Allow ID(anihpj)"  │
│  • toPorts: [{port: "5432"}] → Rule: "...on port 5432/TCP"                  │
│  • L7 rules: [{http: {method: "GET", path: "/api/"}}] → Envoy redirect      │
│  • Compiler produces: "Allow SrcID∈{anihpj_ids} → DstID∈{pg_ids}:5432/TCP"  │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 5: eBPF MAP PROGRAMMING                                                 │
│  • Agent writes compiled rules into eBPF POLICY_MAP (BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASH)     │
│  • Key: (DstIdentity, DstPort, Protocol) → Value: allowed SrcIdentities     │
│  • eBPF lookup: hash(dstID, 5432, TCP) → [12345, 12346] (allowed sources)  │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 6: RUNTIME ENFORCEMENT (PER PACKET)                                      │
│  • Packet arrives → eBPF extracts srcID, dstID, port, protocol               │
│  • eBPF hash lookup in POLICY_MAP: is (dstID, port, proto) allowed for srcID?│
│  • ALLOWED → forward to next stage (CT, LB, delivery)                       │
│  • DENIED  → DROP packet, emit Hubble "Policy denied" event                 │
│  • AUDIT   → LOG violation but ALLOW packet (testing mode)                  │
│                                                                              │
│  WHY DEFAULT DENY WORKS:                                                      │
│  • If NO CNP selects pod → no rules → default ALLOW (K8s default)           │
│  • If ANY CNP selects pod → rules exist → default DENY for unmatched traffic│
│  • This is called "policy-enabled endpoint" — automatic!                    │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 L7 Policy — How HTTP Parsing Works at Kernel Level
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  L7 HTTP POLICY ENFORCEMENT — Kernel-Level HTTP Parsing                        │
│                                                                              │
│  When a CNP has L7 HTTP rules (method, path, headers):                       │
│                                                                              │
│  1. PACKET ARRIVES at eBPF TC hook                                            │
│     • L3/L4 check: is this port 8000 TCP? → YES                              │
│     • Identity check: is srcID allowed? → YES                                │
│     • L7 policy EXISTS for this port → REDIRECT TO PROXY                     │
│                                                                              │
│  2. REDIRECT TO ENVOY PROXY (Userspace)                                        │
│     • eBPF redirects packet → Cilium's embedded Envoy proxy                 │
│     • Envoy terminates TCP connection (acts as transparent proxy)            │
│     • Envoy reads FULL HTTP request (method, path, headers, body)            │
│                                                                              │
│  3. ENVOY ENFORCES HTTP RULES                                                   │
│     • Checks: method == "GET"? path matches "/api/*"?                        │
│     • Checks: headers contain "X-API-Key: valid"?                           │
│     • MATCH → Envoy proxies connection to backend pod                       │
│     • NO MATCH → Envoy returns HTTP 403 Forbidden                           │
│                                                                              │
│  4. ESTABLISHED CONNECTION FAST PATH                                           │
│     • After Envoy approves, connection is recorded in eBPF CT map           │
│     • Subsequent packets on same TCP flow → eBPF fast path (no proxy!)      │
│     • Only the FIRST request of a new connection goes through Envoy         │
│                                                                              │
│  KEY: Only L7 policies trigger proxy redirection. L3/L4 policies are        │
│  100% in kernel eBPF — no userspace involvement, no context switches.       │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 Policy Map Structure — What the eBPF Hash Map Actually Contains
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  eBPF POLICY MAP — The Kernel-Level Data Structure That Enforces Rules         │
│                                                                              │
│  MAP TYPE: BPF_MAP_TYPE_HASH (key → value, O(1) lookup)                      │
│  MAP NAME: cilium_policy_XXXXX (one per endpoint)                            │
│                                                                              │
│  MAP STRUCTURE (simplified):                                                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ KEY: (Destination Identity, Destination Port, Protocol, Direction)    │   │
│  │ VALUE: Bitmask of allowed Source Identities + L7 redirect flag       │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Example entries for postgres pod (Identity 67890):                    │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ KEY                          VALUE                                    │   │
│  │ ─────────────────────────    ──────────────────────────────────────   │   │
│  │ (67890, 5432, TCP, INGRESS)   [12345, 12346] → anihpj pods allowed   │   │
│  │ (67890, 9187, TCP, INGRESS)   [11111]        → metrics scraper only   │   │
│  │ (67890, 5432, TCP, EGRESS)    [0]            → no egress allowed     │   │
│  │ (67890, 53, UDP, EGRESS)      [1, 2]         → DNS to world+cluster  │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ LOOKUP AT RUNTIME (per packet):                                        │   │
│  │ 1. Extract dstID=67890, dstPort=5432, protocol=TCP from packet        │   │
│  │ 2. Hash key → find entry → value = [12345, 12346]                     │   │
│  │ 3. Is srcID=12345 in the allowed list? YES → ALLOW                    │   │
│  │ 4. Is srcID=99999 in the allowed list? NO → DENY (default)            │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  SPECIAL IDENTITIES (Reserved):                                                │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ ID 1:   "host"      — the node itself (kubelet, host processes)       │   │
│  │ ID 2:   "world"     — any IP outside the cluster (internet)          │   │
│  │ ID 3:   "cluster"   — all cluster-internal IPs (pods + services)     │   │
│  │ ID 4:   "health"    — Cilium health checking endpoints               │   │
│  │ ID 5:   "init"      — identity before labels are known               │   │
│  │ ID 6+:  Application identities (derived from pod labels)              │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔀 toFQDNs DNS Interception — How Cilium Watches and Enforces DNS
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DNS-BASED POLICY — The Complete eBPF Interception Flow                         │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ PHASE 1: DNS PROXY INTERCEPTION (eBPF)                                  │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Pod sends DNS query (UDP 53) → eBPF intercepts BEFORE CoreDNS sees it │   │
│  │ • eBPF records: pod_identity=12345, query="api.stripe.com", id=0xABCD │   │
│  │ • eBPF forwards query to Cilium's DNS proxy (not directly to CoreDNS) │   │
│  │ • DNS proxy is a per-node component that caches + enforces policies   │   │
│  │ • DNS proxy forwards to actual CoreDNS → gets response                │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ PHASE 2: DNS RESPONSE INTERCEPTION + CACHING                            │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ CoreDNS responds: api.stripe.com → {54.187.1.1, 54.187.2.2}          │   │
│  │ • Cilium DNS proxy intercepts the response                             │   │
│  │ • Checks: does any CNP/CCNP have a toFQDNs rule matching this domain?  │   │
│  │ • YES → extracts resolved IPs → caches:                                 │   │
│  │   FQDN_CACHE["api.stripe.com"] = {54.187.1.1, 54.187.2.2}           │   │
│  │ • Forwards response to pod (pod gets normal DNS response)             │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ PHASE 3: DYNAMIC IP ALLOW-LISTING                                        │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ • Cilium Agent reads FQDN cache → updates eBPF maps:                   │   │
│  │   IP_TO_IDENTITY[54.187.1.1] = SPECIAL_FQDN_IDENTITY                   │   │
│  │   IP_TO_IDENTITY[54.187.2.2] = SPECIAL_FQDN_IDENTITY                   │   │
│  │ • Policy map now allows egress to these IPs on the specified ports     │   │
│  │ • TTL tracker: starts countdown (e.g., 300 seconds)                    │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ PHASE 4: TTL EXPIRY + CLEANUP                                            │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ • When DNS TTL expires → Cilium REMOVES IPs from eBPF maps            │   │
│  │ • Next pod request to api.stripe.com → must re-resolve DNS            │   │
│  │ • This ensures pod only reaches currently-valid IPs                   │   │
│  │ • Stale IPs (DNS records changed) are automatically cleaned up        │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  WHY DNS PROXY (not raw DNS interception):                                     │
│  • Can enforce: "only allow DNS responses that match policy FQDNs"         │
│  • Can reject: DNS responses for unauthorized domains                      │
│  • Can rate-limit: excessive DNS queries from a pod                        │
│  • Provides visibility: Hubble shows every DNS query + response            │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔄 Policy State Machine — Audit vs Enforce vs Disabled
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  POLICY STATE TRANSITIONS — How a CNP Evolves Through Its Lifecycle             │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────┐     kubectl apply      ┌──────────┐     remove enableAudit    │
│  │ DISABLED │───────────────────────▶│  AUDIT   │─────────────────────────▶  │
│  │ (no CNP) │                        │  MODE    │                            │
│  └──────────┘                        └────┬─────┘                            │
│       ▲                                   │                                   │
│       │                                   │ review audit logs (1-7 days)      │
│       │                                   ▼                                   │
│       │                            ┌──────────────┐                          │
│       │        kubectl delete      │  ENFORCING   │                          │
│       └────────────────────────────│  (no audit)  │                          │
│                                    └──────┬───────┘                          │
│                                           │                                   │
│                                           │ add enableAudit: true back        │
│                                           ▼                                   │
│                                    ┌──────────────┐                          │
│                                    │  ENFORCING   │  (optional hybrid)        │
│                                    │  + AUDITING  │  enforce old rules,       │
│                                    │  (dual mode) │  audit new rules          │
│                                    └──────────────┘                          │
│                                                                              │
│  WHAT HAPPENS IN EACH STATE:                                                   │
│  ┌──────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ AUDIT    │ Matching traffic: ALLOWED (normal)                           │  │
│  │          │ Non-matching traffic: ALLOWED + LOGGED (Hubble: AUDIT)       │  │
│  │          │ Use for: testing new policies, verifying selectors            │  │
│  ├──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │ ENFORCE  │ Matching traffic: ALLOWED (normal)                           │  │
│  │          │ Non-matching traffic: DROPPED (Hubble: DROPPED)              │  │
│  │          │ Use for: production security enforcement                     │  │
│  ├──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │ DISABLED │ No policy → default K8s behavior (ALLOW all)                │  │
│  │          │ Equivalent to: kubectl delete cnp                     │  │
│  └──────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CCA Insight: Network Policy is 20% of the CCA exam. Critical concepts: (1) Default deny activates AUTOMATICALLY when ANY CNP selects a pod — you don't write a "deny all" rule. (2) Multiple CNPs use UNION semantics — the pod gets the MOST permissive combination. (3) L7 policies redirect to Envoy proxy (the ONLY userspace hop in the entire pipeline). (4) CNP takes priority over CCNP — namespace-scoped beats cluster-wide. (5) DNS policies watch DNS responses via eBPF and dynamically update allowed IPs.

📝 Chapter 6 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What does "cilium status" show? Name 6 sections.
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium agent, Operator, Hubble Relay, Hubble UI, ClusterMesh, Encryption status. Also: DaemonSet/Deployment health, image versions, cluster pod count.

Q2
How do you see all Cilium-managed endpoints on a node?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium endpoint list — shows every pod that Cilium manages, including its IP, identity, and policy enforcement status.

Q3
Which command shows real-time packet drops with identity information?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium monitor --type drop — shows source/destination pod names, identities, ports, and the reason for the drop.

Q4
What does "Desired: 3, Ready: 1" in cilium status mean?
Show Answer
Answer

You have 3 nodes (3 Cilium agents desired), but only 1 agent is running and healthy. 2 agents are failing to start. Check those nodes with kubectl describe pod -n kube-system cilium-xxx.

Q5
How do you validate a CiliumNetworkPolicy YAML before applying it?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium policy validate policy.yaml — checks YAML syntax and policy semantics without applying it.

Q6
What command generates a support bundle for troubleshooting?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium bugtool — collects logs, eBPF map dumps, configuration, and cluster state into a tarball for support analysis.

Q7
What's the difference between cilium monitor and cilium monitor --type drop?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium monitor shows ALL eBPF events — every packet, policy decision, connection — like a firehose. cilium monitor --type drop filters to ONLY dropped packets, showing what's being blocked and why. Use unfiltered for deep debugging, filtered for policy troubleshooting.

Explanation

This is like the difference between tcpdump (all packets) and tcpdump port 443 (filtered). The CCA exam expects you to know which monitoring tool to use for which scenario. Monitor = low-level kernel debugging. Hubble = high-level operational visibility.

Q8
How do you check if a specific CiliumNetworkPolicy is actively enforced on a particular pod?
Show Answer
Answer

1) cilium endpoint list — find the pod's endpoint ID. 2) cilium endpoint inspect <ID> — shows all policies applied to that endpoint. 3) hubble observe --from-pod ns/pod --verdict DROPPED — see if policy is actually dropping traffic. 4) cilium policy get -n ns — list all policies in the namespace.

Explanation

CCA Installation domain (12%). The CLI commands map to exam scenarios: status = health check, endpoint = per-pod state, monitor = packet-level debug, policy = rule management. Know which command to use for each diagnostic scenario.

Q9
What does cilium bpf lb list show and why is it useful?
Show Answer
Answer

Shows the raw eBPF load balancer map — the actual kernel-level mapping of Service ClusterIPs → backend pod IPs. Useful for verifying that kube-proxy replacement is working correctly at the kernel level. Compare with cilium service list which shows the userspace view.

Q10
How do you safely upgrade Cilium from v1.15 to v1.16? What command and precautions?
Show Answer
Answer

1) Read release notes at docs.cilium.io. 2) Run cilium preflight to check compatibility. 3) cilium upgrade --version 1.16.0 — upgrades in-place preserving config. 4) cilium status --wait — verify all components healthy. 5) cilium connectivity test — validate functionality. Never skip preflight — it catches breaking changes before the upgrade.

Explanation

CCA Installation domain. Upgrade vs reinstall: upgrade preserves your ConfigMap, CRDs, and running policies. Reinstall (cilium install) replaces everything. Always use upgrade for minor/patch versions within the same major version.

Chapter 8: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy (CCNP) — Cluster-Level Rules

While CNPs are namespace-scoped, CCNPs apply across ALL namespaces. Think of CNPs as room-level locks — each namespace gets its own rules. CCNPs are building-level security — rules that apply to everyone, regardless of which room they're in. CCNPs are essential for cluster-wide concerns like blocking cloud metadata access, allowing monitoring across namespaces, and enforcing DNS security everywhere at once.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour 🌍 Cluster-Wide 🎯 CCA Core

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ When to use CCNP instead of CNP — the decision framework
  • ✅ How CCNP differs structurally (no namespace field!)
  • ✅ Real-world CCNP scenarios: metadata blocking, monitoring, DNS
  • ✅ CNP vs CCNP priority — which wins and why

8.1 When You Need Cluster-Wide Policies

Use CCNP when you need rules that apply everywhere: block external access to kube-system, allow monitoring to scrape all namespaces, block metadata service access cluster-wide.

Why not just use CNPs everywhere? You could — but you'd need to create the same CNP in every single namespace, including future namespaces that don't exist yet. With a CCNP, you write the rule once and it automatically applies to all namespaces — present and future. This is especially important for security rules that should be universal, like blocking the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) which is a common SSRF attack vector.

The priority rule is crucial: Cilium checks CNPs first, then CCNPs. This means a permissive CNP in one namespace can override a restrictive CCNP. For example, if a CCNP blocks all access to 169.254.169.254, but a CNP in the "untrusted" namespace explicitly allows it — the CNP wins. This is by design: more specific policies should have more control. But it also means you need to be careful — a single misconfigured CNP can punch a hole in your cluster-wide security.

💡 CNP vs CCNP Decision Rule

Use CNP when the rule is specific to one namespace (e.g., "protect the anihpj database"). Use CCNP when the rule applies cluster-wide (e.g., "block all pods from accessing 169.254.169.254 cloud metadata").

block-cloud-metadata.yaml — CCNP 
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy  # ← CCNP (NOT CNP!)
metadata:
  name: block-cloud-metadata          # ← NO namespace field!
spec:                                 #    (applies cluster-wide)
  endpointSelector: {}                # ← {} = ALL pods in ALL namespaces
  egress:
  - toCIDR:
    - "169.254.169.254/32"           # Block cloud metadata IP
  # With NO allow rules, Cilium's default is DENY
  # → All egress to 169.254.169.254 is BLOCKED cluster-wide!

# Key differences from CNP:
#   1. kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy (not CiliumNetworkPolicy)
#   2. NO namespace in metadata
#   3. Applies to ALL namespaces simultaneously
#   4. Checked AFTER CNP (CNP takes priority)

8.2 Real-World CCNP Scenarios for anihpj

Here are three CCNP scenarios you'll encounter in real production environments — each solves a problem that would be impractical with namespace-scoped CNPs alone.

🔴 CCNP 1: Block Cloud Metadata Access (SSRF Prevention)

Cloud providers expose a metadata service at 169.254.169.254 that returns sensitive credentials. A Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attack tricks a pod into calling this endpoint, stealing IAM roles or API keys. Blocking this IP cluster-wide with a CCNP is a critical security control — one rule protects every pod in every namespace from this attack vector. The YAML for this is shown in section 8.1 above (block-cloud-metadata).

🟢 CCNP 2: Allow Monitoring Across All Namespaces

Prometheus needs to scrape /metrics endpoints on every pod. Without a CCNP, you'd have to create a CNP in every namespace allowing Prometheus access. Worse, when someone creates a new namespace, they'd forget to add the monitoring CNP — and their pods would be invisible to monitoring. A CCNP solves this elegantly: one rule, all namespaces, forever.

allow-monitoring.yaml — CCNP 
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-monitoring
spec:
  endpointSelector: {}                # All pods in all namespaces
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        app: prometheus               # Only Prometheus pods
        namespace: monitoring          # Only from monitoring namespace
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "9090"                  # Metrics port
        protocol: TCP

# This allows Prometheus (in monitoring namespace) to scrape
# /metrics on port 9090 from ALL pods in ALL namespaces.
# Without this CCNP, you'd need a CNP in EVERY namespace!
🟡 CCNP 3: DNS Allowlist — Prevent DNS Data Exfiltration

DNS tunneling is a technique where attackers encode stolen data into DNS queries to bypass egress controls. By restricting ALL pods to only use the cluster's internal CoreDNS (and blocking external DNS servers like 8.8.8.8), you prevent this attack vector. Combined with a CNP that uses toFQDNs to allow only specific approved external domains, you create a complete DNS security posture. Pods can resolve internal services and approved external APIs — but nothing else.

dns-allowlist.yaml — CCNP 
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: dns-allowlist
spec:
  endpointSelector: {}                # All pods
  egress:
  # Only allow DNS to trusted resolvers
  - toEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        "k8s:app": kube-dns          # Allow CoreDNS
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "53"
        protocol: UDP
  # Block DNS to ANY other destination
  - toFQDNs: []                        # Empty = block all external DNS

# This prevents DNS tunneling/data exfiltration — pods can only
# use the cluster's internal CoreDNS, not external DNS servers.
# Combined with a CNP that allows specific toFQDNs for approved
# external domains, this creates a complete DNS security posture.
🔧 Under the Hood — How CCNP & CNP Precedence Works: Policy Evaluation Order, Union Semantics, and the Identity-Based Selection Pipeline
🗺️ CNP vs CCNP — The Complete Evaluation Order
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  POLICY EVALUATION ORDER — Which Rule Wins When?                                │
│                                                                              │
│  FOR EVERY PACKET, CILIUM CHECKS (in this order):                             │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ PRIORITY 1: CNP (CiliumNetworkPolicy) — NAMESPACE-SCOPED             │   │
│  │ • All CNPs in the pod's namespace that select this pod                │   │
│  │ • UNION semantics: ALL matching allows are combined                   │   │
│  │ • If ANY CNP rule matches → USE IT (stop checking CCNP)              │   │
│  │ • If NO CNP rule matches → go to Priority 2                           │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ PRIORITY 2: CCNP (CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy) — CLUSTER-WIDE     │   │
│  │ • All CCNPs that select this pod                                       │   │
│  │ • UNION semantics: ALL matching allows from ALL CCNPs combined        │   │
│  │ • If ANY CCNP rule matches → USE IT                                    │   │
│  │ • If NO CCNP rule matches → go to Priority 3                           │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ PRIORITY 3: Default Rule                                               │   │
│  │ • If ANY policy (CNP or CCNP) selects this pod → DEFAULT DENY         │   │
│  │ • If NO policy selects this pod → DEFAULT ALLOW (K8s default)        │   │
│  │ • This is automatic — NO explicit "deny" rule needed!               │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  UNION SEMANTICS VISUALIZED:                                                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ CNP-A: Allow Src{anihpj} → Dst{postgres}:5432                        │   │
│  │ CNP-B: Allow Src{prometheus} → Dst{postgres}:9090                    │   │
│  │ CNP-C: Allow Src{all} → Dst{postgres}:80                             │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ EFFECTIVE POLICY for postgres pod = UNION of all three:               │   │
│  │ ✅ anihpj → postgres:5432                                             │   │
│  │ ✅ prometheus → postgres:9090                                          │   │
│  │ ✅ everyone → postgres:80                                              │   │
│  │ ❌ everything else → DENIED (default deny)                             │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Policies NEVER cancel each other. They ONLY ADD allows.               │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  K8s NetPol COMPATIBILITY:                                                     │
│  • Cilium understands BOTH K8s NetworkPolicy AND CNP/CCNP                    │
│  • K8s NetPol → internally translated to same rule format as CNP             │
│  • Precedence: CNP > CCNP > K8s NetPol (CNP is most specific)               │
│  • Allows gradual migration: K8s NetPol → CNP with zero disruption          │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔀 Full Policy Priority Chain — K8s NetPol + CNP + CCNP + Default
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  COMPLETE POLICY PRIORITY CHAIN — Every Policy Type, In Order                  │
│                                                                              │
│  FOR EVERY PACKET, CILIUM WALKS THIS CHAIN (first match wins):               │
│                                                                              │
│  PRIORITY 1: CNP (namespace-scoped)                                           │
│  ├── Most specific — checked FIRST                                            │
│  ├── If ANY CNP rule matches → USE the combined result                       │
│  └── If NO CNP matches → go to Priority 2                                    │
│                                                                              │
│  PRIORITY 2: CCNP (cluster-wide)                                              │
│  ├── Broader scope — checked SECOND                                           │
│  ├── If ANY CCNP rule matches → USE it                                        │
│  └── If NO CCNP matches → go to Priority 3                                    │
│                                                                              │
│  PRIORITY 3: K8s NetworkPolicy (standard)                                      │
│  ├── Standard K8s NetPol — checked THIRD                                      │
│  ├── Cilium translates K8s NetPol to same internal format                    │
│  ├── Allows gradual migration: start with K8s NetPol, add CNP later          │
│  └── If NO K8s NetPol matches → go to Priority 4                              │
│                                                                              │
│  PRIORITY 4: Default Rule                                                      │
│  ├── If ANY policy (CNP/CCNP/NetPol) selects this pod → DEFAULT DENY         │
│  └── If NO policy selects this pod → DEFAULT ALLOW (K8s open default)        │
│                                                                              │
│  REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:                                                           │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Pod: anihpj/web, namespace: anihpj                                     │   │
│  │ Packet: src=some-pod, dst=anihpj/web:8080                              │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Check 1: CNPs in "anihpj" ns selecting anihpj/web?                    │   │
│  │   → CNP-A (allow from frontend:8080): src label doesn't match → skip  │   │
│  │   → CNP-B (allow from monitoring:9090): port doesn't match → skip     │   │
│  │   → No CNP match → continue                                           │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Check 2: CCNPs selecting anihpj/web?                                   │   │
│  │   → CCNP-deny-metadata (egress only): direction doesn't match → skip  │   │
│  │   → No CCNP match → continue                                           │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Check 3: K8s NetPols selecting anihpj/web?                            │   │
│  │   → allow-from-all: matches! → ALLOW                                   │   │
│  │   → RESULT: ALLOWED (K8s NetPol matched)                               │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 CCNP Use Cases — When Cluster-Wide Is the Right Choice
ScenarioCCNP RuleWhy Not CNP?
Block Cloud MetadataDeny egress to 169.254.169.254 for all podsWould need CNP in EVERY namespace — including future ones
Allow MonitoringAllow ingress from monitoring namespace on :9090 for all podsNew namespaces would be invisible to monitoring
Enforce DNS PolicyAllow egress UDP 53 only to kube-system/CoreDNSOne misconfigured CNP could bypass cluster DNS security
Block External EgressDeny all egress to 0.0.0.0/0 except allowed CIDRsDefense-in-depth — CNP can ADD allows but not REMOVE CCNP blocks
PCI-DSS SegmentationDeny all cross-namespace traffic; explicit allows onlyCompliance requires cluster-wide enforcement proof
🔑 CCA Insight: CCNP is a guaranteed CCA exam topic. Key memory aids: (1) CNP = Namespace-scoped, CCNP = Cluster-wide. (2) CCNP has NO namespace field — it applies everywhere. (3) CNP OVERRIDES CCNP — more specific wins. (4) Union semantics = policies ADD, never subtract. You can't write a "deny all" to override an "allow" — you must remove or modify the allow. (5) To block cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), use a CCNP — it's the only way to protect ALL namespaces at once.

📝 Chapter 7 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What's the difference between K8s NetworkPolicy and CiliumNetworkPolicy? Name 4 capabilities Cilium adds.
Show Answer
Answer

1) L7 HTTP/gRPC/Kafka rules, 2) DNS FQDN-based policies (toFQDNs), 3) Identity-based enforcement (labels→IDs), 4) Policy audit mode. K8s NetPol only does L3/L4 IP:port rules.

Q2
Write a CNP that allows ONLY GET requests to /api/v1/ from any source.
Show Answer
Answer

endpointSelector: matchLabels: app: myapp → ingress: fromEndpoints: [{}] → toPorts: ports: [port:"8080"] → rules: http: [{method:"GET", path:"/api/v1/"}]

Q3
What does {} mean in fromEndpoints? When would you use it?
Show Answer
Answer

{} means ALLOW FROM ANY SOURCE (all pods, all namespaces, all CIDRs). Use it for public endpoints like a web frontend that should be accessible. For internal services like databases, use specific label selectors instead.

Q4
How does DNS-based policy (toFQDNs) work? What happens under the hood?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium's eBPF programs watch DNS responses from pods. When a pod resolves api.stripe.com → 54.187.1.1, Cilium caches this mapping and dynamically adds the IP to the allowed egress eBPF map. When the DNS TTL expires, the IP is removed.

Q5
What is policy audit mode and why should you ALWAYS use it before enforcing?
Show Answer
Answer

Audit mode LOGS policy violations but does NOT block traffic. You use it to observe what traffic your policy WOULD block before actually blocking it — preventing "I just broke production!" moments. 3-step process: Audit → Monitor (1-7 days) → Enforce.

Q6
If CNP and CCNP both have rules for the same traffic, which takes priority?
Show Answer
Answer

CNP (namespace-scoped) takes priority over CCNP (cluster-wide). The more specific policy wins. Cilium checks CNP first; if no CNP rule matches, it falls back to CCNP. If neither matches, the DEFAULT is DENY (zero-trust).

Q7
Why does blocking all egress without allowing DNS break applications?
Show Answer
Answer

Pods need DNS (UDP port 53) to resolve service names and external domains. Without DNS, pods can't discover services. Always add an egress rule allowing UDP 53 to kube-system/CoreDNS when writing restrictive policies.

Q8
Write a policy that allows anihpj to call api.stripe.com (HTTPS) but blocks all other egress. Include DNS allowance.
Show Answer
Answer

egress: [toFQDNs: [matchName: "api.stripe.com"], toEndpoints: [matchLabels: {"k8s:app": kube-dns}, toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "53", protocol: UDP}]}]]]

Q9
What is the difference between ingress and egress in a CiliumNetworkPolicy? Provide an anihpj example for each.
Show Answer
Answer

Ingress: Controls who can send traffic TO the selected pods. Example: "Only frontend pods can send traffic to backend pods on port 8000." The backend pod is selected, and the rule protects it from unwanted incoming traffic. Egress: Controls where the selected pods can send traffic OUT to. Example: "Backend pods can only send traffic to postgres on port 5432 and CoreDNS on UDP 53." The backend pod is selected, and the rule restricts its outgoing traffic.

Explanation

CCA Network Policy domain (20%). The direction is ALWAYS from the perspective of the SELECTED pod. Think: "In-gress = IN-coming to my pod" and "E-gress = EX-it from my pod." This is the #4 most common exam mistake — confusing ingress and egress directions.

Q10
How does Cilium handle multiple CNPs selecting the same pod with different rules? What happens if they conflict?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium uses UNION semantics — the pod gets the MOST permissive combination of all policies. If CNP-A allows port 80 and CNP-B allows port 443, the pod gets BOTH. Policies never cancel each other. There is no "deny" rule that overrides an "allow" — to deny, you simply don't allow. Unlike firewalls where "last rule wins," Cilium policies ADD together.

Explanation

This is fundamentally different from traditional firewalls. It means: (1) You can't write a "deny all" rule that overrides existing allows — you must remove or modify the allow rules, (2) Multiple teams can manage policies independently — they won't break each other, (3) The effective policy for a pod is the UNION of all CNPs + CCNPs that select it.

Chapter 9: Network Policy Debugging — "Why Can't My Pod Connect?"

Network policies are powerful but can be tricky. This chapter teaches you a systematic approach to debugging connectivity issues.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours

9.1 The Systematic Debugging Approach

When a pod can't connect, follow this systematic 5-step approach. Never jump to conclusions — work through each step methodically:

Debug Flowchart — "My Pod Can't Connect!"
🔴 "anihpj pod can't reach PostgreSQL!"
     │
     ▼
┌──────────────────────┐
│ ① DNS Check           │
│ nslookup postgres    │──NO──▶ Check CoreDNS + toFQDNs policy
│ Resolves?            │
└────────┬─────────────┘
         │ YES
         ▼
┌──────────────────────┐
│ ② Policy Check        │
│ cilium monitor        │──YES──▶ POLICY_DENIED?
│ --type policy-verdict │         Check policy selectors!
└────────┬─────────────┘
         │ FORWARDED (not blocked)
         ▼
┌──────────────────────┐
│ ③ Route Check         │
│ ping DB pod IP        │──NO──▶ Check routes, tunnel mode
│ Can reach IP?         │        cilium endpoint inspect
└────────┬─────────────┘
         │ YES
         ▼
┌──────────────────────┐
│ ④ Port Check          │
│ nc -zv IP 5432       │──NO──▶ Is PostgreSQL listening?
│ Port open?            │        kubectl exec into DB pod
└────────┬─────────────┘
         │ YES
         ▼
┌──────────────────────┐
│ ⑤ App-Level Check      │
│ Check Django settings │──▶ DATABASE_URL, credentials
│ Check app logs        │
└──────────────────────┘
①
DNS Check — Can the pod resolve the name?

kubectl exec -it anihpj-xxx -- nslookup postgres

If DNS fails → Check CoreDNS pods are running, and verify no policy blocks UDP port 53 to kube-system.

②
Policy Check — Is Cilium dropping the packet?

cilium monitor --type policy-verdict --from-namespace anihpj

If you see verdict DROPPED → Policy is blocking! Check your endpointSelector labels match the actual pod labels.

③
Route Check — Can the pod even reach the target IP?

kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- ping <DB-pod-IP>

If ping fails → Check Cilium tunnel/Geneve/routing mode with cilium status and cilium endpoint list.

④
Port Check — Is the specific port actually open?

kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- nc -zv <target-IP> 5432

If port check fails → Exec into the DB pod and verify PostgreSQL is actually listening on port 5432.

⑤
App-Level Check — Is the application misconfigured?

kubectl logs anihpj-xxx | grep -i error

Check for: connection refused, wrong credentials, missing DATABASE_URL, firewall at app level, TLS misconfiguration.

9.2 Using cilium monitor for Policy Debugging

cilium monitor --type policy-verdict shows real-time policy decisions — DROPPED, FORWARDED, or AUDIT — with full identity information. This is your primary debugging tool for policy issues:

🔍 Essential Debug Filters

--type drop — Only dropped packets

--type policy-verdict — Policy decisions only (MOST USEFUL)

--from-pod anihpj/anihpj-abc123 — Traffic from specific pod

--to-namespace anihpj — Traffic to specific namespace

--related-to-pod anihpj/anihpj-abc123 — Traffic to OR from a pod

terminal — cilium monitor --type policy-verdict
ALLOWED policy matched — anihpj → postgres:5432
flow 0x12345 local EP 67890 remote 11111
src identity 12345@anihpj → dst identity 67890@anihpj
verdict FORWARDED ✓ port 5432/tcp action allow
DENIED no policy matched — external → postgres:5432
flow 0xabcde local EP 67890 remote 22222
src identity 99999@external → dst identity 67890@anihpj
verdict DROPPED ✗ port 5432/tcp action deny
AUDIT logged but not blocked — default → postgres:5432
flow 0xfghij local EP 67890 remote 33333
src identity 55555@default → dst identity 67890@anihpj
verdict AUDIT ◉ port 5432/tcp action audit
📋 verdict
FORWARDED = ALLOWED
DROPPED = BLOCKED
AUDIT = LOGGED
👤 src identity
WHO sent the packet
identity@namespace
🎯 dst identity
WHO receives the packet
identity@namespace
🔌 port
Destination port
5432/tcp = PostgreSQL
⚡ action
allow | deny | audit
🔧 Quick Debug Workflow for Policy Issues
① Open Terminal 1

cilium monitor --type policy-verdict --to-namespace anihpj

② Open Terminal 2

kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- curl postgres:5432

③ If DROPPED

Policy is blocking! Check identity labels match your policy selectors.

④ If FORWARDED

Policy is NOT the issue! → Move to route/port/app checks.

9.3 Common Policy Mistakes and How to Fix Them

These are the top 5 mistakes that even experienced operators make. Memorize these patterns — they will appear on the CCA exam and save you hours of debugging in production.

🔴 HIGH
❌ Label Mismatch (Typo in Selector)
📋 Symptom: Policy has no effect — traffic flows as if policy doesn't exist
🔧 Fix: kubectl get pods --show-labels and verify exact label names match your selectors
🔴 HIGH
❌ Forgot DNS Allow (Port 53 Blocked)
📋 Symptom: Pods work initially, then suddenly can't resolve any hostnames
🔧 Fix: Allow egress UDP 53 to kube-system/CoreDNS in EVERY restrictive policy
🟡 MED
⚠️ Wrong Namespace
📋 Symptom: Policy doesn't apply to intended pods — appears to have no effect
🔧 Fix: Verify -n flag matches the namespace your pods are in. CNPs are namespace-scoped!
🟡 MED
⚠️ Ingress vs Egress Confusion
📋 Symptom: Traffic blocked in wrong direction — pods can't receive or send as expected
🔧 Fix: ingress = INTO the selected pod. egress = OUT FROM the selected pod. For DB protection, use ingress on the DB selector.
🔴 HIGH
❌ Too Restrictive — Default Deny Without Allows
📋 Symptom: Everything breaks! All pods lose connectivity immediately after applying policy
🔧 Fix: Start with audit mode first! Then gradually add explicit allow rules. Never enforce a default-deny without testing.
🔧 Under the Hood — How Cilium Policy Debugging Tools Work: Policy Audit Pipeline, cilium monitor eBPF Events, Hubble Verdict Flow, and the Policy Trace Engine
🗺️ The 3 Debugging Lenses — How Policy Troubleshooting Tools Work
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  POLICY DEBUGGING — 3 TOOLS, 3 LEVELS OF VISIBILITY                            │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ LEVEL 1: Policy Audit Mode ("What WOULD be blocked?")                │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  CNP YAML → spec.enableAudit: true → Agent marks rule as AUDIT        │   │
│  │  eBPF: Instead of DROP, packet is ALLOWED + AUDIT event emitted      │   │
│  │  Hubble: observe --verdict AUDIT shows all "would be dropped" flows  │   │
│  │  Workflow: Audit → Monitor 1-7 days → Change to enforce → DROP       │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ LEVEL 2: cilium monitor (Raw eBPF Events — Kernel-Level)              │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  cilium monitor --type drop → subscribes to Agent's gRPC event stream │   │
│  │  Shows: DROP/POLICY_DENIED events with src/dst identities             │   │
│  │  Use when: "Is my policy actually dropping packets?"                  │   │
│  │  Key filter: --from-pod ns/name --to-pod ns/name                     │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ LEVEL 3: Hubble Observe (Enriched Flows — Application-Level)          │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  hubble observe --from-pod anihpj/web-xxx --verdict DROPPED           │   │
│  │  Shows: pod names, HTTP methods, DNS queries, policy verdicts         │   │
│  │  Hubble enriches raw eBPF events with: pod names, namespace, identity │   │
│  │  Use when: "Why can't my pod reach this service?"                     │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  AUDIT → ENFORCE WORKFLOW (THE GOLDEN RULE):                                  │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. Write policy with enableAudit: true                                │   │
│  │ 2. Deploy → hubble observe --verdict AUDIT → see what WOULD break    │   │
│  │ 3. Adjust policy rules based on audit observations                    │   │
│  │ 4. After 1-7 days of clean audit logs → remove enableAudit            │   │
│  │ 5. Policy now ENFORCES (DROP instead of AUDIT)                        │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 cilium policy trace — How Policy Simulation Works
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  cilium policy trace — Simulating Traffic Without Sending Packets               │
│                                                                              │
│  $ cilium policy trace -s <src-pod> -d <dst-pod> --dport 5432 --proto TCP  │
│                                                                              │
│  WHAT IT DOES (step by step):                                                  │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. Agent receives trace request via gRPC (cilium.sock)                │   │
│  │ 2. Resolves source pod label → finds matching endpoints + identities  │   │
│  │ 3. Resolves destination pod label → finds matching endpoints          │   │
│  │ 4. For EACH (src endpoint, dst endpoint) pair:                        │   │
│  │    a. Looks up policy map: is (srcID → dstID:dport/proto) allowed?    │   │
│  │    b. Checks CNP rules → CCNP rules → K8s NetPol → default            │   │
│  │    c. Checks L7 rules if applicable (HTTP path, method, headers)      │   │
│  │ 5. Returns: ALLOWED (which rule matched) or DENIED (why it was denied)│   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ NO ACTUAL PACKETS ARE SENT — pure simulation against eBPF maps!       │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  EXAMPLE OUTPUT:                                                               │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ $ cilium policy trace -s app=anihpj -d app=postgres --dport 5432     │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Tracing from any endpoint with label app=anihpj                       │   │
│  │   to any endpoint with label app=postgres                             │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  [anihpj/web-xxx (ID:12345)] =>                                      │   │
│  │  [postgres-0 (ID:67890)]:5432/TCP                                     │   │
│  │    ✅ ALLOWED                                                          │   │
│  │    Rule: CNP "protect-postgres" (anihpj namespace)                    │   │
│  │    Ingress rule: fromEndpoints app=anihpj toPorts 5432                │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  [random-pod (ID:99999)] =>                                           │   │
│  │  [postgres-0 (ID:67890)]:5432/TCP                                     │   │
│  │    ❌ DENIED                                                            │   │
│  │    Reason: No policy rule allows ID 99999 → ID 67890 on port 5432     │   │
│  │    Default deny (pod is policy-enabled)                               │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  WHEN TO USE vs OTHER TOOLS:                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ cilium policy trace │ BEFORE applying — "Will this policy work?"      │  │
│  │ cilium monitor      │ DURING debugging — "What's happening NOW?"       │  │
│  │ hubble observe      │ AFTER the fact — "What happened in the last 1h?" │  │
│  └─────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🗺️ Debugging Decision Tree — Which Tool for Which Symptom
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  POLICY DEBUGGING DECISION TREE — Start Here Every Time                         │
│                                                                              │
│  SYMPTOM: "Pod X cannot reach Service Y"                                      │
│  │                                                                           │
│  ├─▶ STEP 1: Is DNS resolving?                                                │
│  │   kubectl exec pod-X -- nslookup service-Y                                │
│  │   ├── NO → DNS issue: check CoreDNS, check egress UDP 53 policy           │
│  │   └── YES → continue                                                       │
│  │                                                                           │
│  ├─▶ STEP 2: Is traffic being dropped by policy?                              │
│  │   hubble observe --from-pod ns/X --to-pod ns/Y --verdict DROPPED          │
│  │   ├── YES (DROPPED shown) → POLICY ISSUE → go to Step 3                   │
│  │   └── NO (no flows at all) → ROUTING/DNS issue → check routes, endpoints  │
│  │                                                                           │
│  ├─▶ STEP 3: WHICH policy is blocking?                                         │
│  │   cilium endpoint inspect <dst-endpoint-id> → see "Active Policies"     │
│  │   ├── CNP found → check its rules (kubectl describe cnp -n ns name)       │
│  │   ├── CCNP found → check its rules (kubectl describe ccnp name)           │
│  │   └── Neither → K8s NetPol might be the cause → check kubectl get netpol  │
│  │                                                                           │
│  ├─▶ STEP 4: Simulate the fix                                                 │
│  │   cilium policy trace -s <src-labels> -d <dst-labels> --dport <port>   │
│  │   ├── Shows ALLOWED → policy should work but isn't → label mismatch?      │
│  │   └── Shows DENIED → confirms which rule needs to be changed              │
│  │                                                                           │
│  └─▶ STEP 5: Fix and verify                                                   │
│      ├── Edit CNP/CCNP YAML → kubectl apply                                   │
│      ├── cilium policy trace again → should show ALLOWED                     │
│      ├── kubectl exec pod-X -- curl service-Y → should work!                 │
│      └── hubble observe --verdict FORWARDED → confirm traffic flows          │
│                                                                              │
│  TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:                                                         │
│  ┌────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ hubble observe     │ "What happened?" — historical + real-time flows    │  │
│  │ cilium monitor     │ "What's happening NOW?" — raw kernel events        │  │
│  │ cilium policy trace│ "What WOULD happen?" — simulation, no packets      │  │
│  │ cilium endpoint    │ "What state is my pod in?" — identity, policies    │  │
│  │ kubectl describe   │ "What does my YAML say?" — the source of truth     │  │
│  └────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CCA Insight: Policy debugging is a critical CCA skill. Know when to use each tool: cilium monitor for raw kernel-level drops (fast, low detail), Hubble for enriched application-level flows (slower, high detail), and audit mode for safe policy testing. The #1 exam scenario: "A pod can't connect — debug it." Answer: hubble observe --from-pod X --verdict DROPPED → identify which policy rule → cilium policy get → fix the CNP. For pre-deployment validation, cilium policy trace simulates traffic against live eBPF maps WITHOUT sending packets — the safest way to test a policy before applying it.

📝 Chapter 8 — CCA Practice Questions (4 Questions)

Q1
When would you use CCNP instead of CNP? Give 3 examples.
Show Answer
Answer

1) Block cloud metadata access cluster-wide, 2) Allow monitoring namespace to access all namespaces, 3) Enforce DNS policy across all namespaces. CCNP is for rules that apply everywhere; CNP is namespace-specific.

Q2
Can a CNP override a CCNP? Which takes precedence?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes, CNP takes precedence over CCNP. Cilium checks CNP first. If a CNP rule matches, it's used. Only if no CNP rule matches does Cilium fall back to CCNP. More specific (namespace-scoped) wins.

Q3
How do you block all pods from accessing 169.254.169.254 using a CCNP?
Show Answer
Answer

Create a CCNP with endpointSelector: {} (all pods) and egress: toCIDR: [169.254.169.254/32] with no matching allow rules — Cilium's default is deny, so this blocks all traffic to that IP.

Q4
What's the YAML kind for a cluster-wide policy?
Show Answer
Answer

CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy (CCNP). Unlike CNP, CCNP has no namespace field in metadata because it applies cluster-wide.

Q5
What is policy audit mode and when should you use it?
Show Answer
Answer

Audit mode (enableAudit: true) logs policy violations WITHOUT blocking traffic. Use it to test new policies before enforcing them — you can see what WOULD be blocked without actually breaking anything. Check audit logs with hubble observe --verdict AUDIT.

Q6
How do you write a CCNP that blocks all pods from accessing external IP 169.254.169.254?
Show Answer
Answer

Create a CCNP with endpointSelector: {} (all pods) and an empty egress: [] that implicitly denies everything, or explicitly deny with toCIDR: [169.254.169.254/32] in an egress rule with no allow counterpart.

Q7
How does Cilium handle policy rule conflicts between multiple CNPs selecting the same pod?
Show Answer
Answer

Rules are UNIONED — the pod gets the MOST permissive combination. If CNP-A allows port 80 and CNP-B allows port 443, the pod gets BOTH. Unlike firewalls where last rule wins, Cilium policies ADD together.

Q8
What's the difference between toEndpoints and toCIDR in egress rules?
Show Answer
Answer

toEndpoints matches by pod labels (identity-based) — survives pod restarts. toCIDR matches by IP address range — simpler but breaks if IPs change. Use toEndpoints for internal traffic (pods), toCIDR for external traffic (services outside the cluster).

Q9
Can a CCNP have a namespace field? Why or why not?
Show Answer
Answer

No, CCNP has NO namespace field because it applies cluster-wide — there's no namespace to scope to. If you need namespace-scoped rules, use CNP (CiliumNetworkPolicy) instead. CCNP is for rules that span every namespace.

Q10
You have a default-deny-all CCNP. How do you allow Prometheus in the monitoring namespace to scrape metrics from all pods?
Show Answer
Answer

Create a CCNP with endpointSelector: {} and an ingress rule allowing fromEndpoints with matchLabels: {app: prometheus, io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: monitoring} on the metrics port (9090). The namespace label ensures only Prometheus from the monitoring namespace gets access.

🌐 Part 5: Service Mesh & Load Balancing Chapters 10-12 · CCA 20%

Chapter 10: Cilium's Built-In Service Mesh — No Sidecar Required!

Traditional service meshes like Istio add a sidecar proxy (Envoy) to every pod — that's 200MB+ of extra RAM per pod. Cilium's service mesh runs entirely in the kernel via eBPF — zero sidecars, zero extra containers, zero RAM overhead. This chapter shows you how Cilium delivers mTLS, canary deployments, and traffic splitting at kernel-native speed.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔀 Mesh 🎯 CCA 20%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What a service mesh is and why traditional ones are heavy
  • ✅ How Cilium's sidecar-less mesh works at the kernel level
  • ✅ Enabling mTLS between anihpj services without sidecars
  • ✅ Canary deployments with identity-based traffic splitting
🎓 CCA Relevance
Service Mesh 20% CRITICAL: Sidecar-less Architecture

10.1 What is a Service Mesh? (And Why Traditional Ones Are Heavy)

A service mesh solves three problems for microservices: secure communication (mTLS), traffic control (canary, retries, timeouts), and observability (metrics, traces). Traditional meshes like Istio/Linkerd do this by injecting a sidecar proxy container into every pod:

Sidecar Mesh vs Cilium Sidecar-less Mesh
  ISTIO (Sidecar Mesh)                     CILIUM (Sidecar-less)
  ┌─────────────────────────┐             ┌─────────────────────┐
  │         POD              │             │        POD          │
  │  ┌──────┐ ┌──────────┐  │             │  ┌──────┐          │
  │  │ App  │ │  Envoy   │  │             │  │ App  │          │
  │  │100MB │ │  200MB   │  │             │  │100MB │          │
  │  └──┬───┘ └────┬─────┘  │             │  └──┬───┘          │
  │     └──localhost──┘     │             │     │ eBPF kernel  │
  │      extra hop! 😱      │             │     │ 0 MB extra   │
  └─────────────────────────┘             │     │ ⚡ native!   │
  ❌ 200MB overhead per pod               └─────────────────────┘
  ❌ Extra network hop (latency)          ✅ 0 MB overhead
  ❌ Complex to manage + upgrade          ✅ No extra hop
                                          ✅ Kernel-native speed
🔴 The Sidecar Problem — By The Numbers

In a 100-pod cluster with Istio, that's 20GB of RAM just for sidecars. Each request takes an extra network hop (app→localhost→sidecar→network), adding ~0.5ms latency. When you upgrade Istio, you must restart EVERY pod. Cilium eliminates all of this — the eBPF programs are already in the kernel, waiting for packets.

10.2 How Cilium Service Mesh Works Under the Hood

Cilium uses eBPF programs attached at the socket level to intercept, inspect, and route L7 traffic — entirely in the kernel. No proxy process, no context switch to userspace:

What "socket level" means in plain English: When your application calls connect("postgres", 5432), that's a Linux syscall. Normally, this goes straight to the TCP stack. Cilium's eBPF program intercepts this syscall before the TCP stack sees it. At this point, the eBPF program can: check the destination identity, verify mTLS certificates, apply L7 policy rules, select a backend via Maglev hashing, and encrypt with WireGuard — all before a single TCP packet is created. The application code never knows this happened — it just gets a connection to postgres:5432.

eBPF Socket-Level Service Mesh
  APP (anihpj) wants to call postgres:5432
       │ connect("postgres", 5432)
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  eBPF SOCKET PROGRAM (kernel level)           │
  │                                               │
  │  ① Intercept connect() syscall               │
  │  ② Look up destination identity (ID:67890)   │
  │  ③ mTLS: Perform handshake with cert         │
  │  ④ Policy: Allow ID:12345→ID:67890? ✅       │
  │  ⑤ Load balance: Maglev hash → 10.0.1.99     │
  │  ⑥ Encrypt: WireGuard (if enabled)           │
  │  ⑦ Forward: Direct socket connection         │
  │                                               │
  │  ⏱️ All 7 steps in ~10 microseconds          │
  │  💡 No userspace process involved!            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

10.3 Enabling Mutual TLS (mTLS) for anihpj

Mutual TLS (mTLS) means BOTH sides of a connection prove their identity with certificates — the client verifies the server AND the server verifies the client. Cilium automates certificate issuance and rotation using cert-manager or its built-in SPIFFE-based certificate authority:

cilium-config — Enable mTLS 
# Enable mTLS cluster-wide with one flag:
cilium install --set encryption.enabled=true \
               --set encryption.type=wireguard \
               --set authentication.mutual.spire.enabled=true

# Or patch an existing installation:
cilium config set authentication-mutual-spire-enabled true

# Verify mTLS is working:
cilium status | grep Authentication
# → Authentication: OK (SPIFFE)
🔐 How Cilium mTLS Works — 4 Steps

1. Identity Provisioning: SPIFFE assigns each pod a cryptographic identity based on its labels (e.g., spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/default).

2. Certificate Issuance: Cilium's SPIRE agent automatically issues short-lived X.509 certificates to each pod.

3. Automatic Rotation: Certificates are rotated before expiry — no pod restarts, no application changes.

4. eBPF Enforcement: The eBPF socket program performs the TLS handshake at the kernel level. Application code doesn't change — it still calls connect("postgres", 5432).

10.4 Traffic Management — Canary Deployments with Cilium

A canary deployment sends a small percentage of traffic to a new version (v2) while keeping most traffic on the stable version (v1). If v2 has no errors, gradually increase its traffic share. Cilium does this with identity-based traffic splitting — no sidecar, no Envoy, just eBPF:

Canary Deployment — 90% v1 / 10% v2
  USER REQUESTS → INGRESS → eBPF LOAD BALANCER
                                │
                    ┌───────────┴───────────┐
                    │   Traffic Split       │
                    │   90%       10%        │
                    ▼           ▼
  ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────┐
  │ anihpj v1 (stable)  │ │ anihpj v2 (canary)  │
  │ Identity: 12345     │ │ Identity: 12346     │
  │ Label: version:v1   │ │ Label: version:v2   │
  └─────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────┘

  POLICY: 90% of traffic → ID:12345 | 10% → ID:12346
  If v2 errors > 1% → auto-rollback to 100% v1
🎯 Why Identity-Based Canary is Superior

Traditional canary deployments use IP-based routing — fragile and manual. Cilium's identity-based approach means: (1) Pods can restart with new IPs — same identity, same routing. (2) Traffic splitting is enforced at the kernel level — no proxy latency. (3) New pods automatically get the correct identity based on labels — zero manual configuration.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 10

❌ MISTAKE 1: Thinking you need Istio for mTLS → Cilium handles mTLS at the kernel level with SPIFFE/SPIRE — no sidecars needed.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Assuming canary deployments need a service mesh → Cilium's identity-based traffic splitting works at the eBPF socket level without any mesh infrastructure.
