📊 Gateway API vs Ingress — Cilium's Next-Gen Routing
FeatureK8s IngressGateway API (Cilium)
HTTP Header Matching❌ Not supported✅ Route by headers (e.g., canary: v2)
Weighted Traffic Splitting❌ Not supported✅ 90% stable, 10% canary
Cross-Namespace Routing❌ Same namespace only✅ Route to any namespace
Role-Based Access❌ Anyone can edit✅ Gateway admin vs route author RBAC
TCP/UDP Routing❌ HTTP/HTTPS only✅ L4 routing for non-HTTP protocols
Cilium IntegrationBasic (via Ingress controller)✅ Native CiliumEnvoyConfig + NetworkPolicies
Enable--set ingressController.enabled=true--set gatewayAPI.enabled=true
🔑 CCA Insight: Cilium's service mesh is "sidecar-less" — no injection, no sidecar containers, no pod restarts. One Envoy proxy per NODE handles L7 traffic for all pods on that node. eBPF redirects only the traffic that needs L7 processing (HTTP/gRPC/Kafka). All other traffic stays in kernel. This is fundamentally different from Istio/Linkerd where every pod gets its own sidecar. CiliumEnvoyConfig (CEC) CRD configures the per-node Envoy — it's like VirtualService + DestinationRule combined.

📝 Chapter 9 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What's the first thing to check when a pod can't connect to another service?
Show Answer
Answer

DNS resolution. Run nslookup or dig from the pod to verify it can resolve the service name. If DNS fails, check CoreDNS and any policies blocking UDP 53.

Q2
How do you see policy verdicts in real time with identity information?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium monitor --type policy-verdict — shows source/destination pod names, identities, ports, and verdict (FORWARDED/DROPPED/AUDIT) for every policy decision.

Q3
What happens if a label selector in a CNP doesn't match any pods?
Show Answer
Answer

The policy applies to ZERO pods — it has no effect. Always verify your selectors with kubectl get pods -l <your-labels> to ensure they match the intended pods.

Q4
You apply a policy and suddenly all pods lose connectivity. What's the most likely cause?
Show Answer
Answer

Too restrictive — likely blocking DNS (UDP 53) or using a default-deny without explicit allows. Fix: rollback the policy, add audit mode, then gradually add explicit allow rules.

Q5
How do you check if a specific policy is actually being enforced on a pod?
Show Answer
Answer

Use cilium endpoint inspect <id> to see all policies applied to that endpoint. Or use hubble observe --from-pod ns/pod --verdict DROPPED to verify the policy is dropping the traffic you expect.

Q6
What does cilium policy trace do and when should you use it?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium policy trace simulates traffic between two endpoints to show whether it would be allowed or denied — without actually sending packets. Use it to test policies before applying them or to debug why specific traffic is blocked.

Q7
Your anihpj frontend can reach the backend, but the backend can't reach PostgreSQL. What's the debugging sequence?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Check DNS: kubectl exec backend-pod -- nslookup postgres. 2. Check policy: hubble observe --from-pod anihpj/backend-xxx --to-port 5432 --verdict DROPPED. 3. Check policy selectors: cilium policy get -n anihpj. 4. Check the backend egress rules for database access.

Q8
How can you test a policy before enforcing it in production?
Show Answer
Answer

Use audit mode (enableAudit: true in the policy spec). This logs violations without blocking. Observe audit logs via Hubble, verify the policy catches what you expect, then remove enableAudit to enforce.

Q9
What's the difference between cilium monitor and hubble observe for policy debugging?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium monitor shows raw eBPF events from ONE node — use for low-level per-node debugging. hubble observe shows cluster-wide flows through Hubble Relay — better for cross-node policy debugging.

Q10
Why might a CiliumNetworkPolicy appear to "not work" even though the YAML is correct?
Show Answer
Answer

Three common reasons: (1) Forgot DNS egress rule — pods can't resolve names, (2) Another CNP is unioning with yours — policies ADD, they don't replace, (3) Label selectors don't match. Always check with hubble observe --verdict DROPPED.

9.6 CiliumCIDRGroup & CiliumEndpointSlice — Advanced Policy & Scalability CRDs

Two important CRDs extend Cilium's network policy capabilities: CiliumCIDRGroup (CCG) simplifies managing large sets of external CIDRs, and CiliumEndpointSlice (CES) improves scalability in large clusters by batching endpoint updates.

📦 CiliumCIDRGroup (CCG) — Group External CIDRs

Instead of listing dozens of CIDRs in every CiliumNetworkPolicy, define them once in a CCG and reference by name or label:

CCG: Centralize CIDR Management, Reference in Policies
  WITHOUT CCG (painful):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CNP-1: fromCIDRs: [10.48.0.0/24, 10.16.0.0/24, ...]       │
  │  CNP-2: fromCIDRs: [10.48.0.0/24, 10.16.0.0/24, ...]  ← DUPLICATED!
  │  CNP-3: fromCIDRs: [10.48.0.0/24, 10.16.0.0/24, ...]       │
  │  Change one CIDR → must update ALL policies                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WITH CCG (clean):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CiliumCIDRGroup: vpn-example-1                             │
  │    spec.externalCIDRs: [10.48.0.0/24, 10.16.0.0/24]         │
  │    labels: {role: vpn}                                      │
  │                          │                                   │
  │         ┌────────────────┼──────────────────┐               │
  │         ▼                ▼                  ▼               │
  │  CNP-1: cidrGroupRef  CNP-2: cidrGroupRef  CNP-3           │
  │         vpn-example-1        vpn-example-1                  │
  │                                                             │
  │  Change CCG once → all policies update automatically!       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
YAML — Defining and Using CiliumCIDRGroup
# Step 1: Define the CIDR group
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2alpha1
kind: CiliumCIDRGroup
metadata:
  name: vpn-example-1
  labels:
    role: vpn
spec:
  externalCIDRs:
    - "10.48.0.0/24"
    - "10.16.0.0/24"
---
# Step 2: Reference in CNP by name OR label
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: from-vpn
spec:
  endpointSelector: {}
  ingress:
  - fromCIDRSet:
    - cidrGroupRef: vpn-example-1        # By name
    # OR:
    - cidrGroupSelector:                  # By label
        matchLabels:
          role: vpn
💡 Scalability Impact

CCGs create a single security identity per group regardless of how many CIDRs it contains. For large groups, this dramatically reduces identity table size. Hubble flows are annotated with CCG name and labels for easy identification.

📊 CiliumEndpointSlice (CES) — Scalability for Large Clusters

Beta In large clusters (1000+ nodes, 100k+ pods), every new pod creates a CiliumEndpoint (CEP) object that ALL agents must watch — causing API server overload. CES batches CEPs into slices, reducing the number of objects agents must track:

CES: Batching CEPs for Scalability
  WITHOUT CES (100k pods):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  API Server: 100,000 CEP objects                     │
  │  Each agent: watches 100,000 objects                 │
  │  Each new pod: 100,000 watch notifications           │
  │  Result: API server crushed at scale                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WITH CES (100k pods, 100 CEPs per slice):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  API Server: ~1,000 CES objects                      │
  │  Each agent: watches ~1,000 objects (100x fewer!)    │
  │  Cilium Operator: batches CEPs → CES                 │
  │  Trade-off: Slightly longer identity propagation     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Shell — Enable CES (Operator first, then Agents)
# 1. Enable CES on Operator first
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.5 \
  --namespace kube-system --reuse-values \
  --set ciliumEndpointSlice.enabled=true

# 2. Verify CRD registered
kubectl get crd ciliumendpointslices.cilium.io

# 3. Verify CES objects created
kubectl get ces
# NAME                  AGE
# ces-2fvynpvzn-4ncg9   1m17s

# 4. Then upgrade agents
# Agents automatically switch to watching CES instead of CEPs

# Optional: Prioritize critical namespaces
kubectl annotate ns anihpj cilium.io/ces-namespace=priority
⚠️ CES Limitations

• Not compatible with Egress Gateway — if you use Egress Gateway, keep CES disabled.
• CEPs must be enabled (don't set --disable-endpoint-crd=true).
• CES is a Cilium-specific concept — not related to Kubernetes EndpointSlice (they solve different problems: CES for policy/routing, K8s EndpointSlice for Service backends).

💡 CCA Exam Tip — CCG & CES

CiliumCIDRGroup: CRD for grouping external CIDRs. Referenced via cidrGroupRef (by name) or cidrGroupSelector (by label). Creates one identity per group. Purpose: simplify policy management and improve scalability.
CiliumEndpointSlice: Beta CRD for batching CEPs. Operator creates CES, agents watch CES instead of individual CEPs. Purpose: reduce API server load in large clusters. Migration: upgrade Operator first, then Agents.

📝 Chapter 9 — Advanced CRDs Practice Questions (5 Additional)

CQ1
What problem does CiliumCIDRGroup solve?
Show Answer
Answer

It centralizes management of external CIDR blocks. Instead of repeating CIDRs across multiple CiliumNetworkPolicies, define them once in a CCG and reference by name (cidrGroupRef) or label (cidrGroupSelector). Change the CCG and all referencing policies update.

CQ2
How does CiliumEndpointSlice help with scalability?
Show Answer
Answer

CES batches individual CiliumEndpoint (CEP) objects into slices. Instead of every agent watching 100k+ CEP objects, they watch ~1k CES objects. The Cilium Operator handles the batching. This reduces API server load significantly in large clusters.

CQ3
What's the migration order for enabling CES?
Show Answer
Answer

Operator first, then Agents. Enable CES on Operator → let it create all CES objects → verify with kubectl get ces → then upgrade Agents to watch CES. For downgrade: disable on Agents first, then Operator.

CQ4
Is CiliumEndpointSlice related to Kubernetes EndpointSlice?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Despite the similar name, they solve different problems: K8s EndpointSlice tracks Service backends for load balancing. CiliumEndpointSlice batches CiliumEndpoint (CEP) objects for network routing and policy decisions. Enabling one doesn't affect the other.

CQ5
How do you prioritize policy updates for critical namespaces with CES?
Show Answer
Answer

Annotate the namespace with cilium.io/ces-namespace=priority. This tells the Operator to process CEP updates from that namespace before non-priority namespaces, ensuring faster policy enforcement for critical workloads like production anihpj.

Chapter 11: Cilium as kube-proxy Replacement — Faster Load Balancing

kube-proxy is Kubernetes' built-in service load balancer — and it's one of the biggest performance bottlenecks in any cluster. Cilium replaces kube-proxy entirely with eBPF socket-level load balancing, delivering O(1) hash lookups instead of O(n) iptables rule walking. For large clusters with 100+ services, this is the difference between microsecond and multi-second service updates.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours ⚖️ Load Balancing 🎯 CCA Core

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ How kube-proxy works and why it's slow (iptables vs IPVS)
  • ✅ How Cilium's eBPF load balancer replaces kube-proxy
  • ✅ Maglev consistent hashing — even distribution + connection affinity
  • ✅ How to enable, verify, and test kube-proxy replacement
🎓 CCA Relevance
Service Mesh 20% kube-proxy Replacement
kube-proxy Replacement is a Key CCA Topic
  • O(n) vs O(1): iptables walks rules sequentially; eBPF does hash lookups. Know this difference cold.
  • Maglev Hashing: Understand why consistent hashing matters — backend changes affect only ~1/N connections.
  • KubeProxyReplacement Modes: "Strict" (fully eBPF) vs "Partial" (fallback to kube-proxy for some features).
  • Verification: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep kube-proxy should return NOTHING after enabling replacement.

11.1 How kube-proxy Works (and Why It's Slow)

kube-proxy watches the Kubernetes API for Services and Endpoints, then programs iptables rules on every node to implement load balancing. The problem: iptables rules are evaluated sequentially — every packet must walk through every rule until it finds a match:

📖 A simple analogy: Imagine a security guard checking IDs at a building with 5000 employees. With iptables (O(n)), the guard checks each person against a list of 5000 names — one by one — until finding a match. With eBPF (O(1)), the guard has a lookup table — "Bob → desk 42" — and finds the answer instantly, regardless of how many employees there are. Now imagine doing this for every single packet — millions per second. That's why iptables doesn't scale and eBPF does.

kube-proxy iptables — O(n) Rule Walking
  PACKET: dst=10.96.42.100:8000 (anihpj ClusterIP)
       │
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  iptables nat PREROUTING chain               │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ RULE 1:   dst 10.96.0.10:53 → DNS ❌    │ │
  │  │ RULE 2:   dst 10.96.0.1:443 → API ❌    │ │
  │  │ RULE 3:   dst 10.96.42.100:8000 → ✅    │ │
  │  │ ...                                       │ │
  │  │ RULE 5000: dst 10.96.99.50:9090 → ❌     │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                               │
  │  😱 5000 rules × every packet = SLOW          │
  │  😱 Adding 1 service = rewrite ALL rules      │
  │  😱 100+ services = 30+ second updates        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  IPVS MODE (better but still netfilter):
  • Uses hash table → O(1) lookup
  • BUT: Still goes through netfilter/conntrack
  • Limited to L4 (no L7 awareness)
  • Connection tracking table can overflow

11.2 Cilium's eBPF Load Balancer — How It Replaces kube-proxy

Cilium's eBPF load balancer operates at the socket level, before packets even enter the TCP/IP stack. Services are stored in eBPF hash maps — lookup is O(1) regardless of how many services you have. Maglev consistent hashing ensures even backend distribution and connection affinity:

terminal — Before vs After kube-proxy Replacement 
# BEFORE: kube-proxy running (iptables mode)
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep kube-proxy
kube-proxy-abcde   1/1  Running
kube-proxy-fghij   1/1  Running
kube-proxy-klmno   1/1  Running

$ iptables -t nat -L | wc -l
5234   # ← 5000+ rules! Takes 30 seconds to list!

# AFTER: Cilium kube-proxy replacement enabled
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep kube-proxy
(no output — kube-proxy is GONE!) ⚡

$ cilium service list
ID   Frontend            Backend
1    10.96.0.10:53       kube-dns
2    10.96.42.100:8000   anihpj:8000 (3 endpoints)
3    10.96.99.50:9090    prometheus:9090
# Instant output — O(1) eBPF map lookup!
🔑 Maglev Hashing — Why It Matters

Maglev is a consistent hashing algorithm developed by Google. It ensures: (1) Backend changes only affect ~1/N of connections (not all), (2) Connections to the same 5-tuple always go to the same backend (affinity), (3) Load is evenly distributed across backends. When a backend pod dies, only its connections are rehashed — all other connections remain undisturbed.

📡 How Cilium Handles Each Service Type

ClusterIP: eBPF socket-level NAT — connect() syscall is intercepted and destination IP:port is rewritten before the packet enters the TCP stack. No iptables, no netfilter.

NodePort: eBPF programs attached to the host network namespace intercept packets arriving at the NodePort. The packet is DNAT'd to the backend pod — all in kernel eBPF.

ExternalIPs: eBPF programs answer ARP requests for the external IP and route incoming traffic to backend pods. Combined with BGP, this provides full external load balancing.

11.3 Enabling kube-proxy Replacement

Enabling kube-proxy replacement is a single flag during installation. Cilium automatically detects your cluster's capabilities and uses the best mode:

terminal — Enable & Verify 
# Install with kube-proxy replacement:
cilium install --set kubeProxyReplacement=true

# Verify kube-proxy is gone:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep kube-proxy
# (should show NO pods)

# Verify Cilium is handling services:
cilium service list
# Should show ALL your Kubernetes Services

# Run connectivity test to confirm:
cilium connectivity test
# → All service tests should pass ✅
⚠️ kube-proxy Replacement Requirements

Requires Linux kernel ≥ 5.10 with eBPF cgroup/sock support. Not all cloud providers support it (check Cilium's compatibility matrix). If unsupported, Cilium gracefully falls back to the standard kube-proxy integration mode. Use cilium status to check: look for "KubeProxyReplacement: Strict" (fully enabled) vs "Partial" (limited mode).

⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 11

❌ MISTAKE 1: Not checking kernel compatibility → kube-proxy replacement requires kernel ≥ 5.10 with cgroup/sock eBPF support. Check cilium status for "KubeProxyReplacement: Strict" vs "Partial".

❌ MISTAKE 2: Forgetting to verify → After enabling, always run cilium connectivity test to confirm services are working through eBPF, not iptables.

🔧 Under the Hood — How Cilium's eBPF Load Balancer Replaces kube-proxy: Maglev Consistent Hashing, Socket-Level LB, Direct Server Return, and Why It's O(1)
🗺️ eBPF Load Balancer Architecture — Socket-Level vs Netfilter
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  kube-proxy (iptables) vs Cilium eBPF Load Balancer                           │
│                                                                              │
│  kube-proxy/iptables PATH:                                                    │
│  App → socket() → TCP stack → Netfilter (PREROUTING) →                      │
│  → Walk ALL iptables rules (O(n)) → DNAT to backend →                       │
│  → conntrack table update → forward                                          │
│  Each step: context switch, spinlock contention at scale                     │
│                                                                              │
│  Cilium eBPF PATH (Socket-Level LB):                                          │
│  App → socket() → CILIUM eBPF INTERCEPTS HERE! →                            │
│  → Hash lookup: ServiceIP:Port → Maglev backend (O(1)) →                    │
│  → Rewrite destination at socket level → DIRECT to backend pod              │
│  → NO netfilter, NO conntrack, NO context switches                           │
│                                                                              │
│  MAGLEV CONSISTENT HASHING:                                                    │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ • Each backend pod gets MULTIPLE positions on a hash ring             │   │
│  │ • Connection 5-tuple → hash → nearest backend position on ring       │   │
│  │ • Backend failure → only 1/N connections disrupted (not ALL!)        │   │
│  │ • Backend addition → minimal redistribution                          │   │
│  │ • Connection affinity: same 5-tuple → same backend (sticky)          │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  RING: [A B A C B C A B C ...]  (each backend appears multiple times) │   │
│  │  Connection X → hash → position 47 → backend B                       │   │
│  │  Connection Y → hash → position 12 → backend A                       │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  DIRECT SERVER RETURN (DSR) — No Reverse Path Through LB:                     │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ WITHOUT DSR: Client → LB → Backend → LB → Client (LB bottlenecks!)   │   │
│  │ WITH DSR:    Client → LB → Backend → Client (direct reply!)          │   │
│  │ Cilium: eBPF rewrites dst MAC at TC hook, backend replies directly   │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 Socket-Level LB — How connect() Interception Works
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SOCKET-LEVEL LOAD BALANCING — Intercepting connect() Before TCP Starts        │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ WITHOUT CILIUM (iptables kube-proxy path):                             │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  Pod app: connect("10.100.50.10", 5432)  ← Service ClusterIP         │   │
│  │  → socket() → TCP handshake to 10.100.50.10:5432                      │   │
│  │  → Kernel routing: "10.100.50.10? That's local!" → OUTPUT chain       │   │
│  │  → iptables KUBE-SERVICES: walk ALL 5000 rules → find match            │   │
│  │  → iptables DNAT: 10.100.50.10:5432 → 10.0.1.7:5432 (backend pod)    │   │
│  │  → conntrack: record mapping for reply packets                         │   │
│  │  → TCP handshake restarts to 10.0.1.7:5432                             │   │
│  │  Steps: syscall → TCP stack → netfilter → DNAT → conntrack = SLOW     │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ WITH CILIUM SOCKET LB (eBPF cgroup/connect4 hook):                    │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  Pod app: connect("10.100.50.10", 5432)  ← Service ClusterIP         │   │
│  │  → syscall connect() ENTERS KERNEL                                     │   │
│  │  → CILIUM eBPF INTERCEPTS HERE (cgroup/connect4 hook!)               │   │
│  │  → eBPF hash lookup: ServiceIP:Port → backend list                     │   │
│  │  → Maglev: selects 10.0.1.7:5432 (backend pod)                        │   │
│  │  → eBPF REWRITES dst IP+Port IN-PLACE in the syscall arguments        │   │
│  │  → connect() proceeds to 10.0.1.7:5432 directly                       │   │
│  │  → NO netfilter, NO iptables, NO conntrack, NO extra syscalls         │   │
│  │  Steps: syscall → eBPF intercept → rewrite → TCP = FAST              │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  KEY ADVANTAGE: The application NEVER knows about the backend pod.           │
│  It asked for 10.100.50.10 but eBPF silently rewrote to 10.0.1.7.           │
│  The TCP handshake happens with the REAL backend, not a proxy.               │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 KPR Modes — Partial vs Strict Comparison
AspectPartial (kubeProxyReplacement=partial)Strict (kubeProxyReplacement=strict)
ClusterIP Services✅ eBPF Socket LB✅ eBPF Socket LB
NodePort Services❌ Falls back to kube-proxy iptables✅ eBPF at TC hook (no iptables!)
ExternalIPs❌ Falls back to kube-proxy✅ eBPF handled
LoadBalancer❌ Falls back to kube-proxy✅ eBPF handled
HostPort❌ Falls back to kube-proxy✅ eBPF handled
Kernel RequirementAny kernel with eBPF supportKernel ≥ 5.10 (full eBPF features)
kube-proxy Still Runs?✅ Yes (handles NodePort etc.)❌ No (can be scaled to 0)
Verifycilium status | grep KPR → "Partial"cilium status | grep KPR → "Strict"
⚡ Performance Benchmarks — Why eBPF Wins at Scale
Metriciptables kube-proxyIPVS kube-proxyCilium eBPF KPR
10 Services~1,000 pps~5,000 pps~50,000 pps
1,000 Services~200 pps~3,000 pps~48,000 pps
10,000 Services~8 pps~1,500 pps~47,000 pps
Rule Update Time~30 seconds~5 seconds~0.1 seconds
CPU at 5K Services80% (1 core saturated)40%5%
Connection TrackingGlobal conntrack table (lock contention)Global conntrackeBPF LRU map (no locks)
🔑 CCA Insight: Cilium's kube-proxy replacement is enabled with a SINGLE flag: --set kubeProxyReplacement=true. All existing Services, NodePorts, and LoadBalancers work without changes. The difference is HOW they work: iptables = O(n) chain walk through 5000+ rules, eBPF = O(1) hash lookup regardless of scale. Maglev ensures minimal disruption during backend changes (only 1/N connections affected). At CCA exam scale questions, always answer: "eBPF is O(1), iptables is O(n)."

📝 Chapter 10 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What's the biggest advantage of Cilium's sidecar-less mesh over Istio?
Show Answer
Answer

Zero RAM overhead per pod (Istio's Envoy uses ~200MB/pod), zero extra network hops (no localhost proxy), and no pod restarts for mesh upgrades. eBPF programs run in the kernel — already present and waiting.

Q2
How does Cilium handle mTLS without sidecars?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium uses SPIFFE for identity provisioning + SPIRE for certificate issuance. eBPF socket programs intercept connect() syscalls and perform TLS handshakes at the kernel level. Certificates are auto-rotated, and application code doesn't change.

Q3
What is a canary deployment and how does Cilium enable it?
Show Answer
Answer

A canary sends a small % of traffic to a new version to test it safely. Cilium uses identity-based traffic splitting — pods with different labels get different identities, and eBPF load balancers distribute traffic by identity. New pods get correct routing automatically based on labels.

Q4
How much RAM overhead does Cilium add per pod for service mesh?
Show Answer
Answer

Zero (0 MB). Cilium's service mesh runs entirely in the kernel via eBPF programs. No sidecar container, no proxy process, no extra memory allocation per pod. Compare to Istio's ~200MB per pod for the Envoy sidecar.

Q5
What's the difference between L4 load balancing and L7 load balancing in Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

L4 (TCP/UDP) is handled by eBPF socket programs — fast, kernel-level, no proxy. L7 (HTTP/gRPC) uses per-node Envoy proxy for protocol-aware routing. L7 adds header-based routing, retries, and rate limiting at the cost of some overhead.

Q6
How do you enable Cilium's Ingress controller? What makes it different from nginx ingress?
Show Answer
Answer

Enable with --set ingressController.enabled=true. Cilium's Ingress uses Envoy (per-node, not per-pod) and integrates with CiliumNetworkPolicies — L7 rules apply to Ingress traffic too. No separate ingress deployment needed; it's built into Cilium.

Q7
What Cilium CRD enables traffic splitting for canary deployments?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium doesn't need a separate CRD for basic canary traffic splitting — it uses Kubernetes standard Services with pod labels. Pods with version: stable and version: canary labels get different Cilium identities, and the Service distributes traffic based on backend pod count. For advanced splitting, use the Gateway API.

Q8
How does Cilium's per-node Envoy differ from Istio's sidecar Envoy?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium runs ONE Envoy per NODE (shared by all pods on that node). Istio runs ONE Envoy per POD (sidecar). Per-node is more efficient: fewer proxy instances, shared memory, less overhead. Traffic reaches Envoy via eBPF redirect — no localhost hop.

Q9
What is Gateway API and how does Cilium support it?
Show Answer
Answer

Gateway API is the next-gen Kubernetes networking API (replacing Ingress). Cilium supports Gateway API for advanced routing: HTTP header matching, weighted traffic splitting, cross-namespace routing. Enable with --set gatewayAPI.enabled=true.

Q10
What happens to existing connections when you deploy a new version of your backend with Cilium's canary approach?
Show Answer
Answer

Existing connections to stable backend pods continue uninterrupted (connection affinity via Maglev). New connections are distributed based on the current backend pod ratio (e.g., 90% stable, 10% canary). No connections are dropped during the rollout.

Chapter 12: BGP and External Load Balancing — Reaching Your Services from Outside

In cloud environments, LoadBalancer services are handled automatically. But in bare metal or on-premise data centers, you need BGP to announce your Service IPs to the physical network. Cilium has built-in BGP support and a LoadBalancer IPAM that works without any cloud provider.

Service Mesh 20% External Connectivity
BGP & LB IPAM — Know When You Need Them
  • Cloud ≠ Bare Metal: EKS/GKE/AKS handle LoadBalancer IPs automatically. BGP is for on-premise/bare metal.
  • CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy: The CRD name — know the apiVersion (cilium.io/v2alpha1) and key fields (localASN, peerAddress, peerASN).
  • LB IPAM Pool: Defined before services are created. Services stay Pending if no pool matches.
  • BGP + LB IPAM: Together they provide cloud-like LoadBalancer on bare metal. LB IPAM assigns the IP, BGP announces it.

12.1 What is BGP? (Border Gateway Protocol — The Internet's Routing Protocol)

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is how the internet routes traffic between networks. Think of it as GPS for network packets — routers use BGP to tell each other "I know how to reach IP range X." Cilium uses BGP to tell your physical network "Service IP 192.168.1.100 can be reached through this Kubernetes node."

BGP — Cilium Announces Service IPs to Physical Network
  INTERNET / CORPORATE NETWORK
       │
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │  UPSTREAM ROUTER             │
  │  Learns via BGP:             │
  │  "192.168.1.100 via Node1"  │
  │  "192.168.1.101 via Node2"  │
  └──────────┬──────────────────┘
             │
    ┌────────┴────────┐
    ▼                 ▼
  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐
  │ NODE 1   │   │ NODE 2   │
  │ Cilium   │   │ Cilium   │
  │ BGP peer │   │ BGP peer │
  │ AS 65001 │   │ AS 65001 │
  └──────────┘   └──────────┘

  External user accesses 192.168.1.100:80
  → Router knows it's at Node1 → forwards → Cilium eBPF LB → pod
🌍 When Do You Need BGP?

Cloud (EKS/GKE/AKS): You DON'T need BGP — the cloud provider handles LoadBalancer IP assignment automatically.

Bare Metal / On-Premise: You NEED BGP — there's no cloud controller to assign external IPs. Cilium's BGP support lets you announce Service IPs to your existing network infrastructure.

Edge / IoT: BGP enables direct service reachability without cloud dependencies.

12.2 Cilium BGP Configuration

Cilium uses the CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy CRD to configure BGP peers. This tells Cilium which routers to peer with and which Service IPs to announce:

bgp-peering-policy.yaml 
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2alpha1
kind: CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy
metadata:
  name: upstream-routers
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    matchLabels:
      kubernetes.io/os: linux
  virtualRouters:
  - localASN: 65001              # Your AS number
    exportPodCIDR: true           # Announce pod IPs too
    serviceSelector:
      matchExpressions:
      - key: somekey
        operator: NotIn
        values: ["never-match"]
    neighbors:
    - peerAddress: "10.0.0.1/32" # Upstream router IP
      peerASN: 65000              # Router's AS number

# What Cilium can advertise via BGP:
#   ✅ LoadBalancer IPs (external access)
#   ✅ ClusterIP ranges (internal service reachability)
#   ✅ Pod CIDRs (direct pod access from outside)
#   ❌ Not for: cloud envs (EKS/GKE/AKS handle this natively)
🌐 BGP Configuration Essentials

localASN: Your private AS number (64512-65534 for private use).

peerAddress: Upstream router IP that Cilium peers with.

peerASN: The router's AS number.

exportPodCIDR: Set to true if you want external access directly to pod IPs (advanced).

serviceSelector: Controls which Service IPs are advertised. Use label selectors to be selective.

12.3 LoadBalancer IPAM (LB IPAM) — External IPs Without a Cloud

LB IPAM lets Cilium assign external IPs to LoadBalancer services without needing a cloud provider. You define an IP pool, and Cilium automatically allocates IPs as services are created:

lb-ipam-config.yaml 
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2alpha1
kind: CiliumLoadBalancerIPPool
metadata:
  name: anihpj-pool
spec:
  blocks:
  - start: "192.168.1.240"
    stop: "192.168.1.250"      # 11 IPs for LoadBalancer
  serviceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj               # Only for anihpj services

# Now create a LoadBalancer service:
# kubectl expose deploy anihpj --port=80 --type=LoadBalancer
# Cilium auto-assigns an IP from 192.168.1.240-250!
💡 BGP + LB IPAM — The Complete External Access Solution

LB IPAM assigns the IP. BGP announces it to the network. Together, they provide cloud-like LoadBalancer functionality on bare metal — no external cloud controller, no MetalLB, no third-party tools. Just Cilium.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 12

❌ MISTAKE 1: Using BGP in cloud environments → Cloud providers handle LoadBalancer IPs automatically. BGP is for bare metal/on-premise only.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Not defining LB IPAM pools before creating LoadBalancer services → Services will stay in Pending state forever. Define the IP pool first.

🔧 Under the Hood — How BGP Peering and L2 Announcements Work: CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy, Route Advertisement, ARP/NDP Responder, and LoadBalancer IPAM
🗺️ BGP vs L2 Announcements — Two Ways to Expose Services
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BGP ROUTE ADVERTISEMENT (Layer 3 — Network-Wide)                              │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────┐  BGP Session (TCP 179)  ┌──────────────────┐                  │
│  │  Cilium  │◄══════════════════════►│  Upstream Router  │                  │
│  │  Node    │  Advertise:            │  (AS 65001)       │                  │
│  │          │  10.96.100.50/32       │                   │                  │
│  │          │  Next-hop: node IP     │  Updates routing  │                  │
│  └──────────┘                        │  table → Internet │                  │
│                                       └──────────────────┘                  │
│                                                                              │
│  HOW IT WORKS:                                                                │
│  1. CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy CRD defines: local ASN, peer IP + ASN, services  │
│  2. Cilium Agent starts BGP session with upstream router                     │
│  3. When a LoadBalancer Service is created with an IP from the BGP pool:     │
│     → Cilium announces /32 route for that Service IP                         │
│     → Next-hop = node's IP (where the service endpoint lives)               │
│  4. Router learns route → forwards traffic to correct node                   │
│  5. Node failure → route withdrawn → router uses alternative path            │
│                                                                              │
│  L2 ANNOUNCEMENTS (Layer 2 — Local Subnet Only):                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  ┌──────────┐   Gratuitous ARP    ┌──────────────┐                    │   │
│  │  │  Cilium  │  "10.96.100.50     │  L2 Switch   │                    │   │
│  │  │  Node    │   is at MAC:AA:BB" │  (no BGP!)   │                    │   │
│  │  │ (Leader) │───────────────────►│              │                    │   │
│  │  └──────────┘                    └──────┬───────┘                    │   │
│  │                                        │                              │   │
│  │  LEADER ELECTION via K8s Lease:        │ Clients on same subnet      │   │
│  │  • One node becomes leader             │ send traffic to leader      │   │
│  │  • Leader responds to ARP "who has IP X?" → "ME!"                     │   │
│  │  • Leader failure → lease expires → new leader → new ARP             │   │
│  │  • Failover: 10-20 seconds                                           │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  COMPARISON:                                                                  │
│  ┌──────────┬────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │ Aspect   │ BGP                │ L2 Announcements                     │    │
│  │ Scope    │ Entire network     │ Local L2 subnet only                 │    │
│  │ Router   │ BGP-capable needed │ ANY L2 switch works                  │    │
│  │ Failover │ ~1-3 seconds       │ ~10-20 seconds (ARP update)          │    │
│  │ Setup    │ Complex (ASN, peer)│ Simple (just enable the feature)     │    │
│  │ Scale    │ Unlimited          │ Limited to subnet size               │    │
│  └──────────┴────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 LB IPAM — How Cilium Assigns External IPs Without a Cloud Provider
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LOADBALANCER IPAM — Automatic External IP Assignment for Bare Metal            │
│                                                                              │
│  WITHOUT LB IPAM:                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ apiVersion: v1                                                         │   │
│  │ kind: Service                                                           │   │
│  │ spec:                                                                   │   │
│  │   type: LoadBalancer                                                    │   │
│  │   → Status: Pending FOREVER (no cloud controller to assign IP!)        │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  WITH LB IPAM (Configured in cilium-config ConfigMap):                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ lb-ipam-cidrs: "192.168.100.0/24"   ← IP pool for LoadBalancer SVcs  │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Service: anihpj-frontend   type: LoadBalancer                          │   │
│  │ → Cilium Operator allocates: 192.168.100.5 from the pool              │   │
│  │ → Service gets ExternalIP: 192.168.100.5                               │   │
│  │ → BGP announces 192.168.100.5/32 to upstream routers                  │   │
│  │ → External clients can now reach the service!                          │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  IP ALLOCATION LIFECYCLE:                                                      │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. User creates LoadBalancer Service (no spec.loadBalancerIP set)    │   │
│  │ 2. Cilium Operator watches Services → detects new LB Service         │   │
│  │ 3. Operator checks LB IPAM pool for available IPs                    │   │
│  │ 4. Allocates next free IP → updates Service.status.loadBalancer      │   │
│  │ 5. Cilium Agent programs eBPF: this IP → backend pods                │   │
│  │ 6. BGP/L2 announces the IP to external network                        │   │
│  │ 7. Service deleted → IP returned to pool → available for reuse       │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔀 BGP Session Lifecycle — From Peering to Route Withdrawal
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BGP SESSION LIFECYCLE — How Cilium Maintains Router Peering                    │
│                                                                              │
│  PHASE 1: SESSION ESTABLISHMENT (TCP 179)                                      │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy CRD applied                                │   │
│  │    localASN: 65001, peerAddress: "10.0.0.1", peerASN: 65000         │   │
│  │ 2. Cilium Agent on matching node opens TCP connection to 10.0.0.1:179│   │
│  │ 3. BGP OPEN message: exchange AS numbers, hold timer, capabilities   │   │
│  │ 4. BGP KEEPALIVE: periodic (30s default) — "I'm still here"          │   │
│  │ 5. Session state: IDLE → CONNECT → ACTIVE → ESTABLISHED              │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  PHASE 2: ROUTE ADVERTISEMENT                                                  │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. LoadBalancer Service created with external IP 192.168.100.5       │   │
│  │ 2. Cilium Agent: "I have a route to 192.168.100.5/32"               │   │
│  │ 3. BGP UPDATE message: NLRI=192.168.100.5/32, NEXT_HOP=node IP       │   │
│  │ 4. Router adds route to its forwarding table                         │   │
│  │ 5. Router propagates to other BGP peers (if configured)              │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  PHASE 3: FAILURE DETECTION + ROUTE WITHDRAWAL                                 │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. Node goes down → BGP KEEPALIVE missed (hold timer expires)        │   │
│  │ 2. Router detects session DOWN → removes ALL routes from that node   │   │
│  │ 3. If another node also advertises same IP (ECMP/anycast):           │   │
│  │    → Router switches to alternative next-hop automatically            │   │
│  │ 4. If no alternative: traffic to Service IP → BLACKHOLE               │   │
│  │ 5. Node recovers → re-establishes BGP session → re-advertises routes │   │
│  │ 6. Failover time: BGP hold timer (default 90s) + convergence        │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  L2 ANNOUNCEMENT LEADER ELECTION (detailed):                                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ • Uses K8s Lease API (coordination.k8s.io/v1)                         │   │
│  │ • Lease name: "cilium-l2announce-{service-name}"                     │   │
│  │ • Each node tries to acquire lease → ONE wins → becomes leader       │   │
│  │ • Leader responds to ARP "who has Service IP?" → "ME! (MAC:...)"    │   │
│  │ • Non-leader nodes: DO NOT respond to ARP for that IP                 │   │
│  │ • Leader renews lease every leaseDurationSeconds/2 (default 7.5s)    │   │
│  │ • Leader dies → lease expires after leaseDurationSeconds (15s)       │   │
│  │ • Another node acquires lease → new leader → Gratuitous ARP           │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🗺️ Decision Tree — BGP vs L2 vs Cloud LoadBalancer
EnvironmentRecommended ApproachWhy
EKS/AKS/GKECloud LoadBalancer (automatic)Cloud controller assigns external IP, creates cloud LB — zero config
Bare metal + BGP routerCilium BGP + LB IPAMFull network reachability, fast failover (1-3s), enterprise-grade
Bare metal + L2 switch onlyCilium L2 Announcements + LB IPAMWorks with ANY switch, simple setup, local subnet reachability
Multi-cloud / HybridCluster Mesh + BGPCross-cluster Service discovery, global load balancing
Edge / IoT / LabNodePort or L2 AnnouncementsMinimal infrastructure requirements, works without routers
Data center with MetalLBReplace MetalLB with Cilium BGPConsolidate stack — one tool for CNI + LB + Policy + Observability
🔑 CCA Insight: BGP and L2 Announcements are key CCA topics for bare metal/external access. Remember: BGP = Layer 3, requires BGP-capable router, whole-network scale. L2 = Layer 2, works with ANY switch, local subnet only. Both use the CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy CRD or CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy CRD. The LoadBalancer IPAM pool is configured via ConfigMap (cilium-config). For the exam: know which approach to recommend based on the environment description.

📝 Chapter 11 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What flag enables kube-proxy replacement in Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

--set kubeProxyReplacement=true during cilium install. This replaces iptables-based kube-proxy with Cilium's eBPF socket-level load balancer using Maglev consistent hashing.

Q2
How does eBPF load balancing differ from iptables kube-proxy?
Show Answer
Answer

iptables: O(n) sequential rule walking — 5000+ rules, 30s updates. eBPF: O(1) hash map lookups at socket level, before TCP/IP stack. No iptables rules, no netfilter traversal, no connection tracking table overflow. Maglev hashing ensures even distribution and connection affinity.

Q3
What is Maglev hashing and why is it important?
Show Answer
Answer

Maglev is Google's consistent hashing algorithm. It provides: (1) Even load distribution across backends, (2) Connection affinity (same 5-tuple → same backend), (3) Minimal disruption — when a backend changes, only ~1/N connections are affected, not all connections.

Q4
What is Socket LB and how does it work in Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

Socket LB (Load Balancing) intercepts connect() syscalls at the socket layer using eBPF cgroup hooks. When a pod calls connect("service-ip", port), Cilium's eBPF program redirects it to a real backend pod IP BEFORE the TCP handshake. No DNAT hop, no iptables.

Q5
What are the two modes of kube-proxy replacement?
Show Answer
Answer

Partial: Only replaces ClusterIP services (works on any kernel). Strict: Replaces ALL kube-proxy functionality including NodePort, ExternalIPs, and LoadBalancer (requires kernel 5.10+). Check with cilium status | grep KubeProxyReplacement.

Q6
How does DSR (Direct Server Return) work in Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

DSR lets the backend pod respond directly to the client, bypassing the load balancer on the return path. Cilium rewrites the destination MAC address (not IP) at the node level. The backend sees the original client IP. Faster than SNAT but requires specific network configuration.

Q7
How does Cilium handle NodePort services with KPR enabled?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium's eBPF programs intercept NodePort traffic at the network device level (TC hook) and redirect to backend pods. No iptables DNAT rules. Traffic can be directed to backends on the same node (local) or any node (cluster), depending on externalTrafficPolicy.

Q8
What happens to existing connections when a Service backend changes with Maglev?
Show Answer
Answer

Maglev's consistent hashing ensures that only connections that mapped to the removed backend are affected. All other connections continue to their original backends. This minimizes disruption compared to random hashing where ALL connections could be redistributed.

Q9
How do you verify kube-proxy replacement is active and working?
Show Answer
Answer

Check cilium status | grep KubeProxyReplacement — should show "Strict" or "Partial". Verify with cilium service list to see services managed by Cilium. Run cilium connectivity test which includes service connectivity tests.

Q10
Why is Cilium's KPR 587x faster than iptables kube-proxy?
Show Answer
Answer

iptables walks rules sequentially (O(n)) — with 10,000 services, every packet traverses 10,000+ rules. Cilium uses eBPF hash maps (O(1)) — one lookup finds the backend regardless of service count. Additionally, socket-level interception avoids the entire netfilter stack and DNAT hop.

11.4 Bandwidth Manager — eBPF-Based Rate Limiting & BBR Congestion Control

Cilium's Bandwidth Manager uses eBPF to enforce bandwidth limits on pod traffic and enables BBR congestion control — a game-changer for internet-facing services. Unlike the legacy Kubernetes bandwidth CNI plugin (which uses TBF — Token Bucket Filter), Cilium uses EDT (Earliest Departure Time) for precise, scalable rate limiting directly in the kernel.

Bandwidth Manager Architecture — EDT vs TBF
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              CILIUM BANDWIDTH MANAGER (EDT)                   │
  │                                                              │
  │  Pod A                    Pod B                    Pod C     │
  │  ┌─────────┐            ┌─────────┐            ┌─────────┐   │
  │  │ 10 Mbps │            │ 50 Mbps │            │ 100 Mbps│   │
  │  │ limit   │            │ limit   │            │ limit   │   │
  │  └────┬────┘            └────┬────┘            └────┬────┘   │
  │       │                      │                      │        │
  │       ▼                      ▼                      ▼        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │         eBPF EDT (Earliest Departure Time)           │    │
  │  │  • Per-packet pacing — not "allow X then wait"      │    │
  │  │  • Multi-queue (MQ) + Fair Queue (FQ) scheduling    │    │
  │  │  • Native integration — no CNI chaining needed      │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │       │                                                      │
  │       ▼                                                      │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │              Physical NIC (eth0)                     │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  VS Legacy TBF (Token Bucket Filter):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  • Coarse "allow burst then block" — causes jitter           │
  │  • Queue-based (FIFO) — no fairness across flows             │
  │  • CNI chaining required — additional complexity             │
  │  • Poor multi-queue support — scalability issues             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📋 Enabling Bandwidth Manager

Shell — Install with Bandwidth Manager
helm install cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.5 \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set bandwidthManager.enabled=true

# Or enable on existing install:
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.5 \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set bandwidthManager.enabled=true
kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart ds/cilium

Verify it's active:

Shell — Check Bandwidth Manager Status
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status | grep BandwidthManager
# Output: BandwidthManager: EDT with BPF [BBR] [eth0]

🏷️ Pod Bandwidth Annotations

Use standard Kubernetes pod annotations to set per-pod limits:

AnnotationDirectionMechanismExample
kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidthEgress (pod→outside)EDT pacing"10M"
kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidthIngress (outside→pod)eBPF Token Bucket"20M"
YAML — anihpj Pod with Bandwidth Limits
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-server
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth: "10M"   # 10 Mbit/s egress
    kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth: "20M"  # 20 Mbit/s ingress
spec:
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: anihpj:latest
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
Shell — Verify Limits from BPF
kubectl exec -it -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg bpf bandwidth list
# IDENTITY   DIRECTION   PRIO   BANDWIDTH (BitsPerSec)
# 724        Egress      0      10M
# 724        Ingress     0      20M

🚀 BBR Congestion Control for Pods

BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time) is Google's congestion control algorithm. It achieves up to 2,700x higher throughput and 25x lower latency than traditional loss-based algorithms (CUBIC) on internet paths:

BBR vs CUBIC — Why It Matters for Internet-Facing Services
  CUBIC (Traditional):
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Internet Client  ──packet loss──▶  CUBIC: "Must be   │
  │  (high latency,                     congestion! Cut    │
  │   packet loss)                      window by 50%!"   │
  │                                                        │
  │  Problem: Wireless/wifi packets lost ≠ congestion      │
  │  Result: Unnecessarily low throughput, high latency    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  BBR (Cilium Bandwidth Manager):
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Internet Client  ──probes──▶  BBR: "What's the REAL   │
  │                               bottleneck bandwidth?    │
  │                               What's the REAL RTT?"    │
  │                                                        │
  │  BBR models the pipe, not packet loss                  │
  │  Result: Near-optimal throughput + minimal queues      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Enable BBR:

Shell — Enable BBR for Pods
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.5 \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set bandwidthManager.enabled=true \
  --set bandwidthManager.bbr=true
kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart ds/cilium
📋 BBR Requirements

Kernel 5.18+ is required for BBR to work for pods. Older kernels lose packet timestamps when switching from pod to host network namespace, breaking BBR's pacing. BBR also requires eBPF Host-Routing enabled to preserve socket association through the stack. For legacy routing mode, use bandwidthManager.bbrHostNamespaceOnly=true to enable BBR only for host-network processes.

🏗️ anihpj Bandwidth Management Example

For the anihpj Django application serving external clients:

YAML — anihpj Deployment with Bandwidth Limits
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth: "50M"   # 50 Mbit/s
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: anihpj:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
---
# High-priority job processing — higher bandwidth
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-worker
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth: "200M"
    kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth: "200M"
spec:
  containers:
  - name: worker
    image: anihpj-worker:latest

⚠️ Bandwidth Manager Limitations

⚠️ Important Limitations

• Bandwidth enforcement does NOT work with L7 Cilium Network Policies — if an L7 policy selects the pod at egress, bandwidth enforcement is disabled for that pod.
• Does NOT work with nested network namespaces (e.g., Kind clusters) — they lack access to global sysctl /proc/sys/net/core.
• Strongly recommended to use with BPF Host Routing — legacy routing through the upper stack causes undesired high latency.
• Bandwidth limits apply per-pod, not per-deployment. Each replica gets the full limit individually.

💡 CCA Exam Tip — Bandwidth Manager

Key exam points: (1) Uses EDT (Earliest Departure Time) for egress, eBPF Token Bucket for ingress. (2) Configured via standard Kubernetes annotations kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth and kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth. (3) BBR requires kernel 5.18+ and BPF Host Routing. (4) Does NOT work with L7 policies. (5) Verify with cilium-dbg bpf bandwidth list. (6) Each pod replica gets the full bandwidth limit independently.

📝 Chapter 11 — Bandwidth Manager Practice Questions (5 Additional)

BQ1
What mechanism does Cilium use for egress bandwidth enforcement?
Show Answer
Answer

EDT (Earliest Departure Time) with eBPF. Unlike legacy TBF (Token Bucket Filter) which uses crude "allow X then block," EDT paces packets precisely using MQ/FQ (Multi-Queue / Fair Queue) scheduling at the physical NIC level.

BQ2
What kernel version is required for BBR congestion control to work for pods?
Show Answer
Answer

Kernel 5.18+. Older kernels lose packet timestamps when switching from pod to host network namespace, breaking BBR's pacing mechanism. BBR also requires eBPF Host-Routing enabled.

BQ3
How do you set bandwidth limits on a pod?
Show Answer
Answer

Use Kubernetes pod annotations: kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth: "10M" for egress and kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth: "20M" for ingress. These are standard Kubernetes annotations, not Cilium-specific CRDs.

BQ4
Why doesn't bandwidth enforcement work with L7 network policies?
Show Answer
Answer

L7 policies require deep packet inspection (proxying) which changes the packet path through the kernel. The bandwidth enforcement relies on EDT pacing at the physical NIC — when traffic is proxied through Envoy for L7 inspection, the pacing mechanism is bypassed.

BQ5
How do you verify bandwidth limits are being enforced?
Show Answer
Answer

Use cilium-dbg bpf bandwidth list to see per-identity limits. Test with iperf3 between pods: deploy netperf server/client pods with bandwidth annotations and run iperf3 -c <server-ip> to verify the actual throughput matches the configured limit.

🔭 Part 6: Observability — Seeing Everything with Hubble Chapters 13-15 · CCA 18%

Chapter 13: Hubble — The Microscope for Your Kubernetes Network

Hubble is Cilium's built-in observability platform — think of it as "tcpdump for Kubernetes, but 100x better." While tcpdump shows raw IPs and ports, Hubble shows pod names, namespaces, identities, HTTP methods, DNS queries, and policy verdicts — all collected from eBPF with zero overhead. This chapter teaches you to see everything happening in your cluster.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔭 Observability 🎯 CCA 18%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What Hubble is and why it beats tcpdump for Kubernetes
  • ✅ Hubble architecture — how flow data gets from eBPF to your screen
  • ✅ Hubble CLI — the essential commands for flow inspection
  • ✅ Hubble UI — the beautiful service map and flow browser
🎓 CCA Relevance
Observability 18% CRITICAL EXAM TOPIC

13.1 What is Hubble? — "tcpdump for Kubernetes, But 100x Better"

Hubble is Cilium's built-in observability platform that shows you who talked to whom, how much data, was it allowed or denied, and why. Unlike tcpdump, Hubble understands Kubernetes identities — pod names, namespaces, labels — not just raw IP addresses:

tcpdump vs Hubble — Same Traffic, Different Understanding
  tcpdump (raw packets):
  10.0.0.55.54321 > 10.0.0.99.5432: Flags [S], ...
  "What is 10.0.0.55? Who is 10.0.0.99? Who knows..."

  Hubble (identity-aware flows):
  anihpj/anihpj-55 (app=anihpj) → anihpj/postgres-0 (app=postgres)
  Port 5432, TCP, FORWARDED, 2.5 MB, 15ms latency
  "Ah! The Django pod connected to PostgreSQL. Makes sense!"

Hubble gets its data directly from Cilium's eBPF programs — every packet that passes through the eBPF datapath generates a flow event. These events include: source/destination pod name and namespace, source/destination identity, IP addresses and ports, L7 protocol info (HTTP method/path, DNS query), verdict (FORWARDED/DROPPED/AUDIT), and the specific policy rule that matched. All of this is collected with zero overhead — no agents, no sidecars, no extra containers.

📹 Think of Hubble as CCTV for your cluster: tcpdump is like a security camera that records license plates (IP addresses) but doesn't know who the drivers are. Hubble is like a smart camera system that knows every person by name (pod identity), what room they entered (namespace), what they did there (HTTP method + path), and whether security stopped them (policy verdict). And unlike real CCTV, Hubble records everything with zero performance impact — the eBPF programs are already processing every packet anyway.

13.2 Hubble Architecture — How Flow Data Gets to You

Hubble has a distributed architecture that scales with your cluster:

Hubble Data Flow — eBPF → Agent → Relay → UI/CLI
  WORKER NODE 1                        WORKER NODE 2
  ┌──────────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ anihpj Pod            │            │ postgres Pod          │
  │ (10.0.0.55)           │            │ (10.0.0.99)           │
  │    │                   │            │    │                   │
  │    ▼ eBPF Ring Buffer │            │    ▼ eBPF Ring Buffer │
  │ Cilium Agent           │            │ Cilium Agent           │
  │ exports flows via gRPC │            │ exports flows via gRPC │
  └──────────┬───────────┘            └──────────┬───────────┘
             │                                    │
             └──────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                            ▼
              ┌─────────────────────────┐
              │     HUBBLE RELAY         │ ← Aggregates ALL flows
              │     (Deployment)         │    from every agent
              └────────────┬────────────┘
                           │
            ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
            ▼              ▼              ▼
   ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐
   │ HUBBLE CLI │ │ HUBBLE UI  │ │ PROMETHEUS │
   │ (terminal) │ │ (browser)  │ │ (metrics)  │
   └────────────┘ └────────────┘ └────────────┘
🏗️ Hubble Components — 4 Pieces

1. Cilium Agent (per node): Exports flow events from eBPF Ring Buffer to Hubble Relay via gRPC. One per node — always running.

2. Hubble Relay (cluster-wide): Aggregates flows from ALL Cilium agents. This is what the CLI and UI connect to. Without Relay, you'd need to query each node individually.

3. Hubble CLI: Terminal-based flow viewer. Connects to Relay. Supports powerful filtering — by pod, namespace, verdict, port, HTTP method, and DNS query.

4. Hubble UI: Web dashboard at localhost:12000. Shows service map, flow browser, and real-time traffic visualization.

13.3 Hubble CLI — Your Detective Toolkit

hubble observe is the main command — it shows ALL flows. Without filters, this is a firehose. With filters, it's surgical:

terminal — Hubble CLI Essential Commands 
# Show ALL flows (firehose — use filters!)
hubble observe

# Only traffic FROM our Django pod
hubble observe --from-pod anihpj/anihpj-abcde

# Only traffic TO the anihpj namespace
hubble observe --to-namespace anihpj

# Only DROPPED traffic (debug policies!)
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED

# Only FORWARDED traffic (see what's working)
hubble observe --verdict FORWARDED

# Only PostgreSQL traffic (port 5432)
hubble observe --port 5432

# JSON output for scripting
hubble observe -o json | jq .

# HTTP-specific: see methods and paths
hubble observe --http-method GET --http-path /jobs/
🔍 Most Common Hubble Commands for anihpj

See all traffic to the database: hubble observe --to-namespace anihpj --port 5432

Find what's being blocked: hubble observe --verdict DROPPED -n anihpj

See HTTP requests to /admin: hubble observe --http-path /admin/

Monitor one pod's activity: hubble observe --from-pod anihpj/anihpj-abcde

13.4 Hubble UI — The Beautiful Web Dashboard

Hubble UI provides a visual service map and flow browser at localhost:12000 (port-forward the hubble-ui service). The service map shows all your services as nodes with edges representing traffic — green for allowed, red for denied. The flow browser is a searchable, filterable log of every flow in your cluster.

🖥️ Accessing Hubble UI

Step 1: cilium hubble ui — Opens a browser tab automatically.

Step 2: Or manually: kubectl port-forward -n kube-system svc/hubble-ui 12000:80

Step 3: Open http://localhost:12000 in your browser.

What you'll see for anihpj: nginx → Django → PostgreSQL as connected nodes, with traffic volume, latency, and HTTP status codes visible on click. Dropped traffic shows as red edges — instantly visible policy violations.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 13

❌ MISTAKE 1: Hubble Relay not running → CLI shows no flows. Check with cilium status — Hubble Relay must show OK.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Not using filters → firehose of all flows is overwhelming. Always filter by namespace, verdict, or port.

🔧 Under the Hood — How Hubble Captures and Streams Network Flows: eBPF Ring Buffer, Per-CPU Events, gRPC Streaming, and the Relay Aggregation Architecture
🗺️ Hubble Architecture — From eBPF Event to Your Terminal
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HUBBLE FLOW PIPELINE — 5 Stages from Packet to Dashboard                      │
│                                                                              │
│  STAGE 1: eBPF EVENT GENERATION (Kernel)                                      │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Cilium's eBPF programs emit a "perf event" for each flow decision:   │   │
│  │ {srcID, dstID, srcIP, dstIP, srcPort, dstPort, protocol, verdict,    │   │
│  │  L7 info (HTTP method/path, DNS query, Kafka topic), timestamp}      │   │
│  │ Written to BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF (lock-free circular buffer)          │   │
│  │ Each CPU has its own ring buffer → NO lock contention!               │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  STAGE 2: CILIUM AGENT COLLECTION (Userspace)                                 │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Agent reads ring buffers from ALL CPUs via bpf() syscall              │   │
│  │ Enriches events with metadata: pod name, namespace, labels, identity  │   │
│  │ Converts raw event → Hubble Flow protobuf                            │   │
│  │ Stores recent flows in in-memory ring buffer (default: 4095 flows)   │   │
│  │ Exposes via gRPC on Unix socket (/var/run/cilium/hubble.sock)        │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  STAGE 3: HUBBLE RELAY AGGREGATION (Cluster-Wide)                             │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Hubble Relay connects to ALL Cilium Agents via gRPC                  │   │
│  │ Uses Hubble Peer Service to discover agents dynamically              │   │
│  │ Aggregates flows from all nodes into ONE stream                      │   │
│  │ Provides cluster-wide querying: "Show ALL DROPPED flows everywhere"  │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  STAGE 4: HUBBLE CLI / API (Query Interface)                                  │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ hubble observe --from-pod X --verdict DROPPED                        │   │
│  │ → CLI translates to gRPC query → Relay filters + aggregates → returns│   │
│  │ Supports: pod/namespace/IP filters, verdict filters, HTTP/DNS filters│   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  STAGE 5: HUBBLE UI (Web Visualization)                                       │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Service Map: auto-generates topology from observed flows              │   │
│  │ Flow Browser: real-time stream with filtering                        │   │
│  │ HTTP/DNS tabs: protocol-specific views                               │   │
│  │ Access: kubectl port-forward -n kube-system svc/hubble-ui 12000:80   │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  WHY RING BUFFER: Lock-free, per-CPU, no memory allocation at runtime.       │
│  256KB per CPU — at 10M flows/sec, the buffer holds ~25ms of data.           │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 Hubble Peer Service — How Relay Discovers Cilium Agents
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HUBBLE PEER SERVICE — Dynamic Agent Discovery Without Hardcoded IPs            │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ PROBLEM: How does Hubble Relay find ALL Cilium Agents?                │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ ❌ Hardcoded IPs: breaks on node restart, scaling, replacement       │   │
│  │ ❌ K8s API polling: adds latency, API server load                     │   │
│  │ ✅ Hubble Peer Service: dynamic gRPC-based agent discovery            │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  DISCOVERY FLOW:                                                               │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. Each Cilium Agent registers with the Hubble Peer K8s Service       │   │
│  │ 2. Hubble Relay connects to hubble-peer.kube-system.svc.cluster.local │   │
│  │ 3. Peer Service returns list of ALL agent IPs + ports (gRPC)         │   │
│  │ 4. Relay opens gRPC streams to each agent simultaneously              │   │
│  │ 5. Agent joins/leaves → Peer Service notifies Relay → add/remove     │   │
│  │ 6. Relay continuously watches for changes (not periodic polling!)     │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  BENEFITS:                                                                     │
│  • New nodes → agents auto-discovered (no config change)                     │
│  • Node failures → agent removed from peer list (no stale connections)      │
│  • Scaling → Relay handles 100s of agents (streaming, not polling)          │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
