🔑 CCA Insight: Hubble is 18% of the CCA exam. Key architectural facts: (1) Hubble flows come from the SAME eBPF programs that enforce policies — zero additional overhead. (2) Ring buffers are per-CPU = lock-free = scales linearly with CPU count. (3) Hubble Relay is needed for cluster-wide queries — without it, you can only query one node at a time. (4) hubble observe connects to Relay (not directly to agents). (5) The Service Map is auto-generated from observed flows — no configuration needed.

📝 Chapter 12 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
When would you use BGP with Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

In bare metal or on-premise data centers where there's no cloud provider to handle LoadBalancer IP assignment. BGP announces Service IPs to upstream routers so external traffic can reach your services.

Q2
What CRD configures BGP peering in Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy (apiVersion: cilium.io/v2alpha1). It defines the local AS number, neighbor router IP/ASN, and which Service IPs to advertise.

Q3
What is LB IPAM and when is it useful?
Show Answer
Answer

LB IPAM (LoadBalancer IP Address Management) lets Cilium assign external IPs to LoadBalancer services from a defined pool — without a cloud provider. Combined with BGP, it provides complete cloud-like LoadBalancer functionality on bare metal.

Q4
What does localASN and peerASN mean in CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy?
Show Answer
Answer

localASN: Your network's Autonomous System Number (private ASNs: 64512-65534). peerASN: Your neighbor router's ASN. These numbers uniquely identify networks in BGP. Cilium uses them to establish peering sessions with upstream routers.

Q5
How does Cilium select which nodes participate in BGP peering?
Show Answer
Answer

Using nodeSelector in CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy. Only nodes with matching labels (e.g., bgp: enabled) participate in BGP peering. Label the nodes you want as BGP speakers: kubectl label node worker-1 bgp=enabled.

Q6
What is the difference between BGP in Cilium vs MetalLB?
Show Answer
Answer

Both provide BGP-based LoadBalancer services for bare metal. Cilium's BGP is built-in — no separate deployment needed — and integrates with CiliumNetworkPolicies for security. MetalLB is a standalone solution that works with any CNI. Cilium's BGP leverages eBPF for the data plane.

Q7
How do you configure LB IPAM in Cilium? What pool sizes should you use?
Show Answer
Answer

Configure via --set lbIPAM.enabled=true and define pools in a CiliumLoadBalancerIPPool CRD. Pool size depends on expected LoadBalancer services — a /24 (254 IPs) is common for medium clusters. Each LoadBalancer Service gets one IP from the pool.

Q8
What happens if the BGP peer router becomes unreachable?
Show Answer
Answer

The BGP session times out (typically 90-180 seconds with hold timers). The router withdraws the routes to your Service IPs — external traffic stops reaching your services. When connectivity restores, BGP re-establishes automatically. For HA, peer with multiple routers.

Q9
What is a LoadBalancer Service and how does it differ from NodePort?
Show Answer
Answer

NodePort: Exposes the service on a port on EVERY node (30000-32767). Client hits any node IP:port. LoadBalancer: Gets a dedicated external IP that routes to the service. With Cilium + BGP, this IP is announced to the network and reachable directly — no need to know node IPs.

Q10
Which CCA exam domain does BGP fall under and why?
Show Answer
Answer

BGP falls under Service Mesh & Load Balancing (20%). It's part of how Cilium enables external access to services. Know the CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy CRD, the difference between BGP and cloud LoadBalancers, and when to use LB IPAM.

12.5 L2 Announcements / L2 Aware LB — Bare Metal Load Balancing Without BGP

Beta L2 Announcements is an alternative to BGP for bare metal environments without BGP-capable routers — think office networks, campus LANs, or small data centers. Instead of BGP route advertisements, Cilium responds to ARP/NDP requests for Service LoadBalancer IPs, making them reachable on the local network segment.

L2 Announcements vs BGP — Two Bare Metal Approaches
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    BARE METAL CLUSTER                            │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Approach A: BGP (Section 12.1-12.4)                            │
  │  ┌──────────┐     BGP Session     ┌──────────────┐             │
  │  │  Cilium  │◄───────────────────►│  Upstream    │             │
  │  │  Node    │   Route Advertise   │  Router      │             │
  │  │          │   Service IP/32     │  (AS 65001)  │             │
  │  └──────────┘                     └──────┬───────┘             │
  │                                         │                       │
  │  Requires: BGP-capable router           │                       │
  │  Scale: Entire network / Internet        │                       │
  │                                         │                       │
  │  Approach B: L2 Announcements (This Section)                     │
  │  ┌──────────┐   ARP Reply "10.0.0.100   ┌──────────┐          │
  │  │  Cilium  │   is at MAC aa:bb:cc"      │  Client  │          │
  │  │  Node    │◄──────────────────────────►│  on same │          │
  │  │ (Leader) │   ARP Request "Who has     │  L2 net  │          │
  │  └──────────┘    10.0.0.100?"           └──────────┘          │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Requires: Same L2 broadcast domain                              │
  │  Scale: Local network segment only                               │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🎯 When to Use L2 Announcements vs BGP

FeatureL2 AnnouncementsBGP
Network requirementSame L2 broadcast domain (ARP)Routed network (L3)
Router supportAny standard switchBGP-capable router needed
Failover time~10-20s (default)Seconds (fast reconvergence)
Load distributionOne node handles all traffic per serviceECMP — multiple paths possible
ScaleSingle L2 domain onlyEntire network / internet
ComplexityLower — just enable flagHigher — need BGP config
Best forOffice, campus, small DCLarge DC, multi-site, internet

📋 Enabling L2 Announcements

Prerequisites: Kube-proxy replacement must be enabled. Required kernel: same as KPR.

Shell — Install with L2 Announcements
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.5 \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set l2announcements.enabled=true \
  --set kubeProxyReplacement=true \
  --set k8sServiceHost=${API_SERVER_IP} \
  --set k8sServicePort=${API_SERVER_PORT} \
  --set k8sClientRateLimit.qps=50 \
  --set k8sClientRateLimit.burst=100
⚠️ Client Rate Limit is Critical!

L2 announcements use Kubernetes Leases for leader election, which generates significant API traffic. The default rate limit (5 QPS / 10 burst) is quickly exceeded. Size according to: QPS = #services × (1 / leaseRenewDeadline). For 65 services with 2s renew deadline: 32.5 QPS minimum.

📜 L2 Announcement Policy

Policies control which services are announced, on which nodes, and via which interfaces:

YAML — CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2alpha1"
kind: CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy
metadata:
  name: anihpj-l2-policy
spec:
  serviceSelector:          # Which services to announce
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  nodeSelector:             # Which nodes can announce
    matchExpressions:
      - key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
        operator: DoesNotExist   # Workers only
  interfaces:               # Which NICs to announce on
  - ^eth[0-9]+
  externalIPs: true         # Announce .spec.externalIPs
  loadBalancerIPs: true     # Announce .status.loadBalancer.ingress

🗳️ Leader Election — One Node Per Service

ARP/NDP works by associating one IP with one MAC address. So only one node can answer ARP requests for a given Service IP at a time. Cilium uses Kubernetes Leases for leader election:

Leader Election via Kubernetes Leases
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Service: anihpj-web (IP: 10.0.0.100)                       │
  │                                                              │
  │  ┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐        │
  │  │  Worker-1   │   │  Worker-2   │   │  Worker-3   │        │
  │  │  (Leader!)  │   │  (Standby)  │   │  (Standby)  │        │
  │  │  Holds      │   │  Waiting    │   │  Waiting    │        │
  │  │  Lease      │   │  for lease  │   │  for lease  │        │
  │  │  Answers    │   │             │   │             │        │
  │  │  ARP for    │   │             │   │             │        │
  │  │  10.0.0.100 │   │             │   │             │        │
  │  └──────┬──────┘   └─────────────┘   └─────────────┘        │
  │         │                                                     │
  │         │  Lease: cilium-l2announce-default-anihpj-web        │
  │         │  Holder: worker-1                                   │
  │         │  Duration: 15s (default)                            │
  │         │  Renew: every 5s                                    │
  │         │                                                     │
  │  ┌──────▼──────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
  │  │  If worker-1 fails:                                  │      │
  │  │  • Lease expires after leaseDuration (15s)           │      │
  │  │  • Worker-2 or Worker-3 acquires lease               │      │
  │  │  • New leader sends Gratuitous ARP                   │      │
  │  │  • Clients update ARP cache → new MAC                │      │
  │  │  • Failover time: 10-20s (typical)                   │      │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Shell — View L2 Announcement Leases
kubectl -n kube-system get lease | grep cilium-l2announce
# NAME                                  HOLDER        AGE
# cilium-l2announce-default-anihpj-web  worker-1      2d20h

kubectl -n kube-system get lease cilium-l2announce-default-anihpj-web -o yaml
# spec:
#   holderIdentity: worker-1
#   leaseDurationSeconds: 15
#   renewTime: "2025-06-02T12:15:26Z"

🔧 Tuning Lease Parameters

ParameterDefaultPurposeTrade-off
l2announcements.leaseDuration15sHow long before lease expiresLonger = less API load, slower failover
l2announcements.leaseRenewDeadline5sHow often leader renewsShorter = faster detection, more API calls
l2announcements.leaseRetryPeriod2sRetry interval after renew failureMust be less than renewDeadline by 20%

⚠️ L2 Announcements Limitations

⚠️ Key Limitations

• No load balancing before cluster: ARP maps one IP→one MAC. All external traffic for a service goes to ONE node, which then load balances to backends. The leader node can become a bottleneck.
• No intra-policy balancing: Nodes within the same policy may be asymmetrically loaded due to first-come-first-serve lease acquisition.
• Incompatible with externalTrafficPolicy: Local: IPs may be announced on nodes without pods, causing traffic drops.
• Not a security feature: Services are still reachable via hard-coded ARP entries even if not announced.
• L2 domain only: Traffic must be on same broadcast domain — no routing across subnets.

🔍 Troubleshooting L2 Announcements

Shell — Troubleshooting Checklist
# 1. Verify feature is enabled
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg config --all | grep EnableL2Announcements
# EnableL2Announcements : true

# 2. Check policies exist
kubectl get CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy

# 3. Check leases created
kubectl -n kube-system get lease | grep cilium-l2announce

# 4. Check agent internal state
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg shell -- db/show l2-announce

# 5. Check known devices
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg shell -- db/show devices

# 6. Test ARP from another node
kubectl exec -n kube-system pod/cilium-xxxxx -- arping -i eth0 <service-ip>

# 7. Check BPF map for ARP responder
kubectl exec -n kube-system pod/cilium-xxxxx -- \
  bpftool map dump pinned /sys/fs/bpf/tc/globals/cilium_l2_responder_v4
💡 CCA Exam Tip — L2 Announcements

Key points: (1) Beta feature for bare metal without BGP routers. (2) Uses ARP/NDP (L2) instead of BGP (L3). (3) One leader per service via Kubernetes Leases. (4) Requires kube-proxy replacement enabled. (5) Policy CRD: CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy. (6) Watch the client rate limit — each service creates a lease with API overhead. (7) Failover: 10-20s default. (8) All traffic enters through a single leader node per service. (9) L2 Pod Announcements is a separate feature for announcing individual pod IPs.

📝 Chapter 12 — L2 Announcements Practice Questions (5 Additional)

L2Q1
What's the key difference between L2 Announcements and BGP in Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

L2 Announcements use ARP/NDP at Layer 2 — requires same broadcast domain, no special router needed. BGP operates at Layer 3 — requires BGP-capable routers but works across routed networks and the internet.

L2Q2
How does Cilium ensure only one node responds to ARP for a given Service IP?
Show Answer
Answer

Via Kubernetes Leases. Each service gets a lease object. The node holding the lease is the leader and responds to ARP. If the leader fails to renew, another node acquires the lease and takes over. Leases are visible with: kubectl -n kube-system get lease | grep cilium-l2announce.

L2Q3
Why must you increase the client rate limit when using L2 Announcements?
Show Answer
Answer

Each service generates a Kubernetes Lease that needs periodic renewal. The default 5 QPS limit is quickly saturated. Formula: QPS = #services × (1 / leaseRenewDeadline). For 65 services with 2s renew: ~32.5 QPS needed.

L2Q4
What happens when the leader node for a service fails?
Show Answer
Answer

The lease expires after leaseDuration (default 15s). Another node acquires the lease, becomes the new leader, and sends a Gratuitous ARP reply. Clients that accept gratuitous ARP update their tables immediately. Failover takes 10-20s with defaults. Not all clients accept gratuitous ARP — some wait for TTL expiry.

L2Q5
What CRD and API version is used for L2 Announcement policies?
Show Answer
Answer

CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy with apiVersion: cilium.io/v2alpha1. It uses serviceSelector (which services), nodeSelector (which nodes), interfaces (which NICs), externalIPs (bool), and loadBalancerIPs (bool) to control announcements.

Chapter 14: Hubble Metrics — Prometheus + Grafana Integration

Hubble doesn't just show flows — it exports Prometheus metrics for HTTP request rates, latency, TCP drops, DNS queries, and more. This chapter shows you how to connect Hubble to Prometheus and build Grafana dashboards for anihpj.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour 📊 Metrics

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What metrics Hubble exports and what each one means
  • ✅ How to configure Prometheus to scrape Hubble metrics
  • ✅ Building a Grafana dashboard for anihpj observability
🎓 CCA Relevance
Observability 18%
Hubble Metrics — Know These for the CCA Exam
  • Enable Metrics: Set hubble.metrics.enabled="{flow,tcp,http,dns,drop}" during install. Metrics are OFF by default.
  • Prometheus Integration: Hubble exposes metrics on port 9965. Use ServiceMonitor for Prometheus Operator or a scrape config.
  • Key Metric Types: flow (TCP), http (L7), dns (queries), drop (policy denies). Each answers a different question about your cluster.

14.1 Hubble Metrics — Turning Flows into Numbers

Hubble doesn't just show you flows — it exports Prometheus metrics so you can build dashboards, set alerts, and track trends over time. Each metric type answers a specific question about your cluster. Enable them during installation with hubble.metrics.enabled:

Metric TypeWhat It TracksExample for anihpj
flowTCP flow counts, bytes, durationTotal traffic between Django and PostgreSQL
httpHTTP requests, responses, latencyGET /jobs/ rate, POST /admin/ errors
tcpTCP flags, handshake latencySYN retransmits, connection setup time
dnsDNS queries and responsesCoreDNS query rate, NXDOMAIN errors
icmpICMP (ping) trafficHealth check latency
dropDropped packet counts and reasonsPolicy denied drops per pod

14.2 Setting Up Prometheus to Scrape Hubble Metrics

Hubble exposes a Prometheus metrics endpoint. Configure a ServiceMonitor (if using Prometheus Operator) or a scrape config:

hubble-metrics-config.yaml 
# Enable Hubble metrics during install:
cilium install \
  --set hubble.metrics.enabled="{flow,tcp,http,dns,drop}" \
  --set hubble.metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled=true

# Or patch existing config:
cilium config set hubble-metrics-enabled "flow,tcp,http,dns,drop"

# Key Prometheus queries for anihpj:
# HTTP error rate:
sum(rate(hubble_http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))

# Database latency (p99):
histogram_quantile(0.99, hubble_tcp_flow_duration_seconds{port="5432"})

# Policy drops per pod:
sum(rate(hubble_drop_total[5m])) by (pod)

14.3 Grafana Dashboard for anihpj

Hubble provides pre-built Grafana dashboards. Import them and customize panels for your application:

📊 Essential Grafana Panels for anihpj

🌐 HTTP Dashboard: Request rate by endpoint (/jobs/, /admin/), status code distribution (2xx/4xx/5xx), p50/p95/p99 latency per endpoint.

🗄️ Database Dashboard: Connection rate to PostgreSQL, query latency, connection duration, dropped connections.

🛡️ Security Dashboard: Dropped traffic by policy, top blocked sources, audit mode violations.

🔍 DNS Dashboard: DNS query rate, response time, NXDOMAIN rate (sign of DNS exfiltration attempts).

Import the dashboard JSON from Cilium's GitHub: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/tree/main/install/kubernetes/cilium/charts/hubble-ui/templates

⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 14

❌ MISTAKE 1: Metrics not enabled → Hubble shows flows but Prometheus sees nothing. Enable with hubble.metrics.enabled during install.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Enabling ALL metrics in production → High cardinality. Only enable what you need: flow, http, drop are usually enough.

🔧 Under the Hood — How Hubble Metrics Export Works: Prometheus Integration, Metric Collection from eBPF Maps, Context Labels, and Grafana Dashboard Architecture
🗺️ Hubble Metrics Pipeline — From eBPF Counter to Grafana Dashboard
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HUBBLE METRICS ARCHITECTURE — Zero-Overhead Metric Collection                 │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ METRIC SOURCE: eBPF Maps (NOT /proc scraping!)                        │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  hubble_drop_total{reason,protocol,direction}                         │   │
│  │  ↑ eBPF increments a per-CPU counter ON DROP — atomic, lock-free      │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  hubble_tcp_flags_total{flag,family}                                  │   │
│  │  ↑ eBPF increments on each TCP flag observation                       │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  hubble_dns_queries_total{query,rcode}                                │   │
│  │  ↑ eBPF increments on each DNS query/response observation             │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  hubble_http_requests_total{method,path,status}                        │   │
│  │  ↑ eBPF increments on each HTTP request observation                   │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  hubble_flows_processed_total{protocol,verdict,type}                   │   │
│  │  ↑ eBPF increments on each flow processed                             │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ METRIC EXPORT PATH:                                                     │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  eBPF Map → Cilium Agent (reads via bpf syscall) →                     │   │
│  │  → Internal metric registry → HTTP /metrics endpoint (:9965) →         │   │
│  │  → Prometheus scrape (every 15-60s) → Prometheus TSDB →               │   │
│  │  → Grafana (PromQL queries → dashboards)                               │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  NO separate exporter process needed!                                  │   │
│  │  NO node_exporter needed!                                              │   │
│  │  Metrics are a BYPRODUCT of policy enforcement.                        │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  CONTEXT LABELS (What Makes Hubble Metrics Rich):                             │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ source_pod, source_namespace, source_identity                         │   │
│  │ destination_pod, destination_namespace, destination_identity         │   │
│  │ → These are auto-populated from eBPF identity maps!                   │   │
│  │ → No configuration needed — labels come from K8s metadata             │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📈 Key PromQL Queries — What to Ask Your Hubble Metrics
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ESSENTIAL PROMQL QUERIES — Hubble Metrics in Action                            │
│                                                                              │
│  DETECT DROPPED TRAFFIC:                                                       │
│  rate(hubble_drop_total[5m]) > 0                                               │
│  → "Is any policy blocking traffic right now?"                               │
│                                                                              │
│  MOST BLOCKED DESTINATIONS:                                                    │
│  topk(10, sum(rate(hubble_drop_total[5m])) by (destination_pod))              │
│  → "Which pods are being blocked from the most?"                              │
│                                                                              │
│  HTTP 5XX ERROR RATE BY ENDPOINT:                                              │
│  sum(rate(hubble_http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])) by (path, method)  │
│  → "Which API endpoints are returning server errors?"                         │
│                                                                              │
│  P99 HTTP LATENCY:                                                             │
│  histogram_quantile(0.99,                                                      │
│    sum(rate(hubble_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, path))  │
│  → "Where's the bottleneck? 99% of requests are slower than X seconds"       │
│                                                                              │
│  DNS EXFILTRATION DETECTION:                                                   │
│  sum(rate(hubble_dns_queries_total{rcode=~"NXDOMAIN|REFUSED"}[5m])) by (query)│
│  > 10                                                                          │
│  → "Is a compromised pod trying to exfiltrate data via DNS?"                  │
│                                                                              │
│  SYN FLOOD DETECTION:                                                          │
│  rate(hubble_tcp_flags_total{flag="SYN"}[1m])                                  │
│  /                                                                             │
│  rate(hubble_tcp_flags_total{flag="SYN-ACK"}[1m]) > 10                        │
│  → "SYN/SYN-ACK ratio > 10 = likely SYN flood attack"                        │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔑 CCA Insight: Hubble metrics are NOT sampled or polled — they're incremented atomically by eBPF programs at the point of decision. This means: (1) Zero CPU overhead for metric collection, (2) No missed events (every drop/flags/DNS query is counted), (3) Context labels (pod, namespace, identity) are auto-populated from eBPF maps. Key exam metric: hubble_drop_total tells you WHY traffic was dropped. Combine with policy verdicts for complete debugging.

📝 Chapter 13 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What does Hubble show that tcpdump doesn't?
Show Answer
Answer

Pod names, namespaces, Kubernetes identities, policy verdicts (FORWARDED/DROPPED/AUDIT), HTTP methods and paths, DNS queries, and the specific policy rule that matched. tcpdump only shows raw IPs, ports, and packet data.

Q2
How does Hubble get flow data from the kernel?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium Agent exports flow events from the eBPF Ring Buffer to Hubble Relay via gRPC. The Relay aggregates flows from ALL agents. CLI and UI connect to the Relay. This is zero-overhead — eBPF already processes every packet.

Q3
What command shows only DROPPED traffic in the anihpj namespace?
Show Answer
Answer

hubble observe --verdict DROPPED -n anihpj — shows all traffic that was blocked by network policies in the anihpj namespace.

Q4
What is Hubble Relay and why is it needed?
Show Answer
Answer

Hubble Relay aggregates flow data from ALL Cilium agents across all nodes. Without Relay, you'd need to query each node's agent individually. Relay provides a single point of access for the CLI, UI, and Prometheus.

Q5
How do you filter Hubble flows to show only HTTP GET requests from a specific pod?
Show Answer
Answer

hubble observe --from-pod anihpj/anihpj-xxx --protocol http --http-method GET. Add --http-path /api/.* for path filtering. Combine with --verdict FORWARDED or DROPPED for policy debugging.

Explanation

CCA Observability domain (18%). Hubble filters are additive — each flag narrows the results. Know the key flags: --from-pod, --to-pod, --verdict, --protocol, --http-method, --http-path, --since. The exam may ask which combination of flags solves a specific monitoring scenario.

Q6
What is the Hubble Service Map and what does red vs green mean?
Show Answer
Answer

The Service Map is a real-time dependency graph in Hubble UI showing service-to-service communication. Green edges = allowed traffic (FORWARDED). Red edges = dropped traffic (policy denied). Thickness = traffic volume. Click any edge to see the flows between those services.

Q7
What's the difference between cilium monitor and hubble observe?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium monitor shows raw eBPF events from a SINGLE node — packet-level, low-level debugging. hubble observe shows cluster-wide flow data aggregated through Hubble Relay — higher-level, policy-aware, with pod names and verdicts. Monitor = per-node kernel debug. Hubble = cluster-wide operational visibility.

Q8
How do you access Hubble UI after installation?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium hubble ui — opens a local proxy to the Hubble UI service. Or manually: kubectl port-forward -n kube-system svc/hubble-ui 12000:80 then open localhost:12000. Requires Hubble UI to be enabled during install (--set hubble.ui.enabled=true).

Q9
How do you export Hubble flows to JSON for scripting or external analysis?
Show Answer
Answer

hubble observe -o json outputs each flow as a JSON object with fields: source/destination pod, namespace, identity, IP, port, verdict, protocol, HTTP details, and timestamp. Pipe to jq for filtering: hubble observe -o json | jq 'select(.verdict=="DROPPED")'.

Q10
What Hubble command shows DNS queries being made by pods in the anihpj namespace?
Show Answer
Answer

hubble observe -n anihpj --to-port 53 --protocol UDP or hubble observe -n anihpj --dns-query. Shows which domains pods are resolving, response codes, and whether DNS queries are being dropped by policy. Critical for debugging "pod can't reach external API" issues.

Chapter 15: Troubleshooting with Hubble — Real-World Debugging

Hubble isn't just for monitoring — it's your primary debugging tool when things go wrong. This chapter walks through 4 real-world scenarios you'll encounter with anihpj, showing exactly how to diagnose and fix each one using Hubble.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🔧 Debug

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Debug HTTP 500 errors using Hubble flow inspection
  • ✅ Identify database flood sources with top talkers
  • ✅ Troubleshoot network policy blocks
  • ✅ Verify canary deployment health
🎓 CCA Relevance
Observability 18% Troubleshooting
Troubleshooting with Hubble — CCA Exam Skills
  • The 4 Debug Scenarios: 500 errors, DB floods, policy blocks, canary health — expect at least one troubleshooting question on the exam.
  • Key Commands: hubble observe --verdict DROPPED (policy debug), hubble observe --http-status 5xx (error investigation).
  • Top Talkers: Know how to use -o json | jq to find which pod is generating the most traffic to a service.

15.1 Scenario 1: "Why is my pod getting 500 errors?"

Users report intermittent 500 errors on /jobs/. Application logs show "Database connection timeout." Let's use Hubble to find the root cause:

Debug Walkthrough — 500 Error Investigation
  STEP 1: Check HTTP status codes
  $ hubble observe --http-status 500 -n anihpj
  anihpj/anihpj-abc → anihpj/postgres-0:5432 500 2.3s
  ↑ 2.3 SECOND response time! Normal is 5-15ms

  STEP 2: Check database latency
  $ hubble observe --to-pod anihpj/postgres-0 --port 5432
  Shows all queries → 2-3 second response times

  STEP 3: Check for drops (is policy blocking retries?)
  $ hubble observe --verdict DROPPED -n anihpj
  No drops → policy is not the issue

  STEP 4: Root cause identified
  PostgreSQL is overloaded → connection pool exhausted
  FIX: Increase max_connections or add read replicas

15.2 Scenario 2: "Who is flooding the database?"

PostgreSQL CPU is at 100%. Someone is sending an abnormal amount of queries. Hubble can identify the culprit:

terminal — Identify DB Top Talkers 
# Find top talkers to PostgreSQL (count flows by source pod)
hubble observe --to-namespace anihpj --port 5432 -o json | \
  jq -r '.source.pod_name' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

# Output:
#   15234 anihpj-worker-xyz    ← THIS pod is flooding the DB!
#     423 anihpj-abc
#      15 monitoring-grafana

# FIX: Investigate the worker pod's code for a query loop,
# or apply a CiliumNetworkPolicy to rate-limit it.

15.3 Scenario 3: "My network policy is blocking legitimate traffic!"

You applied a new CNP and suddenly the frontend can't reach the backend. Use Hubble to see exactly what's being blocked:

Policy Block Debug — 3-Step Fix
  SYMPTOM: Frontend returns 502 Bad Gateway

  STEP 1: See what's being DROPPED
  $ hubble observe --verdict DROPPED -n anihpj
  anihpj/nginx-xyz → anihpj/anihpj-abc:8000 DROPPED
  Reason: Policy denied
  ↑ Frontend can't reach backend! Policy is blocking port 8000.

  STEP 2: Check the policy
  $ kubectl describe cnp -n anihpj
  endpointSelector: app=anihpj  ← applies to BACKEND
  ingress: fromEndpoints: matchLabels: app=frontend ← nginx label?

  STEP 3: The fix
  $ kubectl get pods -n anihpj nginx-xyz --show-labels
  app=nginx-ingress  ← Label is "nginx-ingress", NOT "frontend"!
  FIX: Update policy selector to matchLabels: app=nginx-ingress
🔧 Policy Debug Quick Reference

1. hubble observe --verdict DROPPED -n <ns> — See WHAT is being blocked.

2. kubectl get pods --show-labels — Verify labels match policy selectors.

3. cilium policy get -n <ns> — See active policies and their selectors.

4. Fix the selector mismatch → blocked traffic should now show FORWARDED.

15.4 Scenario 4: "Is our new canary deployment healthy?"

You deployed anihpj v2 to 10% of traffic. Is it working better or worse than v1? Hubble HTTP metrics give you the answer:

terminal — Compare v1 vs v2 with Hubble 
# Compare error rates between versions
hubble observe --to-pod anihpj/anihpj-v2-* --http-status 5xx
# vs
hubble observe --to-pod anihpj/anihpj-v1-* --http-status 5xx

# Compare latency (using Hubble metrics in Prometheus):
# v1 p99 latency:
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  hubble_http_request_duration_seconds{pod=~"anihpj-v1-.*"})

# v2 p99 latency:
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  hubble_http_request_duration_seconds{pod=~"anihpj-v2-.*"})

# DECISION:
# If v2 errors > v1 errors → ROLLBACK to 100% v1
# If v2 latency < v1 latency → INCREASE v2 to 50%
# If v2 is stable for 1 hour → PROMOTE to 100%
⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 15

❌ MISTAKE 1: Not using --verdict filter → Seeing ALL traffic when you only need DROPPED. Always filter by verdict when debugging policies.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Debugging in production without audit mode → Always audit before enforcing. Use Hubble to verify policies in audit mode before switching to enforce.

🔧 Under the Hood — How Hubble Enables Real-World Debugging: Flow Correlation Across Hops, L7 Protocol Decoding, Timeline Reconstruction, and the Timescape Replay Engine

│  HUBBLE DEBUGGING METHODOLOGY — The 5-Step Diagnostic Pattern                  │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 1: IDENTIFY THE SYMPTOM                                                  │
│  • "Pod X can't reach Service Y"                                              │
│  • "HTTP 500 errors in anihpj backend"                                       │
│  • "External API calls timing out"                                            │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 2: CHECK POLICY VERDICTS                                                 │
│  hubble observe --from-pod anihpj/web-xxx --to-pod anihpj/backend-yyy         │
│  → FORWARDED?  Policy OK, go to step 3                                        │
│  → DROPPED?    Policy issue! Check CNP/CCNP rules                             │
│  → NOT FOUND?  No traffic at all — DNS, routing, or pod is dead              │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 3: CHECK L7 PROTOCOL DETAILS                                             │
│  hubble observe --http-method POST --http-path /admin/                        │
│  → Shows exact HTTP requests, response codes, latency                        │
│  → HTTP 403? L7 policy is blocking it                                         │
│  → HTTP 500? Application error — not a network issue                         │
│  → No HTTP data? Traffic is non-HTTP or L7 parsing disabled                  │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 4: CHECK DNS RESOLUTION                                                  │
│  hubble observe --dns-query api.stripe.com                                    │
│  → Query seen? DNS is working                                                 │
│  → Query DROPPED? DNS policy is blocking it                                   │
│  → No query? Pod isn't even trying DNS — app config issue                    │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 5: TRACE THE FULL PATH (Multi-Hop Correlation)                           │
│  hubble observe --from-pod frontend --to-pod backend --http-path /api/jobs/  │
│  → Then: hubble observe --from-pod backend --to-pod postgres (port 5432)    │
│  → Reveals: frontend→backend latency + backend→DB latency                    │
│  → Pinpoints which HOP is slow or failing                                    │
│                                                                              │
│  TIMESCAPE REPLAY (Historical Forensics):                                      │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ • Records ALL flows (not sampled) to persistent storage               │   │
│  │ • Replay any time window: "Show me all traffic between 2-3 AM"       │   │
│  │ • Security forensics: trace attacker's lateral movement               │   │
│  │ • Compliance: prove what traffic occurred during an audit window     │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 Hubble JSON Output — Scripting and Analysis with jq
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HUBBLE JSON + jq — Advanced Flow Analysis                                      │
│                                                                              │
│  TOP TALKERS (most active source pods):                                        │
│  hubble observe -o json | jq -r '.source.pod_name' | sort | uniq -c |        │
│    sort -rn | head -10                                                        │
│  → Shows which 10 pods are generating the most traffic                        │
│                                                                              │

│    jq -r '"from \(.source.pod_name) to \(.destination.pod_name):\(.l4.TCP. │
│    destination_port)"' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10                │

│                                                                              │

│  hubble observe --since 1h --http-status 500 -o json |                        │
│    jq -r '"\(.Time) \(.source.pod_name) → \(.destination.pod_name)          │

│  hubble observe --protocol UDP --to-port 53 -o json |                         │

│  → All domains being resolved — look for unexpected domains                   │
│                                                                              │
│  LATENCY ANALYSIS (HTTP response times):                                       │
│  hubble observe --protocol http -o json |                                     │
│    jq -r '"\(.l7.http.url) \(.l7.http.latency_ms)ms"' |                      │
│    sort -t' ' -k2 -rn | head -20                                               │
│  → Top 20 slowest HTTP endpoints                                              │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🗺️ Real Debug Scenario — HTTP 500 Investigation End-to-End
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SCENARIO: Users report "anihpj is returning errors"                           │
│                                                                              │
│  🕐 10:00 AM — Incident starts                                                 │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 1: IDENTIFY THE SCOPE                                                    │
│  $ hubble observe --http-status 500 --since 30m                               │
│  → Shows 500 errors from anihpj-backend pods                                 │
│  → ALL errors coming from POST /api/jobs/ endpoint                           │
│  → Source: anihpj-frontend pods (normal — they're allowed)                   │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 2: CHECK LATENCY                                                         │
│  $ hubble observe --http-path /api/jobs/ --http-method POST -o json |        │
│    jq '.l7.http.latency_ms'                                                    │
│  → P50: 120ms (normal), P95: 450ms (normal), P99: 2800ms (SLOW!)            │
│  → Some requests are taking 2.8 seconds — likely timing out                   │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 3: CHECK DOWNSTREAM (PostgreSQL)                                         │
│  $ hubble observe --from-pod anihpj/backend-xxx --to-port 5432 --since 30m   │
│  → Shows many forwarded connections (policy OK)                               │
│  → But some connections show TCP RST after 3 seconds                          │
│  → Database connection pool exhausted?                                        │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 4: CONFIRM ROOT CAUSE                                                    │
│  $ kubectl logs anihpj-backend-xxx | grep "connection pool"                  │
│  → "Connection pool exhausted — waiting for connections"                     │
│  → ROOT CAUSE: PostgreSQL connection pool size too small for load            │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 5: FIX + VERIFY                                                          │
│  • Increase DB connection pool: DATABASE_POOL_SIZE=50                         │
│  • Restart backend pods                                                        │
│  • Watch hubble observe --http-status 500 — should drop to 0                  │
│  • Monitor P99 latency — should return to normal (< 500ms)                    │
│                                                                              │
│  🕐 10:25 AM — Incident resolved (25 min, no Hubble = 2+ hours)               │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 CCA Insight: Hubble troubleshooting scenarios are a guaranteed CCA exam topic. The exam WILL give you a symptom ("pod can't connect") and ask which Hubble command diagnoses it. Remember: DROPPED = policy issue, HTTP 403/503 = L7 policy or app error, no flows = routing/DNS, high latency per-hop = which service is slow. Timescape is the historical replay feature — distinct from real-time observe.

📝 Chapter 14 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What metrics does Hubble export? Name 4 categories.
Show Answer
Answer

Flow (TCP flows, bytes), HTTP (requests, responses, latency), TCP (flags, handshake), DNS (queries, responses), ICMP, and Drop (denied packets, reasons).

Q2
How does Prometheus scrape Hubble metrics?
Show Answer
Answer

Hubble exposes a Prometheus metrics endpoint. Configure with hubble.metrics.enabled and hubble.metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled=true for Prometheus Operator. Or add a scrape config targeting the Hubble metrics port (default 9965).

Q3
What metric would you use to detect a DDoS attack on anihpj?
Show Answer
Answer

hubble_http_requests_total filtered by endpoint — a sudden spike in requests to /jobs/ or /admin/ from a single source. Combine with hubble_drop_total to see policy enforcement kicking in.

Q4
How do you enable Hubble metrics during Cilium installation?
Show Answer
Answer

--set hubble.metrics.enabled="{dns,drop,tcp,flow,http}". Choose specific metric categories to avoid high cardinality. For Prometheus Operator, also add --set hubble.metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled=true for automatic scraping.

Q5
What Grafana panels would you create to monitor anihpj's health?
Show Answer
Answer

1) HTTP request rate by endpoint, 2) Status code distribution (2xx/4xx/5xx), 3) P95/P99 latency per endpoint, 4) Database connection rate and latency, 5) Dropped traffic by policy, 6) DNS query rate. Import Cilium's pre-built dashboards from GitHub as a starting point.

Q6
What does hubble_drop_total metric track and why is it important?
Show Answer
Answer

Counts packets dropped by Cilium policies, with labels for source/destination identity, port, and protocol. Critical for security monitoring — a spike in drops means a policy is blocking something (legitimate or attack). Combine with alerts to notify when unexpected drops occur.

Q7
How do you use Hubble metrics with Prometheus alerting rules?
Show Answer
Answer

Create Prometheus alerting rules on Hubble metrics: (1) rate(hubble_drop_total[5m]) > 10 for unexpected policy drops, (2) rate(hubble_http_requests_total{status="500"}[5m]) > 5 for HTTP errors, (3) histogram_quantile(0.99, hubble_http_request_duration_seconds) > 2 for high latency. Route alerts to Slack/PagerDuty.

Q8
Why shouldn't you enable ALL Hubble metric categories in production?
Show Answer
Answer

High cardinality — each metric generates multiple time series per pod, per endpoint, per status code. Enabling all categories in a 100-pod cluster can generate thousands of time series, overwhelming Prometheus. Enable only what you need: flow, http, and drop are usually sufficient for most monitoring.

Q9
How does Hubble metrics integration differ from standalone Prometheus node exporters?
Show Answer
Answer

Hubble metrics come directly from eBPF programs in the kernel — no separate exporter process, no polling, no overhead. Node exporters run as separate processes scraping /proc and /sys. Hubble's eBPF-based approach has near-zero CPU overhead because the data is already being collected by Cilium's datapath for policy enforcement.

Q10
What does hubble_tcp_flags_total tell you and how would you use it to detect SYN floods?
Show Answer
Answer

Counts TCP flags (SYN, SYN-ACK, FIN, RST) per flow. A SYN flood shows as a massive spike in SYN flags with very few SYN-ACK responses. Alert rule: rate(hubble_tcp_flags_total{flag="SYN"}[1m]) > 1000. Combine with drop metrics to see if Cilium's policy enforcement is mitigating the attack.

🔴 Part 7: Advanced Cilium — Encryption, Cluster Mesh & Egress Chapters 16-18

Chapter 16: Transparent Encryption — WireGuard for Free

Cilium can encrypt ALL pod-to-pod traffic with WireGuard — one flag, zero application code changes. Your Django app still connects to postgres:5432 as before. Cilium transparently encrypts every packet at the kernel level. This is defense-in-depth: even if an attacker compromises your physical network, all pod traffic is unreadable.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~1 hour 🔒 Encryption

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why encrypting pod traffic matters (compliance + zero-trust)
  • ✅ WireGuard vs IPSec — which to choose
  • ✅ Enabling transparent encryption with one flag
  • ✅ How node-to-node encryption works
🎓 CCA Relevance
Architecture 30% Security Features

16.1 Why Encrypt Pod Traffic?

In a default Kubernetes cluster, pod-to-pod traffic travels in plain text over the network. Anyone with access to the physical network (a compromised switch, a rogue network admin, a misconfigured VLAN) can sniff database passwords, API keys, and user data.

📬 Think of encryption like sending a sealed envelope vs a postcard: Without WireGuard, your pod traffic is like a postcard — anyone handling it along the way can read the contents (passwords, API keys, user data). With WireGuard, every packet is sealed in an unbreakable envelope — only the intended recipient can open it. And the best part? Your application doesn't even know the envelope exists — it just sends the postcard as usual, and Cilium seals it at the kernel level.

Encryption provides three critical benefits:

Without vs With WireGuard Encryption
  WITHOUT ENCRYPTION                  WITH WIREGUARD
  anihpj ── plain text ──▶ postgres  anihpj ──🔒 encrypted──▶ postgres
  😱 Anyone can sniff                ✅ Data is unreadable
     "SELECT * FROM users"              on the wire
     passwords visible!                 Even if network is compromised!

  🔧 APPLICATION CODE: UNCHANGED!
  Django still: connect("postgres", 5432)
  Cilium handles encryption transparently at the kernel level
📋 Why Encryption Matters — 3 Reasons

1. Defense in Depth: Network policies protect at L3/L4/L7. Encryption protects the data itself. If policies fail, data is still safe.

2. Compliance: HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and GDPR require data encryption in transit. WireGuard encryption satisfies these requirements.

3. Zero-Trust Networking: Assume the network is hostile. Encrypt everything. Trust nothing. Verify always.

16.2 WireGuard vs IPSec — Which Should You Choose?

FeatureWireGuardIPSec
Performance⚡ Very Fast (in-kernel)Moderate (user-space or kernel)
Complexity✅ Simple (~4000 lines of code)Complex (IKE, multiple modes)
Key Management✅ Auto-rotated by CiliumManual or external tools
Hardware SupportSoftware only✅ Hardware offload (NICs)
Cilium Recommendation✅ DEFAULT (best choice)Use if hardware offload needed

💡 Recommendation: Use WireGuard unless you have specific hardware offload requirements. It's faster, simpler, and Cilium handles all key management automatically.

16.3 Enabling Transparent Encryption — One Flag, Zero Code Changes

terminal — Enable & Verify WireGuard Encryption 
# Install Cilium with WireGuard encryption:
cilium install \
  --set encryption.enabled=true \
  --set encryption.type=wireguard

# Or enable on an existing cluster:
cilium config set encryption-enabled true
cilium config set encryption-type wireguard

# Verify encryption is active:
cilium status | grep Encryption
# → Encryption: OK (WireGuard)

# Check encryption status per node:
cilium encrypt status
# Shows: node-to-node encryption status, key age, peer count
🔑 Key Insight — Zero Application Changes

Your Django application code doesn't change AT ALL. It still calls connect("postgres", 5432). Cilium's eBPF programs intercept the connection at the socket level, perform the WireGuard key exchange, and encrypt every packet — all transparently. The application has no idea encryption is happening.

16.4 Node-to-Node Encryption — How Cross-Node Encryption Works

When pods are on different nodes, Cilium establishes a WireGuard tunnel between the nodes. Each node has a WireGuard key pair, and Cilium automatically distributes public keys to all other nodes:

Cross-Node WireGuard Encryption
  NODE 1 (10.0.0.1)                        NODE 2 (10.0.0.2)
  ┌─────────────────────────┐             ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │ anihpj pod (10.0.1.5)   │             │ postgres pod (10.0.2.9) │
  │     │                    │             │     ▲                    │
  │     │ plaintext inside   │             │     │ plaintext inside   │
  │     │ the node           │             │     │ the node           │
  │     ▼                    │             │     │                    │
  │ Cilium eBPF intercepts   │             │ Cilium eBPF decrypts    │
  │     │                    │             │     │                    │
  │     ▼                    │             │     ▲                    │
  │ WireGuard encrypts ──────┼── Tunnel ──▶ WireGuard decrypts       │
  │ (kernel-level)           │  🔒 UDP     │ (kernel-level)          │
  └─────────────────────────┘             └─────────────────────────┘

  ⏱️ WireGuard overhead: ~3-5% throughput reduction (negligible!)
  🔄 Key rotation: Automatic, every few minutes
  📦 Packet overhead: 60 bytes (WireGuard header)
⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 16

❌ MISTAKE 1: Not checking kernel support → WireGuard requires kernel ≥ 5.6. Check with uname -r.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Enabling encryption mid-flight → Existing connections break. Enable encryption during initial cluster setup if possible.

🔧 Under the Hood — How Cilium's Transparent Encryption Works: WireGuard Key Exchange, Node-to-Node Tunnel, IPSec Fallback, and Why Applications Don't Know They're Encrypted
🗺️ Transparent Encryption Architecture — WireGuard in the Kernel
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WIREGUARD ENCRYPTION — How It Works (Node-to-Node)                            │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ NODE A (10.0.0.1)                    NODE B (10.0.0.2)                │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Pod: anihpj-web                      Pod: postgres-0                   │   │
│  │ IP: 10.244.1.5                       IP: 10.244.2.9                   │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ 1. Pod sends packet:                                                    │   │
│  │    src: 10.244.1.5 → dst: 10.244.2.9:5432                             │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ 2. Cilium eBPF routes to node B:                                        │   │
│  │    ENCAPSULATE (VXLAN):                                                │   │
│  │    Outer: src: 10.0.0.1 → dst: 10.0.0.2                               │   │
│  │    Inner: src: 10.244.1.5 → dst: 10.244.2.9                           │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ 3. WIREGUARD ENCRYPTS outer packet:                                     │   │
│  │    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │   │
│  │    │ WireGuard Header │ Encrypted Payload (entire VXLAN packet)  │    │   │
│  │    │ src: 10.0.0.1:51820 → dst: 10.0.0.2:51820                   │    │   │
│  │    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ 4. WIREGUARD ON NODE B DECRYPTS:                                         │   │
│  │    Inner VXLAN packet → pod packet → delivered to postgres             │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  KEY PROPERTIES:                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ • TRANSPARENT: Applications have NO IDEA they're encrypted            │   │
│  │ • NO CODE CHANGES: Your app doesn't need TLS/SSL — WireGuard does it  │   │
│  │ • IN-KERNEL: WireGuard runs IN the Linux kernel → line-rate speed    │   │
│  │ • NODE-TO-NODE: All inter-node traffic is encrypted automatically    │   │
│  │ • POD-TO-POD: Traffic on the SAME node is NOT encrypted (localhost)  │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  KEY EXCHANGE:                                                                │
│  • Each node generates a Curve25519 keypair                                  │
│  • Public keys exchanged via Cilium's KVstore (etcd/CRD)                    │
│  • No certificate authority needed — just public keys!                      │
│  • Keys rotate automatically (no manual intervention)                       │
│                                                                              │
│  WIREGUARD vs IPSEC:                                                          │
│  ┌──────────┬──────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │ WireGuard│ 4000 lines of code   │ Simple, fast, modern crypto          │    │
│  │ IPSec    │ 400,000 lines of code│ Complex, feature-rich, older         │    │
│  │ Cilium   │ Both supported       │ --set encryption.type=wireguard/ipsec│    │
│  └──────────┴──────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 Key Rotation — How Cilium Handles WireGuard Key Lifecycle
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WIREGUARD KEY ROTATION — Seamless, Automated, Zero-Downtime                    │
│                                                                              │
│  INITIAL KEY GENERATION:                                                       │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. cilium install --set encryption.enabled=true                      │   │
│  │ 2. Each Cilium Agent generates a Curve25519 keypair                  │   │
│  │ 3. Public key stored in CiliumNode CRD (status.encryption.key)       │   │
│  │ 4. Private key stored in agent memory (never on disk!)               │   │
│  │ 5. All agents read all CiliumNode CRDs → build peer list             │   │
│  │ 6. Each agent creates WireGuard tunnel to every other node           │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  KEY ROTATION (every 5 minutes by default):                                    │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. Agent generates NEW keypair                                        │   │
│  │ 2. Updates CiliumNode CRD with new public key                         │   │
│  │ 3. Other agents detect CRD change → add new peer with new key        │   │
│  │ 4. Both old + new keys valid during transition (~30s overlap)         │   │
│  │ 5. Old key expires → tunnels using it tear down                       │   │
│  │ 6. ZERO packet loss during rotation (WireGuard handles it natively)   │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  MANUAL ROTATION (security incident):                                          │
│  $ cilium encrypt flush                                                        │
│  → Forces immediate regeneration of ALL keys on ALL nodes                    │
│  → All tunnels re-established within seconds                                 │
│  → Existing connections: brief pause, no drops                              │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 Encryption + Hubble — Observability Without Compromise
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ENCRYPTION + HUBBLE — How Cilium Sees Encrypted Traffic                        │
│                                                                              │
│  THE MAGIC: Hubble sees traffic BEFORE it's encrypted!                        │
│                                                                              │
│  Pod App → eBPF (Hubble captures flow here) → WireGuard encrypt → Network    │
│            │                                                                  │
│            └── Hubble flow event: {src:anihpj, dst:postgres, method:SELECT,  │
│                                     latency:2ms, verdict:FORWARDED}          │
│                                                                              │
│  WHAT HUBBLE STILL SEES (even with encryption enabled):                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ ✅ Pod names + namespaces                                              │   │
│  │ ✅ Policy verdicts (FORWARDED/DROPPED/AUDIT)                           │   │
│  │ ✅ HTTP methods + paths + status codes                                 │   │
│  │ ✅ DNS queries + responses                                              │   │
│  │ ✅ gRPC methods                                                         │   │
│  │ ✅ Latency (per-flow, per-hop)                                         │   │
│  │ ✅ Connection tracking (new/established/closed)                        │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ ❌ Hubble does NOT see: encrypted packet payload (irrelevant!)         │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🗺️ Encryption Scenarios — What Gets Encrypted and What Doesn't
Traffic TypeEncrypted?Notes
Pod→Pod (different nodes)✅ YESWireGuard encrypts the VXLAN/Geneve tunnel between nodes
Pod→Pod (same node)❌ NOTraffic stays on localhost — never leaves the node
Pod→Service (ClusterIP)✅ YES (if backend on different node)eBPF LB rewrites to backend pod IP, then encrypted if cross-node
Pod→External (egress)❌ NOWireGuard only encrypts node-to-node — egress traffic leaves as-is
Node→Node (host traffic)❌ NO (by default)Host traffic not encrypted — use Host Firewall for node-level security
Hubble flows (gRPC)❌ NO (by default)Hubble gRPC between agent and relay; enable TLS for Hubble
🔑 CCA Insight: Cilium's transparent encryption is a key CCA exam topic. Critical facts: (1) Encryption is NODE-TO-NODE, not pod-to-pod — same-node traffic is NOT encrypted. (2) Enabled with a SINGLE Helm flag: --set encryption.enabled=true --set encryption.type=wireguard. (3) Requires kernel ≥ 5.6 for WireGuard. (4) Verify with cilium encrypt status. (5) Performance impact: ~3-5% overhead (WireGuard is extremely efficient). (6) Applications are COMPLETELY unaware — no TLS/SSL configuration needed.

📝 Chapter 15 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
How do you find which pod is sending the most traffic to PostgreSQL?
Show Answer
Answer

hubble observe --to-namespace anihpj --port 5432 -o json | jq -r '.source.pod_name' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn — counts flows per source pod, showing the top talkers.

Q2
What Hubble command shows HTTP 500 errors in real time?
Show Answer
Answer

hubble observe --http-status 500 -n <namespace> — shows all flows where the HTTP response code is 500, including source/destination pods and latency.

Q3
How do you debug a network policy that's too restrictive?
Show Answer
Answer

1) hubble observe --verdict DROPPED -n <ns> to see what's blocked. 2) kubectl get pods --show-labels to verify label selectors. 3) Fix the policy selector mismatch or add missing allow rules. 4) Verify with Hubble that traffic now shows FORWARDED.

Q4
How do you use Hubble to compare canary v1 vs v2 performance?
Show Answer
Answer

Filter by pod name patterns: hubble observe --to-pod anihpj/anihpj-v2-* --http-status 5xx for v2 errors, and --to-pod anihpj/anihpj-v1-* for v1. In Prometheus: hubble_http_request_duration_seconds{pod=~"v2-.*"} vs v1. Compare error rates, latency, and throughput to decide rollout.

Q5
What Hubble command identifies the top talker to a specific service?
Show Answer
Answer

hubble observe --to-namespace ns --port 5432 -o json | jq -r '.source.pod_name' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn. Shows which pods generate the most traffic to a service. Use to identify misbehaving pods (infinite query loops, excessive API calls, data exfiltration attempts).

Q6
How do you verify a canary deployment is healthy before full rollout?
Show Answer
Answer

1) Hubble: check --http-status 5xx for canary pods — should be 0. 2) Prometheus: compare p99 latency of canary vs stable. 3) Hubble: verify canary pods are receiving correct % of traffic. 4) Check --verdict DROPPED — if canary traffic is dropped, fix policies. Promote only when canary metrics match or beat stable for ≥1 hour.

Q7
What's the most common label selector mistake when debugging policy blocks with Hubble?
Show Answer
Answer

Assuming pod labels match policy selectors without verifying. Always run kubectl get pods --show-labels to see actual labels. Common issues: typos ("frontend" vs "front-end"), missing labels, wrong namespace, or labels that exist on the Deployment but not inherited by pods (check pod template in spec).

Q8
How do you diagnose "Connection Refused" errors in anihpj using Hubble?
Show Answer
Answer

Connection Refused means the target port is closed — different from policy DROP. Hubble shows DROPPED for policy blocks but may show FORWARDED for connection refused (packet reached target but port was closed). Check: (1) Is the backend pod actually listening? (2) Is the port number correct? (3) kubectl exec into the pod and netstat -tlnp.

Q9
How do you trace the full path of a specific request through anihpj using Hubble?
Show Answer
Answer

Chain Hubble commands: (1) --from-pod nginx --to-pod backend (frontend→backend), (2) --from-pod backend --to-pod postgres (backend→DB), (3) Check verdicts at each hop. Use --http-path /specific/endpoint to isolate a particular API call. Export to JSON for timeline reconstruction.

Q10
What is the Hubble Timescape feature and what CCA exam domain does it relate to?
Show Answer
Answer

Hubble Timescape records and replays historical flow data for forensic analysis and compliance auditing. It captures ALL flows (not sampled) for later investigation — useful for security incident response and debugging intermittent issues. Relates to CCA Observability domain (18%) — know that Hubble provides both real-time AND historical flow visibility.

Chapter 17: Cluster Mesh — Connecting Multiple Kubernetes Clusters

Cluster Mesh connects multiple Kubernetes clusters into a single virtual network. Pods in a US cluster can talk directly to pods in an EU cluster — same IP space, same policies, same identities. This enables global high availability, disaster recovery, and multi-region deployments without complex VPNs or service meshes.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🌍 Multi-Cluster

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why connect multiple clusters (HA, DR, compliance)
  • ✅ How Cluster Mesh enables direct pod-to-pod communication across clusters
  • ✅ Setting up Cluster Mesh step by step
  • ✅ Service affinity — prefer local, fail over to remote
🎓 CCA Relevance
Architecture 30% Advanced Networking
Cluster Mesh — CCA Exam Essentials
  • Unique IDs: Each cluster must have a unique cluster.id and cluster.name — and non-overlapping Pod CIDRs.
  • Service Affinity: Know that Cilium prefers local pods by default. Remote pods are used only when local pods are unavailable.
  • Direct Pod-to-Pod: Cluster Mesh enables direct pod communication across clusters — no VPN, no service mesh, just eBPF tunnels.

17.1 Why Connect Multiple Clusters?

🌐 Think of Cluster Mesh like a corporate VPN between offices: Your company has offices in New York and London. Each office has its own local network. Without a VPN, employees in NY can't access servers in London. Cluster Mesh is like a zero-configuration VPN between Kubernetes clusters — once connected, pods in any cluster can reach pods in any other cluster using the same service names, as if they were all in one big building. No manual VPN tunnels, no complex routing — Cilium handles it all automatically.

Cluster Mesh enables three critical use cases for production deployments:

Cluster Mesh — anihpj Global Deployment
  CLUSTER: us-east (Virginia)          CLUSTER: eu-west (Frankfurt)
  ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │ anihpj pod  postgres pod │         │ anihpj pod  postgres pod │
  │ (10.0.1.5)   (10.0.1.9)  │         │ (10.0.2.5)   (10.0.2.9)  │
  └───────────┬─────────────┘         └───────────┬─────────────┘
              │                                    │
              │    ┌──────────────────┐            │
              └────│  CLUSTER MESH     │────────────┘
                   │  Encrypted Tunnel │
                   │                    │
                   │  us-east pod ◀───▶ eu-west pod  │
                   │  Direct pod-to-pod!              │
                   └──────────────────┘

  💡 anihpj pod in US → postgres.anihpj.svc → routes to EU!
     Same service name. Same identity. Transparent.
🌍 Three Use Cases for Cluster Mesh

1. High Availability: Run anihpj in us-east and eu-west. If us-east fails, traffic automatically routes to eu-west.

2. Data Locality / Compliance: GDPR requires EU user data to stay in EU. Run a separate cluster in Frankfurt with local PostgreSQL.

3. Disaster Recovery: Maintain a standby cluster in a different region. Cluster Mesh enables near-instant failover.

17.2 Setting Up Cluster Mesh — Step by Step

terminal — Cluster Mesh Setup 
# STEP 1: Enable Cluster Mesh on both clusters during install
cilium install --set cluster.id=1 --set cluster.name=us-east \
               --set clustermesh.enabled=true

cilium install --set cluster.id=2 --set cluster.name=eu-west \
               --set clustermesh.enabled=true

# STEP 2: Establish trust (on cluster 1)
cilium clustermesh connect --destination-context=eu-west

# STEP 3: Verify the mesh
cilium clustermesh status
# → us-east: connected ✅
# → eu-west: connected ✅

# STEP 4: Test cross-cluster communication
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-us-east -- \
  curl anihpj.eu-west.svc.cluster.local:8000
# → Should return 200 OK from the EU cluster!

17.3 Service Affinity — "Prefer Local, Fail Over to Remote"

By default, Cilium prefers local pods when routing service traffic. This is called service affinity. If a local pod is available, traffic stays in the same cluster (lower latency). If the local pod is down, traffic automatically fails over to a remote cluster:

Service Affinity — Local First, Remote as Backup
  anihpj pod (us-east) wants to reach postgres
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Is postgres pod available LOCALLY (us-east)? │
  │                                               │
  │  ✅ YES → Route locally (1ms latency)        │
  │  ❌ NO  → Fail over to eu-west (80ms latency) │
  │           (automatic, no config changes!)     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 17

❌ MISTAKE 1: Same cluster ID on both clusters → Identity conflicts. Each cluster MUST have a unique cluster.id and cluster.name.

❌ MISTAKE 2: Overlapping Pod CIDRs → Routing conflicts. Each cluster must use distinct Pod CIDR ranges.

🔧 Under the Hood — How Cilium Cluster Mesh Works: Global Identities, Cross-Cluster Service Discovery, etcd Proxy, and Multi-Cluster NetworkPolicy
