🔑 CCA Insight: Cluster Mesh is a CCA exam topic for multi-cluster scenarios. Key facts: (1) Global identities — same labels = same numeric ID across clusters. (2) Pod CIDRs MUST NOT overlap. (3) Services can span clusters — eBPF load balances globally. (4) Policies are enforced per-cluster but identities are global. (5) HA/DR benefit: if one cluster fails, traffic routes to remaining backends automatically. (6) etcd is used to synchronize identities and state between clusters.

📝 Chapter 16 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What encryption types does Cilium support?
Show Answer
Answer

WireGuard (recommended) and IPSec. WireGuard is modern, simple, and fast. IPSec is older with wider hardware support (NIC offload).

Q2
Do you need to change your application code for encryption?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Encryption is transparent — Cilium's eBPF programs intercept connections at the socket level and encrypt/decrypt in the kernel. Applications connect as normal.

Q3
How do you enable WireGuard encryption in Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

--set encryption.enabled=true --set encryption.type=wireguard during install. Or cilium config set encryption-enabled true on an existing cluster.

Q4
What is the performance impact of WireGuard encryption?
Show Answer
Answer

Minimal — approximately 3-5% throughput reduction. WireGuard uses efficient ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption and runs entirely in the kernel. Packet overhead is 60 bytes per packet.

Q5
How do you verify that WireGuard encryption is actually working between nodes?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium encrypt status — shows encryption status per node. Should display "OK" with WireGuard key for each peer node. Also check: kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium encrypt status from within the agent. All node pairs should show established WireGuard tunnels.

Q6
What's the difference between WireGuard and IPSec for Cilium encryption?
Show Answer
Answer

WireGuard: modern, simple (4000 lines of code), ChaCha20-Poly1305, kernel 5.6+, ~3-5% overhead. IPSec: older, more complex, wider hardware offload support, works on older kernels. WireGuard is recommended for new deployments due to simplicity and auditability.

Q7
What happens to existing connections when you enable WireGuard on a running cluster?
Show Answer
Answer

Existing connections continue unencrypted until they close naturally. Only NEW connections are encrypted. To ensure all traffic is encrypted, enable encryption during initial cluster setup. If enabling mid-flight, restart pods to force new (encrypted) connections.

Q8
How does Cilium handle WireGuard key management and rotation?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium generates WireGuard key pairs per node automatically. Keys are stored in the CiliumNode CRD. To rotate: cilium encrypt flush regenerates all keys and re-establishes tunnels. Key rotation is transparent to applications — connections may briefly pause but don't drop.

Q9
What kernel version is required for WireGuard and how do you check?
Show Answer
Answer

Kernel 5.6+ for native WireGuard. Check: uname -r and modprobe wireguard. If WireGuard module isn't available, Cilium falls back to IPSec. For older kernels, use IPSec or upgrade the kernel. Most modern distros (Ubuntu 20.04+, RHEL 8.4+) include WireGuard.

Q10
How does transparent encryption affect Hubble observability?
Show Answer
Answer

Hubble sees flows BEFORE encryption — so all L7 visibility (HTTP methods, paths, DNS queries) is preserved. Hubble shows the actual application traffic, not encrypted blobs. Encryption happens after Cilium's eBPF programs process the packet, so observability and security are both fully functional simultaneously.

16.5 Host Firewall — Protecting the Node Itself with eBPF

While Cilium Network Policies protect pod-to-pod communication, the Host Firewall protects the Kubernetes nodes themselves. This is crucial because nodes have direct access to the control plane (kube-apiserver, etcd), SSH ports, and node-level services. An attacker who compromises a node gains far more than one who compromises a single pod.

Host Firewall vs Pod Firewall — Two Layers of Defense
                    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │            EXTERNAL NETWORK               │
                    │  (Attackers, Legitimate users, Internet) │
                    └──────┬───────────────┬───────────────────┘
                           │               │
                    ┌──────▼──────┐  ┌─────▼──────────────────┐
                    │ HOST        │  │                         │
                    │ FIREWALL    │  │ Cilium Pod Network      │
                    │ (This       │  │ Policies                │
                    │  Section)   │  │ (Chapters 9-10)         │
                    │             │  │                         │
                    │ Protects:   │  │ Protects:               │
                    │ • SSH (22)  │  │ • pod→pod traffic       │
                    │ • kubelet   │  │ • pod→external traffic  │
                    │ • API server│  │ • L7 HTTP/Kafka/gRPC    │
                    │ • NodePorts │  │ • DNS-based policies    │
                    │ • Host net  │  │                         │
                    └──────┬──────┘  └──────────▲──────────────┘
                           │                    │
                    ┌──────▼────────────────────┴──────────────┐
                    │         LINUX KERNEL (eBPF)               │
                    │  Both firewalls run as eBPF programs in   │
                    │  the kernel — no iptables, no userspace   │
                    └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

🛡️ Why Host Firewall Matters (CCA Relevance)

The host firewall is essential for defense in depth. Pod policies protect workloads but don't protect node-level services:

Risk Without Host FirewallImpactHost Firewall Mitigation
Open SSH port (22) on nodesBrute force attacks, unauthorized accessRestrict SSH to specific IPs only
Exposed kubelet API (10250)Container escape, pod manipulationAllow only control plane access
NodePort services on all nodesBypass external load balancer restrictionsRestrict NodePort access to specific CIDRs
Host-network podsPods with hostNetwork: true bypass pod policiesHost policies apply to host-networking pods
etcd port exposed (2379)Complete cluster compromiseRestrict to control plane nodes only

🔄 Host Endpoint — A Special Identity

In Cilium, each node is represented as a special endpoint with the label reserved:host and identity 1. Host policies use CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy (CCNP) with a nodeSelector to target specific nodes:

Host Endpoint Architecture
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    KUBERNETES CLUSTER                    │
  │                                                         │
  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐              │
  │  │ Control  │  │ Worker   │  │ Worker   │              │
  │  │ Plane    │  │ Node 1   │  │ Node 2   │              │
  │  │          │  │          │  │          │              │
  │  │ EP ID:1  │  │ EP ID:1  │  │ EP ID:1  │  ← All      │
  │  │reserved: │  │reserved: │  │reserved: │    nodes     │
  │  │  host    │  │  host    │  │  host    │    have      │
  │  │          │  │          │  │          │    identity 1│
  │  │ Policies │  │ Policies │  │ Policies │              │
  │  │ match ON │  │ match ON │  │ match ON │              │
  │  │ node     │  │ node     │  │ node     │              │
  │  │ labels!  │  │ labels!  │  │ labels!  │              │
  │  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘              │
  │                                                         │
  │  Host Policies = CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy          │
  │  with nodeSelector: matchLabels: {role: control-plane}  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📋 Enabling the Host Firewall

Enable during Cilium installation via Helm:

Shell — Enable Host Firewall
helm install cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.16.5 \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set hostFirewall.enabled=true \
  --set devices='{eth0,eth1}'

Verify it's active:

Shell — Verify Host Firewall Status
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status | grep 'Host firewall'
# Output: Host firewall: Enabled [eth0, eth1]

🔖 Labeling Nodes for Host Policy Targeting

Host policies use node labels to select which nodes to apply to:

Shell — Label a Node
kubectl label node worker-1 node-access=ssh
kubectl label node control-plane-1 node-role=master

📜 Host Firewall Policy — Restrict SSH Access

Allows SSH (TCP/22) and ICMP ping from within cluster, blocks everything else from outside:

YAML — Host Firewall Policy (CCNP)
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "host-ssh-only"
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    matchLabels:
      node-access: ssh
  ingress:
  - fromEntities:
    - cluster
  - toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "22"
        protocol: TCP
  - icmps:
    - fields:
      - type: 8
        family: IPv4
  egress:
  - toEntities:
    - cluster
  - toEntities:
    - world
⚠️ CAUTION: Lockout Risk!

If a host policy blocks the Cilium agent's access to kube-apiserver, the agent cannot receive policy updates — including the DELETE to remove the bad policy. Always test in audit mode first!

🔍 Policy Audit Mode — Test Before You Enforce

Audit mode logs what WOULD be blocked without actually blocking:

Shell — Enable Audit Mode
NODE_NAME=worker-1
CILIUM_POD=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pods \
  -l "k8s-app=cilium" \
  -o jsonpath="{.items[?(@.spec.nodeName=='$NODE_NAME')].metadata.name}")
HOST_EP_ID=$(kubectl -n kube-system exec $CILIUM_POD -- \
  cilium-dbg endpoint list -o jsonpath='{[?(@.status.identity.id==1)].id}')
kubectl -n kube-system exec $CILIUM_POD -- \
  cilium-dbg endpoint config $HOST_EP_ID PolicyAuditMode=Enabled

Monitor audit verdicts — blocked traffic shows "action audit" not "action deny":

Shell — Monitor Audit Verdicts
kubectl -n kube-system exec $CILIUM_POD -- \
  cilium-dbg monitor -t policy-verdict --related-to $HOST_EP_ID
# Shows "action audit, match none" — NOT dropped, just logged!

🚨 Emergency Recovery from Lockout

🚨 Recovery Steps (requires SSH/console access)

1. SSH to the node
2. CONTAINERID=$(crictl ps -q --label io.kubernetes.container.name=cilium-agent)
3. crictl exec -ti $CONTAINERID bash
4. cilium-dbg endpoint config $(cilium-dbg endpoint get -l reserved:host -o 'jsonpath={$[0].id}') PolicyAuditMode=Enabled
5. Delete bad CCNP via kubectl
6. kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart ds/cilium

💡 CCA Exam Tip — Host Firewall

Key points: (1) Uses CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy, not CiliumNetworkPolicy. (2) Targets via nodeSelector, not endpointSelector. (3) Host endpoint always has identity 1 and label reserved:host. (4) Always use audit mode first. (5) Applies to host-networking pods too. (6) Emergency recovery needs console access.

📝 Chapter 16 — Host Firewall Practice Questions (5 Additional)

HQ1
What CRD does the Host Firewall use for policies?
Show Answer
Answer

CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy (CCNP). Unlike pod policies which can use either CCNP or CiliumNetworkPolicy (namespaced), host policies are always cluster-scoped since nodes are cluster-level resources.

HQ2
How does the host firewall select which nodes to apply policies to?
Show Answer
Answer

Via nodeSelector with matchLabels — policies match nodes based on Kubernetes node labels, NOT pod labels. Nodes must first be labeled (e.g., kubectl label node worker-1 node-access=ssh), then the policy's nodeSelector matches those labels.

HQ3
What special identity number does every node's host endpoint have?
Show Answer
Answer

Identity 1 with label reserved:host. You can find it with: cilium-dbg endpoint list -o jsonpath='{[?(@.status.identity.id==1)].id}'.

HQ4
Why is audit mode especially important for host policies?
Show Answer
Answer

A bad host policy can lock out the Cilium agent from the API server, preventing policy updates — including deleting the bad policy. Audit mode logs what would be blocked without actually blocking it. Always test in audit mode first.

HQ5
How do you recover if a host firewall policy locks you out?
Show Answer
Answer

Requires out-of-band access (SSH/console): (1) Enter Cilium agent via crictl exec, (2) Enable audit mode on host endpoint, (3) Delete bad CCNP, (4) Restart Cilium daemonset. Audit mode temporarily converts drops to warnings.

16.6 Threat Model — Understanding Cilium's Security Posture

Cilium publishes a formal Threat Model using the STRIDE methodology (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege). This is critical CCA knowledge — understanding what Cilium can and cannot protect against helps you design secure deployments and answer exam questions about security boundaries.

Cilium Threat Model — 8 Attacker Profiles

🔐 Key Protection Boundaries (CCA Must-Know)

Attacker TypeCan Bypass Cilium?Cilium's DefenseAdditional Controls Needed
K8s Workload Attacker
(compromised pod, no host access)		❌ NoNetworkPolicy isolates pods, Hubble audits traffic, bandwidth limits prevent DoSResource limits, Tetragon for runtime detection
Limited-priv Host Attacker
(hostNetwork pod, non-root)		⚠️ Partially — bypasses pod policies for own trafficHost Firewall still applies, traffic attributed to node identityMinimize hostNetwork pods, restrict container runtime access
Root Host Attacker
(full root on node)		✅ Yes — can disable eBPFNone at node level — Cilium relies on kernel integrityNode hardening, audit logging, Tetragon, restrict privileged pods
MITM Attacker
(between nodes)		⚠️ Can sniff trafficTransparent Encryption (WireGuard/IPSec) prevents sniffingAlways enable encryption in production
API Server Attacker
(has kubectl access)		✅ Yes — can modify CRDs, exec into Cilium podsNone at Cilium level — relies on K8s RBACStrict RBAC, audit logging, restrict kube-system access

🛡️ STRIDE in Practice — What the CCA Exam Expects

💡 CCA Exam Tip — Threat Model

Key STRIDE mappings for Cilium:
Spoofing: Cilium assigns cryptographic identities — a pod cannot spoof another pod's identity. BUT: root host attacker CAN spoof any identity from that node.
Tampering: Cilium eBPF programs run in kernel — only root can tamper. API server attacker can tamper with CRDs.
Information Disclosure: MITM attacker can sniff UNENCRYPTED traffic. Enable WireGuard/IPSec. Hubble metrics exposed to Prometheus can leak flow data — use TLS.
Denial of Service: Workload without resource limits can starve Cilium. Use bandwidth manager + resource limits.
Elevation of Privilege: hostNetwork: true pod bypasses pod policies and gains node-level network access. Use Host Firewall + restrict hostNetwork.

📋 Cilium's 9 Production Hardening Recommendations

Production Security Checklist (from Official Threat Model)
  ✅ 1. Scoped K8s RBAC — limit access to kube-system, secrets, exec
  ✅ 2. Resource limits on all workloads — prevent DoS against Cilium
  ✅ 3. Minimize privileged pods — only grant CAP_BPF/CAP_NET_ADMIN if essential
  ✅ 4. Network Policies — least-privilege allow rules
  ✅ 5. Transparent Encryption — WireGuard or IPSec for all inter-node traffic
  ✅ 6. K8s Audit Logging — forward to centralized platform, alert on anomalies
  ✅ 7. TLS for Hubble — Hubble Relay, Hubble UI, and all metrics endpoints
  ✅ 8. Tetragon — runtime security for detecting container escapes
  ✅ 9. Constrain toFQDNs DNS trust — prefer cluster DNS only
⚠️ Critical Insight: Root = Game Over

The threat model is clear: if an attacker gains root on a node, Cilium cannot protect that node. Root can disable eBPF, modify programs, spoof any identity, and access IPSec pre-shared keys. If the compromised node runs cilium-operator, the attacker can compromise the entire cluster. Node security is your last line of defense.

📝 Chapter 16 — Threat Model Practice Questions (5 Additional)

TQ1
What methodology does Cilium's threat model use?
Show Answer
Answer

STRIDE — Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege. It analyzes 8 attacker types placed at different parts of the deployment stack.

TQ2
Can a compromised pod (without host access) bypass Cilium network policies?
Show Answer
Answer

No. A compromised pod without host access is fully constrained by Cilium's NetworkPolicy, identity-based enforcement, and Hubble auditing. This is the attacker type Cilium handles best.

TQ3
What's the risk if an attacker gains kubectl exec access to a Cilium agent pod?
Show Answer
Answer

They become a root-equivalent host attacker — can disable eBPF, modify programs, access IPSec keys, spoof any pod identity, and potentially escalate to cluster-wide compromise. This is why RBAC on kube-system namespace is critical.

TQ4
How does a MITM attacker between nodes affect Cilium traffic?
Show Answer
Answer

Without Transparent Encryption, a MITM can inspect all inter-node traffic in both overlay and native routing modes. They can also inject forged packets. Mitigation: Enable WireGuard or IPSec encryption — this makes traffic unreadable to MITM attackers.

TQ5
Why is the threat model important for the CCA exam?
Show Answer
Answer

The CCA exam tests your understanding of Cilium's security boundaries — what Cilium CAN protect against (pod compromise, MITM with encryption) vs what it CANNOT (root on node, API server compromise). Knowing these boundaries helps you answer architecture and security scenario questions correctly.

Chapter 18: Egress Gateway — Controlling Outbound Traffic

When pods call external APIs, their source IP is SNAT'd to the node's IP — which changes with every pod restart or node migration. Egress Gateway solves this by routing outbound traffic through designated gateway nodes with fixed, predictable IPs. Essential for API whitelisting, compliance, and security.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~45 min 🌐 Egress

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The egress problem — why pod IPs are unpredictable externally
  • ✅ How Egress Gateway provides fixed outbound IPs
  • ✅ Egress Gateway with Cluster Mesh for geo-specific APIs
🎓 CCA Relevance
Architecture 30% Egress Control
Egress Gateway — CCA Exam Essentials

  • Use Case: Fixed egress IPs for API whitelisting, compliance, and audit logging. Know when to use it vs default SNAT.
  • Gateway Nodes: Must be labeled (e.g., egress: gateway). Without the label, the policy has no effect.
🎓 CCA Relevance
Architecture 30% Egress Control
Egress Gateway — CCA Exam Essentials
  • CRD Name: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy — know the apiVersion and required fields (selectors, destinationCIDRs, egressGateway).
  • Use Case: Fixed egress IPs for API whitelisting, compliance, and audit logging. Know when to use it vs default SNAT.
  • Gateway Nodes: Must be labeled (e.g., egress: gateway). Without the label, the policy has no effect.

18.1 The Egress Problem — What IP Does Your Pod Use Externally?

🏢 Think of it like a large office building: Every desk (pod) has an internal extension number (10.0.1.5). When someone calls an external number (api.stripe.com), the office phone system replaces the internal extension with the building's main number (the node's IP). The external party sees the building's number — not the individual desk. Now imagine you need Stripe to whitelist your calls. Which number do you give them? The building number changes if you move desks (pod restarts on a different node). Egress Gateway solves this by routing all external calls through a dedicated reception desk with a fixed, permanent phone number.

By default, when a pod calls an external API, Kubernetes performs SNAT (Source NAT) — the pod's internal IP is replaced with the node's IP. This creates two problems:

Default Egress vs Egress Gateway
  DEFAULT (SNAT to Node IP):
  anihpj pod → Node IP (10.0.0.1) → api.stripe.com
  ❌ Node IP changes if pod moves to different node
  ❌ Different pods on different nodes → different IPs
  ❌ Can't whitelist at the API side

  WITH EGRESS GATEWAY:
  anihpj pod → Gateway Node (192.168.1.100) → api.stripe.com
  ✅ Fixed, predictable IP regardless of pod location
  ✅ All anihpj pods egress through the same gateway
  ✅ Whitelist 192.168.1.100 at stripe.com once!

18.2 Cilium Egress Gateway — Fixed IP for Outbound Traffic

egress-gateway-policy.yaml 
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
  name: anihpj-stripe-egress
spec:
  selectors:
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: anihpj              # Apply to anihpj pods
  destinationCIDRs:
  - "54.187.0.0/16"             # Stripe's IP range
  egressGateway:
    nodeSelector:
      matchLabels:
        egress: gateway           # Gateway node label
    egressIP: "192.168.1.100"    # Fixed egress IP

# Now all anihpj → Stripe traffic exits through
# 192.168.1.100 — a fixed, whitelistable IP!

18.3 Egress Gateway with Cluster Mesh

Egress Gateway integrates with Cluster Mesh for geo-specific egress. For example, anihpj pods in eu-west can egress through a Frankfurt gateway (GDPR compliance — data never leaves EU), while us-east pods egress through a Virginia gateway:

🌍 Geo-Specific Egress Example

eu-west cluster: Egress through Frankfurt gateway (192.168.2.100) → European payment processor, European Stripe endpoint.

us-east cluster: Egress through Virginia gateway (192.168.1.100) → US payment processor, US Stripe endpoint.

Result: Each region's traffic exits from its own gateway with a predictable, region-specific IP. GDPR compliance met — EU data never transits through US infrastructure.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls — Chapter 18

❌ MISTAKE 1: Not labeling gateway nodes → Policy has no effect. Gateway nodes must have the matching label (e.g., egress: gateway).

❌ MISTAKE 2: Egress IP not routable → External services can't return traffic. The egress IP must be on the same subnet as the gateway node or have a route back.

🔧 Under the Hood — How Cilium Egress Gateway Works: SNAT Masquerading, Gateway Node Selection, Policy-Based Routing, and the Egress IP Lifecycle

🔄 Gateway Node Failure — What Happens and How Cilium Recovers
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  GATEWAY NODE FAILURE — Detection, Recovery, and Impact                          │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ BEFORE FAILURE:                                                         │   │
│  │ (gateway=node-1, egressIP=203.0.113.10)                                │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  Pod-A → eBPF redirect → node-1 → SNAT (203.0.113.10) → Internet      │   │
│  │  Pod-B → eBPF redirect → node-1 → SNAT (203.0.113.10) → Internet      │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 🔴 node-1 GOES DOWN (power loss, kernel panic, network partition)      │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ PHASE 1: DETECTION (~5-10 seconds)                                      │   │
│  │ • Cilium Operator detects node-1 NotReady (via K8s API watch)          │   │
│  │ • Or: agent heartbeat times out (if using direct health checks)        │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ PHASE 2: GATEWAY RE-SELECTION (~2-5 seconds)                            │   │
│  │ • Operator finds next matching node (nodeSelector: egress-gw=true)     │   │
│  │ • Selects node-2 (also has label egress-gw=true)                        │   │
│  │ • Updates CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy status: gatewayNode=node-2         │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ PHASE 3: eBPF REPROGRAMMING (~1 second)                                 │   │
│  │ • All Cilium Agents detect gateway change → reprogram eBPF redirect     │   │
│  │ • Pod-A → eBPF redirect → node-2 → SNAT (203.0.113.10) → Internet     │   │
│  │ • Pod-B → eBPF redirect → node-2 → SNAT (203.0.113.10) → Internet     │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ IMPACT ON EXISTING CONNECTIONS:                                          │   │
│  │ • TCP connections through node-1: BROKEN (RST, must reconnect)          │   │
│  │ • New connections: transparently use node-2 (no app changes)            │   │
│  │ • Total recovery: ~10-15 seconds (detection + switch + eBPF update)     │   │
│  │ • Applications should implement retry logic (standard best practice)    │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 Egress Gateway Use Cases — When You Need a Fixed IP
ScenarioWhy Fixed IP MattersWithout Egress GW
Stripe/Payment APIStripe whitelists your IP for API accessEvery node has different IP → whitelist impossible
AWS RDS Security GroupRDS SG only allows specific source IPsNode IPs change on scale/replace → constant SG updates
Third-Party VPNVPN peer expects traffic from one IPMultiple node IPs → VPN policy violation
PCI-DSS ComplianceAuditors require known, auditable egress pointsPods egress from random node IPs → audit trail impossible
SOC2 ComplianceAll outbound traffic must pass through known gatewaysUncontrolled egress → compliance failure
GDPR Data ResidencyEnsure data only leaves via specific geo-IPPods may egress from nodes in wrong region
🔑 CCA Insight: Egress Gateway is the solution for "I need my pods to have a fixed, predictable egress IP for firewall whitelisting." Key facts: (1) Configured via CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy CRD. (2) Gateway nodes need a label (nodeSelector) and the egress IP configured on their NIC. (3) eBPF on source nodes redirects to gateway; gateway does SNAT. (4) Required for compliance: PCI-DSS, SOC2 often require known egress IPs. (5) Gateway node failure = existing connections break, new connections use new gateway.

📝 Chapter 17 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What's the main use case for Cluster Mesh?
Show Answer
Answer

Connecting multiple Kubernetes clusters into a single virtual network. Enables high availability across regions, disaster recovery, and data locality/compliance (e.g., GDPR). Pods in different clusters can communicate directly using the same service names.

Q2
Can pods in different clusters communicate directly?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes. With Cluster Mesh, pods in different clusters can communicate directly using the same IP space and identities. A pod in us-east can reach postgres.anihpj.svc which resolves to a pod in eu-west if no local pod is available.

Q3
What is service affinity in Cluster Mesh?
Show Answer
Answer

Service affinity means Cilium prefers local pods (same cluster) over remote pods (different cluster). This minimizes latency. If no local pod is available, traffic automatically fails over to a remote cluster — no configuration changes needed.

Q4
What prerequisites must be met before setting up Cluster Mesh?
Show Answer
Answer

1) Each cluster must have a UNIQUE cluster name and ID, 2) Pod CIDRs must NOT overlap between clusters, 3) Clusters must be able to reach each other on ports 4240 (health) and 4244 (data), 4) Same Cilium major.minor version, 5) TLS certificates configured for mutual authentication.

Q5
What ports need to be open between clusters for Cluster Mesh?
Show Answer
Answer

Port 4240 (TCP) for health checks and cluster discovery. Port 4244 (UDP) for VXLAN-encapsulated pod-to-pod data traffic. Both ports must be open bi-directionally between all clusters in the mesh.

Q6
How do you verify Cluster Mesh connectivity between two clusters?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium clustermesh status --verbose from either cluster. Shows connected clusters, node-to-node tunnel status, and any errors. Also: cilium connectivity test --context kind-cluster1 --multi-cluster kind-cluster2 validates cross-cluster pod communication.

Q7
What happens if two clusters in a mesh have overlapping Pod CIDR ranges?
Show Answer
Answer

Routing conflicts — Cilium won't know which cluster a pod IP belongs to. Traffic to overlapping IPs would be ambiguous. This is a hard requirement: pod CIDRs MUST be unique across all clusters in the mesh. Plan CIDR ranges before creating clusters.

Q8
How does Cilium handle service discovery across clusters in Cluster Mesh?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium creates a global service that spans all clusters. When a pod resolves a service name, Cilium returns backends from ALL clusters (local first via service affinity). If local backends exist, traffic stays local. If none, traffic automatically routes to remote cluster backends.

Q9
What happens to cross-cluster traffic if one cluster in the mesh goes down?
Show Answer
Answer

Pods in the failed cluster become unreachable. Traffic destined for services that had backends in the failed cluster automatically routes to remaining healthy backends in other clusters. This is the HA/DR benefit — no configuration change needed for failover.

Q10
Can you apply CiliumNetworkPolicies across clusters in a Cluster Mesh?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes, partially. CiliumNetworkPolicies are enforced per-cluster (they're namespace-scoped CRDs). However, Cilium identities are global across the mesh, so policies based on identity work across clusters. CCNP is cluster-scoped — each cluster needs its own CCNP for cross-cluster rules.

Chapter 19: CCA Exam Strategy — How to Pass First Time

The CCA (Certified Cilium Associate) exam tests your knowledge across 5 domains in 90 minutes. This chapter gives you the complete strategy: exam format, time allocation, documentation bookmarks, and the top 10 mistakes to avoid. Follow this plan and you'll walk into the exam confident and prepared.

🟢 All Levels ⏱️ ~1 hour 🎯 Exam Strategy
🎯 Why This Chapter Matters for CCA

Exam strategy is the difference between knowing the material and passing the test. The CCA is an open-book, timed exam — you need to know HOW to use the docs efficiently, HOW to manage your 90 minutes, and WHAT mistakes to avoid. This chapter directly prepares you for exam day with a proven strategy.

🧠 CCA Exam Mindset

Think of the CCA like a scavenger hunt, not a memory test. You don't need to memorize every YAML field — you need to know which doc page has the answer and how to find it in under 60 seconds. The exam tests your ability to apply Cilium concepts, not recite facts. Every question is multiple choice, so even if you're unsure, you can eliminate wrong answers.

  • 1.5 min per question — Don't spend 5 minutes on one question. Flag and return.
  • docs.cilium.io is your friend — But only if you know which page has what.
  • Read EVERY answer — Sometimes the "best" answer isn't the first one.
  • Trust your first instinct — Your gut is usually right. Only change answers with evidence.

🔖 How to Use Bookmarks During the Exam

1. Open the docs BEFORE starting: Have docs.cilium.io open in a separate browser tab before the exam begins.

2. Use Ctrl+F to search: Don't browse — search for keywords like "toFQDNs", "Maglev", "CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy".

3. Know which page has what: Memorize the mapping above. When you see a policy question → go straight to /security/policy/.

4. Don't over-rely on docs: You only have ~1.5 minutes per question. Use docs for syntax verification, not to learn concepts from scratch.

19.3 Top 10 CCA Exam Mistakes to Avoid

1 Confusing K8s NetworkPolicy with CiliumNetworkPolicy — CNP has L7, DNS, identity. K8s NetPol is L3/L4 only.
2 Not knowing Hubble CLI flags — --verdict DROPPED, --from-pod, --to-namespace are essential.
3 Forgetting identity-based policies — Cilium enforces by identity (labels→numeric ID), not IP. Pod restarts don't break policies.
4 Mixing up ingress and egress — ingress = INTO selected pod. egress = OUT FROM selected pod. DB protection uses ingress on DB selector.
5 Not understanding eBPF basics — Know the lifecycle (Write→Compile→Verify→JIT→Attach→Execute) and why it's safe (verifier).
6 Overlooking Cluster Mesh — Know why you'd connect clusters (HA, DR, compliance) and that pods communicate directly.
7 Not knowing Cilium CRDs — CiliumNetworkPolicy, CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy, CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy, CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy.
8 Forgetting L7 policy capabilities — Cilium can filter by HTTP method, path, headers, gRPC method, Kafka topic, and DNS FQDN.
9 Not practicing with real YAML — Read the YAML, understand each field. The exam will ask "what does this policy do?" — not "write YAML from scratch."
10 Spending too long on one question — Flag it, move on, come back. 90 min / 60 questions = 1.5 min each. Don't get stuck!

Q1
How long is the CCA exam and how many questions?
Show Answer
Answer

90 minutes, approximately 60 multiple-choice questions across 5 domains. That's about 1.5 minutes per question.

📝 Chapter 18 — CCA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
Why might you need a fixed egress IP for your pods?
Show Answer
Answer

For API whitelisting (external services only accept requests from known IPs), compliance (audit logs show a consistent source IP), and security (identify all outbound traffic from a specific IP range).

Q2
What CRD configures egress gateway in Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy. It defines: which pods (podSelector), which destinations (destinationCIDRs), and which gateway node/IP to use (egressGateway).

Q3
Can egress gateway work with Cluster Mesh?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes. Each cluster in the mesh can have its own egress gateway with region-specific IPs. This enables geo-specific egress — EU pods egress through EU gateway, US pods through US gateway.

Q4
How does CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy select which pods to apply to?
Show Answer
Answer

Via podSelector with matchLabels. Pods matching the selector have their egress traffic routed through the gateway. You can also use namespaceSelector to apply to entire namespaces. Multiple selectors are OR'd together.

Q5
What happens if the egress gateway node fails?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium automatically selects another healthy gateway node (if available). Traffic may briefly pause during failover. For high availability, label multiple nodes as egress gateways — Cilium load-balances across them. External connections to the failed node break; new connections use the new gateway.

Q6
What is the difference between egress gateway and standard Kubernetes egress?
Show Answer
Answer

Standard K8s egress: each pod uses its node's IP (via SNAT) — different pods on different nodes have different source IPs. Egress Gateway: ALL selected pods share ONE consistent source IP regardless of which node they run on. Essential for IP whitelisting with external services.

Q7
How do you specify which external destinations use the egress gateway?
Show Answer
Answer

Via destinationCIDRs in the CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy. 0.0.0.0/0 routes ALL traffic through the gateway. Or specify specific ranges: ["54.187.0.0/16", "34.192.0.0/12"] to only route AWS us-west-2 traffic through the gateway.

Q8
Can you have different egress IPs for different namespaces or pods?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes. Create multiple CiliumEgressGatewayPolicies with different podSelector and egressIP values. Frontend pods egress through 203.0.113.10, backend pods through 203.0.113.11. Each policy is independent, and pods matching multiple policies use the first matching policy.

Q9
What are the requirements for a node to serve as an egress gateway?
Show Answer
Answer

1) Node must have the matching label (e.g., egress-gw: true), 2) The egressIP must be configured on the node's network interface, 3) The egress IP must be routable from the external services, 4) Node must have sufficient bandwidth to handle all selected pods' egress traffic.

Q10
How do you verify that egress gateway is working correctly?
Show Answer
Answer

1) cilium egress list shows active policies, 2) From a selected pod, run curl ifconfig.me — should show the egress IP, not the node IP, 3) Hubble: hubble observe --from-pod ns/pod --verdict FORWARDED to verify traffic is flowing, 4) External service logs should show the egress IP.

Q2
Is the CCA exam open book? What resources are allowed?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes — docs.cilium.io is allowed during the exam. No other websites, notes, or external resources are permitted.

Q3
Which domain has the highest weight on the CCA exam?
Show Answer
Answer

Architecture & Concepts at 30%. Network Policy and Service Mesh are tied at 20% each. Observability is 18%. Installation is 12%.

Q4
What's the most important exam strategy tip?
Show Answer
Answer

Pre-bookmark the Cilium docs pages you'll need. Use Ctrl+F to search. Don't spend more than 1.5 minutes per question — flag difficult ones and return later. The docs are your lifeline, but only if you know exactly which page has what.

Q5
What is the passing score for the CCA exam?
Show Answer
Answer

Isovalent/Cilium has NOT publicly disclosed the exact passing score. Industry estimates suggest ~65-70%. Focus on mastering all 5 domains rather than targeting a specific number — the exam uses statistical scoring that adjusts per question difficulty.

Q6
How should you manage your time across the 5 domains in the CCA exam?
Show Answer
Answer

Spend time proportionally to domain weight: Architecture 25 min (30%), Network Policy 18 min (20%), Service Mesh 18 min (20%), Observability 16 min (18%), Installation 13 min (12%). However, answer easy questions first regardless of domain — don't waste time on hard architecture questions if easy network policy questions are waiting.

Q7
What specific Cilium documentation pages should you bookmark for the exam?
Show Answer
Answer

/security/policy/ (CNP syntax), /observability/hubble/ (CLI flags), /gettingstarted/ (install options), /network/servicemesh/ (mTLS, canary), /network/clustermesh/ (setup), /security/encryption/ (WireGuard), /network/bgp/ (peering), /concepts/ (architecture). Open docs.cilium.io BEFORE the exam starts.

Q8
What should you do if you encounter a question about a topic you've never seen before?
Show Answer
Answer

1) Don't panic — flag it and move on, 2) Use Ctrl+F on docs.cilium.io to search for keywords from the question, 3) Eliminate obviously wrong answers (usually 2 out of 4 are clearly wrong), 4) Make your best guess from remaining options, 5) Return to flagged questions in the last 10 minutes. Never leave a question unanswered.

Q9
What is the CCA exam retake policy and cost?
Show Answer
Answer

The CCA exam costs $250 USD and includes ONE free retake. If you fail, you can retake after a waiting period (typically 7 days). Additional retakes cost $250 each. Schedule your exam when you're consistently scoring 80%+ on practice tests.

Q10
What's the #1 exam day mistake and how do you avoid it?
Show Answer
Answer

Spending too long on one question. At 1.5 min/question, a 5-minute stuck question costs you 3 other questions. Avoid by: (1) Answer easy questions first (5 min skim at start), (2) Flag hard questions immediately, (3) Use docs search (Ctrl+F) not browsing, (4) Return to flagged questions in the last 10 minutes with fresh eyes. Time management beats knowledge depth on timed exams.

Categorize every mistake: knowledge gap (study the concept), distractor trap (learn the pattern), time pressure (practice speed), or docs failure (improve navigation). 20.1 Domain 1: Architecture & Concepts (30%) — 20 Questions

Architecture Practice Questions

Q1
What makes eBPF safe for production kernel use?
Show Answer
Answer

The eBPF verifier — it mathematically proves programs always terminate, never access memory out of bounds, and execute at most 1M instructions. Unsafe programs are rejected before loading.

Q2
Which Cilium component runs as a DaemonSet?
Show Answer
Answer

The Cilium Agent — one per node. The Operator runs as a Deployment (cluster-wide tasks like IPAM).

Q3
How does Cilium assign identities to pods?
Show Answer
Answer

Based on pod labels. All pods with the same set of labels get the same numeric identity. The CiliumIdentity CRD stores this mapping.

Q4
What is the difference between CNP and CCNP?
Show Answer
Answer

CNP (CiliumNetworkPolicy) is namespace-scoped. CCNP (CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy) applies cluster-wide across all namespaces. CNP takes priority over CCNP.

Q5
What CRDs does Cilium create on installation?
Show Answer
Answer

9 CRDs including CiliumNetworkPolicy, CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy, CiliumEndpoint, CiliumIdentity, CiliumNode, CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy, and others.

Q6
What is the eBPF datapath? Why is it faster than iptables?
Show Answer
Answer

The eBPF datapath processes packets directly in the kernel at the lowest hook points (XDP, TC). Unlike iptables which processes rules sequentially (O(n)), eBPF uses hash maps for O(1) lookups — making it up to 587x faster with 10,000 rules.

Q7
What is a CiliumEndpoint? How is it different from a Kubernetes Endpoint?
Show Answer
Answer

A CiliumEndpoint (CEP) is a CRD representing each pod's networking state — its identity, IP, policy enforcement status, and eBPF map references. Kubernetes Endpoints just list pod IP:port pairs for Services. CEP is much richer, tracking per-pod security state.

Q8
What happens when a pod with identity 12345 restarts and gets a new IP?
Show Answer
Answer

The pod keeps identity 12345 (based on labels). All existing policies referencing identity 12345 continue working — no policy updates needed. The new IP is mapped to the same identity. This is why identity-based policies are so powerful.

Q9
What kernel hooks does Cilium use for networking?
Show Answer
Answer

XDP (earliest hook, before SKB allocation), TC ingress/egress (traffic control), socket layer (connect/accept), and cgroup hooks (socket-level enforcement). XDP is the fastest since it processes packets before the kernel allocates memory.

Q10
What is the Cilium Operator and why is it a Deployment, not a DaemonSet?
Show Answer
Answer

The Operator handles cluster-wide tasks: IPAM (allocating pod CIDRs), garbage collecting old CiliumIdentities, synchronizing with KVStore, and managing node heartbeats. It runs as a Deployment (usually 1-2 replicas) because it doesn't need to be on every node — it works at the cluster level.

20.2 Domain 2: Network Policy (20%) — 15 Questions

Network Policy Practice Questions

Q1
What does {} mean in fromEndpoints?
Show Answer
Answer

ALLOW FROM ANY SOURCE — all pods, all namespaces, all CIDRs. Use for public endpoints like frontend. Never use for databases.

Q2
How does toFQDNs work in a CiliumNetworkPolicy?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium watches DNS responses, caches resolved IPs for the FQDN, and dynamically adds them to the allowed egress eBPF map. When DNS TTL expires, IPs are removed.

Q3
What is policy audit mode?
Show Answer
Answer

Audit mode (enableAudit: true) LOGS policy violations but does NOT block traffic. Use it to observe what WOULD be blocked before enforcing.

Q4
Which takes priority: CNP or CCNP?
Show Answer
Answer

CNP (namespace-scoped) takes priority over CCNP (cluster-wide). More specific wins over more general.

Q5
Why must you always allow DNS (UDP 53) in egress policies?
Show Answer
Answer

Pods need DNS to resolve service names and external domains. Without it, pods can't discover services. Always add egress UDP 53 to CoreDNS.

Q6
What is the difference between toPorts and toServices in CNP?
Show Answer
Answer

toPorts filters by port number and protocol (L3/L4). toServices maps to Kubernetes Services by name, allowing Cilium to enforce policy at the service level rather than individual pods. toServices survives pod IP changes automatically.

Q7
What is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy? When would you use it?
Show Answer
Answer

CCNP applies across ALL namespaces in the cluster. Use it for: (1) Monitoring/security tools that need cluster-wide access, (2) Default-deny-all baseline policies, (3) DNS policies that apply everywhere. CNP takes priority over CCNP.

Q8
How do you write a policy that allows HTTP GET to /api/v1 but blocks POST/PUT/DELETE?
Show Answer
Answer

Use L7 rules with toPorts.rules.http: - method: GET; path: /api/v1/.*. Only GET is allowed to that path. POST/PUT/DELETE are implicitly denied (default deny behavior). The policy must also include the standard toPorts for the TCP port.

Q9
What happens when two CNPs select the same pod with conflicting rules?
Show Answer
Answer

Rules are UNIONED — the pod gets the MOST permissive combination. If Policy-A allows port 80 and Policy-B allows port 443, the pod gets both. This is different from firewalls where last rule wins.

Q10
How does Cilium handle DNS-based egress policies differently from IP-based?
Show Answer
Answer

With toFQDNs, Cilium watches DNS responses and dynamically populates the egress eBPF map with resolved IPs. When DNS TTL expires, old IPs are removed and new ones added on the next DNS query. This means policies automatically track changing IPs without manual updates — unlike IP-based rules that break when IPs change.

20.3 Domain 3: Service Mesh & LB (20%) — 15 Questions

Service Mesh Practice Questions

Q1
How much RAM does Cilium's sidecar-less mesh add per pod?
Show Answer
Answer

Zero (0 MB). eBPF programs run in the kernel — no sidecar container, no proxy process, no extra memory.

Q2
What flag enables kube-proxy replacement?
Show Answer
Answer

--set kubeProxyReplacement=true during cilium install.

Q3
What is Maglev hashing used for?
Show Answer
Answer

Consistent hashing for service load balancing. Ensures even backend distribution, connection affinity, and minimal disruption when backends change.

Q4
How does Cilium handle canary deployments?
Show Answer
Answer

Identity-based traffic splitting. Pods with different labels get different identities. eBPF load balancers split traffic by identity — no sidecar needed.

Q5
What CRD configures BGP peering?
Show Answer
Answer

CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy (apiVersion: cilium.io/v2alpha1).

Q6
What is the difference between Cilium's mTLS and Istio's mTLS?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium's mTLS uses the kernel's eBPF + WireGuard/IPSec — no sidecar, no Envoy proxy. Istio uses sidecar Envoy proxies for mTLS. Cilium's approach is lower latency (no userspace proxy hop), lower resource usage, and transparent to applications.

Q7
What is an Ingress resource vs CiliumIngressClass? How do they relate?
Show Answer
Answer

Ingress is the standard K8s resource for HTTP routing. CiliumIngressClass is a custom IngressClass that tells the cluster to use Cilium's built-in Envoy-based ingress controller instead of nginx/traefik. No separate ingress controller deployment needed.

Q8
How does Cilium implement L7 load balancing (HTTP/gRPC)?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium embeds a minimal Envoy proxy (per-node, not per-pod) for L7 processing. eBPF redirects traffic to the local Envoy on the same node, which handles HTTP/gRPC routing, retries, timeouts, and rate limiting. The application pod never sees Envoy — it's transparent.

Q9
What is the difference between DSR and SNAT for Service load balancing?
Show Answer
Answer

DSR (Direct Server Return): Backend pod responds directly to the client, bypassing the load balancer on the return path. Faster, but requires special network setup. SNAT: Load balancer rewrites source IP to its own, so return traffic comes back through it. Simpler but adds a bottleneck. Cilium supports both modes.

Q10
What replaces kube-proxy when kubeProxyReplacement is enabled?
Show Answer
Answer

eBPF programs attached to each node's network devices handle Service ClusterIP translation, NodePort, ExternalIPs, and LoadBalancer services. Maglev consistent hashing distributes traffic. The eBPF socket-level load balancer handles connect() syscall redirection, eliminating the iptables DNAT hop entirely.

20.4 Domain 4: Observability & Hubble (18%) — 12 Questions

Observability Practice Questions

Q1
What command shows only DROPPED traffic?
Show Answer
Answer

hubble observe --verdict DROPPED

Q2
What is Hubble Relay?
Show Answer
Answer

A cluster-wide deployment that aggregates flow data from all Cilium agents. CLI and UI connect to Relay for a unified view.

Q3
What Hubble metrics are available?
Show Answer
Answer

Flow (TCP), HTTP (L7), DNS, TCP flags, ICMP, and Drop (policy denies). Enable with hubble.metrics.enabled.

Q4
How do you access Hubble UI?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium hubble ui or kubectl port-forward -n kube-system svc/hubble-ui 12000:80 then open localhost:12000.

Q5
What does Hubble show that tcpdump doesn't?
Show Answer
Answer

Pod names, namespaces, Kubernetes identities, policy verdicts, HTTP methods/paths, DNS queries, and the specific policy rule that matched.

Q6
How do you filter Hubble flows to show only HTTP traffic from a specific pod?
Show Answer
Answer

hubble observe --from-pod namespace/podname --protocol http or use --from-label app=frontend --http-method GET. Combine with --verdict FORWARDED or --verdict DROPPED for policy troubleshooting.

Q7
What is the Hubble Service Map and how is it generated?
Show Answer
Answer

The Service Map is a real-time dependency graph in Hubble UI showing which services talk to which. It's built from Hubble flow data — each flow between identities becomes an edge in the graph. Green edges = allowed, red edges = dropped, thickness = traffic volume.

Q8
How do you integrate Hubble metrics with Prometheus?
Show Answer
Answer

Enable with hubble.metrics.enabled and configure which metrics to expose. Cilium agents expose a /metrics endpoint. Use a Prometheus ServiceMonitor or PodMonitor to scrape. Common metrics: hubble_flows_processed_total, hubble_tcp_flags_total, hubble_http_requests_total.

Q9
What's the difference between cilium monitor and hubble observe?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium monitor shows raw eBPF events from a SINGLE node — packet-level debugging. hubble observe shows cluster-wide flow data aggregated through Hubble Relay — higher-level, policy-aware, with pod names and verdicts. Use monitor for low-level debugging, hubble for operational visibility.

Q10
How can you troubleshoot why a pod can't reach an external API?
Show Answer
Answer

Step 1: hubble observe --from-pod ns/pod --verdict DROPPED to see if a policy is blocking it. Step 2: Check cilium policy get for the pod's namespace. Step 3: Verify DNS resolution: hubble observe --from-pod ns/pod --to-port 53. Step 4: Check egress gateway and toFQDNs policies if configured.

20.5 Domain 5: Installation & Operations (12%) — 8 Questions

Installation Practice Questions

Q1
What is the minimum Linux kernel for Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

Kernel 5.10 or higher. Recommended 5.15+ or 6.1+ for best eBPF support.

Q2
What does cilium connectivity test verify?
Show Answer
Answer

21+ tests: Pod-to-Pod, Services, DNS, NetworkPolicy, Encryption, Hubble, and Performance.

Q3
Can you run two CNIs simultaneously?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Both will try to assign IPs and manage interfaces, causing conflicts. Remove the old CNI first.

Q4
What does cilium status show?
Show Answer
Answer

Component health (Agent, Operator, Hubble Relay, Hubble UI, Encryption), DaemonSet/Deployment status, and cluster pod count.

Q5
How do you generate a support bundle?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium bugtool — collects logs, eBPF map dumps, configuration, and cluster state into a tarball.

Q6
What is the difference between cilium install and helm install?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium install is the CLI wrapper that auto-detects your cluster (EKS, GKE, AKS, kind) and sets optimal defaults. helm install gives you full control over every Helm value but requires knowing the right settings for your environment. Both produce the same result — cilium install is simpler for most cases.

Q7
How do you migrate from an existing CNI (e.g., Calico) to Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

Generally requires draining nodes and reinstalling. Steps: (1) Cordon and drain one node, (2) Remove old CNI, (3) Install Cilium on that node, (4) Uncordon, (5) Verify pod connectivity, (6) Repeat for remaining nodes. Some cloud providers support in-place migration — check docs.cilium.io for your platform.

Q8
What does cilium connectivity test check that cilium status doesn't?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium status checks component health (are agents running?). cilium connectivity test validates FUNCTIONALITY: Can pods communicate? Do NetworkPolicies block correctly? Does DNS work? Is encryption active? Does Hubble see flows? It's an end-to-end validation, not just a health check.

Q9
What are the prerequisites for running Cilium in a production cluster?
Show Answer
Answer

Linux kernel 5.10+ (5.15+ recommended), eBPF enabled (CONFIG_BPF=y), Kubernetes 1.21+, kube-proxy replacement requires kubeProxyReplacement=true, direct routing or tunnel mode (VXLAN/Geneve), and for WireGuard encryption, kernel 5.6+.

Q10
What does cilium upgrade do and when should you use it vs reinstall?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium upgrade updates the Cilium version in-place, preserving your existing configuration. Use it for minor/patch upgrades within the same major version. Use cilium install (reinstall) when changing major configuration options like switching from tunnel to direct routing. Always read release notes before upgrading.

🚀 Why This Chapter Matters for Your Career

The CCA certification opens doors, but it's what you do AFTER certification that defines your career. This chapter maps out the complete Kubernetes certification journey, gives you real portfolio projects to demonstrate your skills, and connects you with the vibrant eBPF/Cilium community. Companies are actively hiring Cilium expertise — make yourself visible.

🏆 The CCA + CKA Combination Strategy

The most powerful career move you can make: get CCA FIRST (it's easier, more focused), then tackle CKA. Why?

  • CCA teaches you WHY networking works — CKA tests you on HOW to configure it. Understanding the "why" makes the "how" much easier.
  • CCA is newer, less known — Early adopters stand out. Being among the first CCA-certified professionals gives you a unique differentiator.
  • Both certs combined = Kubernetes Networking Expert — You can debug pod communication issues that stump CKA-only admins.
  • Estimated salary bump: Cilium/eBPF skills command a 15-25% premium over standard Kubernetes roles.

📚 Appendices — Quick Reference

Six comprehensive appendices for quick lookup during study and exam preparation. Bookmark this section!

Appendix A: Cilium CLI Command Reference

Every cilium and hubble command you need, organized by category. CCA Exam Tip: You don't need to memorize every flag — but you DO need to know which command solves which problem. Use Ctrl+F during the exam!

🆕 Beginner's Guide: "I just ran cilium install. Now what?"

Congratulations! Cilium is running. Here's the natural progression of commands a beginner should follow:

1. Verify health: cilium status — Is everything green? If not, stop and fix before anything else.

2. See your pods: cilium endpoint list — Every pod is now a Cilium endpoint with an identity and policy state.

3. Run a full test: cilium connectivity test — Validates 21+ scenarios. If this passes, Cilium is working perfectly.

4. Watch traffic: hubble observe — See every packet flowing through your cluster in real-time (add --verdict DROPPED to find blocked traffic).

5. Apply security: Create a CiliumNetworkPolicy YAML (use Appendix B templates!) → cilium policy import my-policy.yaml → verify with cilium policy get.
