Appendix B: Cilium YAML Templates

Ready-to-use YAML templates for common Cilium configurations. CCA Exam Tip: You won't be asked to write YAML from scratch, but you WILL be asked "what does this policy do?" — understand each field's purpose!

B.1 Basic Allow — Ingress from Same Namespace

Allows pods with app: frontend to reach app: backend on port 8000. All other traffic is denied.

YAML
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-same-ns
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        app: frontend
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "8000"
        protocol: TCP
🧩 What Each Field Does (Novice Friendly!)

endpointSelector — "WHO does this policy protect?" Here it protects pods labeled app: backend. Think of it as the "target" of the policy.

ingress — "WHO can talk TO the protected pods?" Inbound traffic rules. (Egress would be "where can protected pods send traffic OUT to?")

fromEndpoints — "Which OTHER pods are allowed in?" Here only pods with app: frontend. Empty {} means "anyone."

toPorts — "On which ports can they connect?" Here only TCP port 8000 is open. Without this, even allowed pods can't actually reach the app!

B.2 L7 HTTP Rules — Allow Only GET to /api/v1

L7 filtering: only HTTP GET requests to /api/v1/* paths are allowed. POST/PUT/DELETE blocked. Regex path matching.

YAML
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: l7-api-get-only
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        app: frontend
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "8000"
        protocol: TCP
      rules:
        http:
        - method: GET
          path: "/api/v1/.*"
💡 L7 vs L3/L4 — The Novice Distinction

L3/L4 (B.1): Only cares about IP addresses and port numbers — "You can knock on port 8000." Simple, fast, but dumb.

L7 (B.2): Reads the actual HTTP request — "You can knock on port 8000, but ONLY with a GET to /api/v1/*." Smarter, but needs Envoy proxy. The rules.http section is nested UNDER toPorts — you must still specify the TCP port FIRST, then add HTTP rules on top.

CCA Exam Pattern: If a question mentions "HTTP method," "path," "headers," or "gRPC" → it's an L7 question. Look for rules: in the YAML.

B.3 DNS-Based Egress — Allow Only api.github.com

Egress policy: first rule allows DNS (UDP 53 to CoreDNS), second rule uses toFQDNs to only allow HTTPS to api.github.com. DNS is a prerequisite!

YAML
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-github-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  egress:
  - toEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
        k8s-app: coredns
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "53"
        protocol: UDP
  - toFQDNs:
    - matchName: api.github.com
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "443"
        protocol: TCP
⚠️ The #1 CCA Mistake: Forgetting DNS!

If you restrict egress but DON'T allow DNS (UDP 53), NOTHING WORKS. Why? Because pods need to resolve domain names before they can connect. Even toFQDNs: api.github.com needs DNS to find the IP addresses.

Rule of thumb: Every egress policy MUST start with a DNS rule allowing UDP 53 to CoreDNS (kube-system). Without it, toFQDNs rules will silently fail because the pod can't look up the domain.

CCA Exam Pattern: If you see a policy with toFQDNs but NO DNS rule → it's broken. The exam WILL test this!

B.4 Default Deny All — Cluster-Wide Baseline

CCNP with empty endpointSelector: {} matches ALL pods. Empty ingress: [] and egress: [] means deny everything. The strongest baseline.

YAML
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
spec:
  endpointSelector: {}
  ingress: []
  egress: []
🔒 Zero-Trust Foundation — Apply This FIRST!

This is the most important policy you'll write. Think of it as locking ALL doors in a building before deciding which ones to unlock. Without it, any pod can talk to any other pod — that's the K8s default.

endpointSelector: {} — empty curly braces = "select EVERY pod in the entire cluster." No exceptions.

ingress: [] — empty list = "nobody can talk TO any pod." All incoming traffic rejected.

egress: [] — empty list = "no pod can talk OUT to anywhere." All outgoing traffic rejected.

After applying this: Every pod is completely isolated. You then apply B.1-B.3 type policies to selectively ALLOW needed traffic. This is called "default-deny, explicit-allow" — the gold standard of zero-trust security.

B.5 CCNP — Monitoring Access (Cluster-Wide Allow)

Cluster-wide policy allowing Prometheus/Grafana monitoring pods to scrape metrics from all pods on port 9090. Uses fromEndpoints with namespace + label selectors.

YAML
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-monitoring
spec:
  endpointSelector: {}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        app: prometheus
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: monitoring
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "9090"
        protocol: TCP
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        app: grafana
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: monitoring
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "3000"
        protocol: TCP
🔭 Why CCNP? The "Cross-Namespace Exception" Pattern

After applying B.4 (default-deny-all), monitoring in the monitoring namespace is blocked from scraping metrics from pods in anihpj namespace. You need a CCNP to punch a cluster-wide hole.

Key difference from CNP: CCNP uses namespace + label together: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: monitoring AND app: prometheus. This means "Prometheus pods from the monitoring namespace ONLY" — not just any pod named Prometheus.

Why two ingress rules? Prometheus scrapes on port 9090, Grafana needs port 3000. Each fromEndpoints block is independent — they're OR'd together (union semantics).

B.6 CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy

Configures BGP peering with an external router (ASN 65000). Cilium nodes with bgp: enabled label advertise Service LoadBalancer IPs via BGP.

YAML
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2alpha1
kind: CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy
metadata:
  name: bgp-peer-router
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    matchLabels:
      bgp: enabled
  virtualRouters:
  - localASN: 65001
    neighbors:
    - peerAddress: 10.0.0.1/32
      peerASN: 65000
🌐 BGP in Plain English — The "Phone Book" Analogy

What BGP does: BGP is like a phone book for networks. Your Cilium nodes tell the router: "Hey, Service IP 192.168.1.100 lives on MY node. Send traffic for that IP to me." The router updates its routing table and forwards accordingly.

localASN: 65001 — "My network's ID number is 65001." Private ASNs are 64512-65534 (for internal use).

peerASN: 65000 — "My neighbor router's network ID is 65000."

peerAddress: 10.0.0.1/32 — "The router lives at IP 10.0.0.1."

CCA Exam Tip: BGP is in the Service Mesh domain (20%). Know that BGP is what makes LoadBalancer Services work without a cloud provider!

B.7 CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy

Routes all egress traffic from app: backend pods through a specific gateway node with static IP 203.0.113.10. Useful for IP whitelisting with external services.

YAML
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-static-ip
spec:
  selectors:
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: backend
  destinationCIDRs:
  - 0.0.0.0/0
  egressGateway:
    nodeSelector:
      matchLabels:
        egress-gw: true
    egressIP: 203.0.113.10
🏢 The "Office Building" Analogy for Egress Gateway

The problem: Your anihpj backend pods run on 10 different nodes, each with a different public IP. An external payment API (Stripe, PayPal) requires you to whitelist IPs. You can't whitelist 10 IPs that change every time pods restart.

The solution: Egress Gateway forces ALL outbound traffic from selected pods through ONE designated node with ONE static IP. The external service sees only 203.0.113.10 — regardless of which pod or node initiated the request.

destinationCIDRs: 0.0.0.0/0 — "route ALL destinations through the gateway." You can narrow this to only specific external services.

CCA Exam Scenario: "A company needs to connect to an external API that requires IP whitelisting. Which Cilium feature?" → Egress Gateway!

B.8 CiliumLocalRedirectPolicy — Local DNS Cache

Redirects DNS queries (UDP 53) to a local DNS cache pod on the same node instead of going through CoreDNS Service. Reduces DNS latency by keeping traffic local.

YAML
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumLocalRedirectPolicy
metadata:
  name: local-dns
spec:
  redirectFrontend:
    toPorts:
    - port: "53"
      protocol: UDP
  redirectBackend:
    localEndpointSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: local-dns-cache
    toPorts:
    - port: "53"
      protocol: UDP
🏠 The "Corner Store vs Supermarket" Analogy

Without Local Redirect: Every DNS query from a pod travels across the network to CoreDNS (the "supermarket" — central but far away). Network hop + queue + processing = latency.

With Local Redirect: Cilium intercepts DNS packets BEFORE they leave the node and redirects them to a local cache pod (the "corner store" — right next door). Same node = near-zero latency.

redirectFrontend — "Which traffic do we intercept?" Here: anything going to UDP port 53 (DNS).

redirectBackend — "Where do we send it instead?" To the local DNS cache pod on the same node.

🚦 Ingress vs Egress — The Direction You ALWAYS Confuse
🟢 INGRESS = INTO the pod
 ┌──────────┐
 │  OTHER   │──┐
 │  PODS    │  │  ┌─────────────┐
 └──────────┘  │  │  PROTECTED  │
               ├─▶│  POD         │
 ┌──────────┐  │  │  (selected)  │
 │  WORLD   │──┘  └─────────────┘
 │  (CIDR)  │     "WHO can reach
 └──────────┘      MY pod?"

YAML key: ingress: → Think: "IN-coming"

🔴 EGRESS = OUT FROM the pod
 ┌─────────────┐
 │  PROTECTED  │──┐  ┌──────────┐
 │  POD        │  │  │  OTHER   │
 │  (selected) │  ├─▶│  PODS    │
 └─────────────┘  │  └──────────┘
                  │  ┌──────────┐
                  └─▶│  WORLD   │
                     │  (CIDR)  │
                     └──────────┘
     "Where can MY pod reach OUT?"

YAML key: egress: → Think: "EX-it"

💡 CCA Exam: "A policy protects pod X. It allows connections FROM pod Y. Is this ingress or egress?" → INGRESS (protecting X, allowing Y INTO X).
⚖️ Policy Precedence Rules — Which Policy Wins?
1 CNP overrides CCNP — Namespace-specific policy ALWAYS wins over cluster-wide. Think of CNP as the "boss" and CCNP as the "company policy" — boss overrides.
2 More specific > Less specific — A policy with app: backend,env: prod (2 labels) beats one with just app: backend (1 label). More labels = more specific.
3 Multiple policies = UNION — If Policy-A allows port 80 and Policy-B allows port 443, the pod gets BOTH. Policies ADD, they don't replace each other.
4 L4 + L7 on same rule = AND — The L4 port must match AND the L7 rule must match. Both conditions must be true for traffic to pass.
🏷️ Common Label Selector Patterns — Cheat Sheet
Selector PatternWhat It MatchesUse Case
matchLabels: {}ALL pods (empty = match everything)Default-deny, "allow world"
matchLabels: {app: frontend}Pods with exactly app=frontendSingle-app targeting
matchLabels: {app: backend, env: prod}Pods with BOTH labels (AND logic)Fine-grained selection
io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: anihpjAll pods in namespace anihpjCross-namespace rules
!io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-systemAll pods NOT in kube-systemExclude system pods
matchExpressions: [{key: app, operator: In, values: [frontend,backend]}]Pods where app is frontend OR backendOR logic (not possible with matchLabels)
matchExpressions: [{key: env, operator: Exists}]Any pod with the env label (any value)Label existence check
🆚 CNP vs CCNP — Visual Comparison
🔵 CNP (CiliumNetworkPolicy)

Scope: Single namespace

Kind: cilium.io/v2

Priority: HIGHER (overrides CCNP)

Examples: B.1, B.2, B.3

Use when: Rules apply to ONE namespace

🟣 CCNP (CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy)

Scope: ALL namespaces

Kind: cilium.io/v2

Priority: LOWER (CNP can override it)

Examples: B.4, B.5

Use when: Baseline, monitoring, global rules

💡 CCA Exam: "This policy should apply to ALL pods" → CCNP. "This policy should apply to pods in namespace X" → CNP.
🏗️ anihpj Policy Stack — How B.1–B.4 Work Together
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LAYER 1: CCNP default-deny-all (B.4)                        │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  ALL pods: ingress ❌  egress ❌                               │
  │  = Every pod in the cluster is completely isolated           │
  └───────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │  "Open only necessary doors"
    ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                     ▼                                     │
    │  LAYER 2: CNP allow-dns (B.3 adapted)                     │
    │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────          │
    │  ALL pods → UDP 53 → kube-system/CoreDNS                  │
    │  = Every pod can resolve domain names                     │
    └─────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
    ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                     ▼                                     │
    │  LAYER 3: CNP allow-backend (B.1)                         │
    │  ────────────────────────────────────────                 │
    │  pod: app=backend ← port 8000 ← pod: app=frontend        │
    │  = Frontend can reach Backend on port 8000                │
    └─────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  RESULT: anihpj is SECURE by default                      │
    │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
    │  ✅ Frontend ↔ Backend on 8000                            │
    │  ✅ DNS resolution works for all pods                     │
    │  ❌ Backend cannot reach Database (no policy yet!)        │
    │  ❌ Pods cannot reach Internet (need egress policy)       │
    │  ❌ No pod can reach any other unexpected destination     │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 The Zero-Trust Formula

Start with B.4 (deny all) → Add DNS (B.3 pattern) → Add app-specific allows (B.1/B.2 patterns) → Add L7 rules (B.2) → Add egress gateway (B.7). Each layer adds permissions; nothing is open by default. This is how Cilium secures real production clusters.

🧭 Which Policy Type Should I Use? — Decision Guide
ScenarioUse ThisKey Field
"Only frontend pods can reach my backend"CNP (B.1)fromEndpoints.matchLabels
"Only allow HTTP GET to /api"CNP with L7 rules (B.2)rules.http
"Pods can only talk to api.github.com"CNP with toFQDNs (B.3)toFQDNs.matchName
"Block everything everywhere as baseline"CCNP (B.4)Empty ingress: [] + egress: []
"Monitoring tools need cluster-wide access"CCNP (B.5)Namespace + label selectors
"Advertise Service IPs via BGP to router"BGPPeeringPolicy (B.6)virtualRouters.neighbors
"Give pods a fixed egress IP"EgressGatewayPolicy (B.7)egressGateway.egressIP
"Keep DNS traffic local on each node"LocalRedirectPolicy (B.8)redirectBackend.localEndpointSelector
💡 CCA Exam Pattern Recognition

Questions often describe a scenario and ask "which policy type?" — memorize this mapping: Single namespace → CNP. All namespaces → CCNP. Egress IP → EgressGatewayPolicy. BGP → BGPPeeringPolicy.

📝 Appendix B — CCA Practice Questions (8 Questions)

Q1
What's the difference between CNP and CCNP?
Show Answer
Answer

CNP (CiliumNetworkPolicy) is namespace-scoped — rules apply only within one namespace. CCNP (CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy) applies across ALL namespaces. CNP has higher priority and can override CCNP rules.

Q2
What does endpointSelector: {} mean?
Show Answer
Answer

Empty curly braces select ALL pods in the scope (all pods in the namespace for CNP, all pods cluster-wide for CCNP). Used in default-deny-all and monitoring access policies.

Q3
Why must every egress policy include a DNS rule (UDP 53 to CoreDNS)?
Show Answer
Answer

Pods need DNS to resolve domain names before connecting to external services. Without it, even toFQDNs rules fail because the pod cannot look up the domain's IP address. The DNS rule must come FIRST in the egress list.

Q4
What is the difference between ingress and egress in a CiliumNetworkPolicy?
Show Answer
Answer

Ingress controls who can send traffic TO the selected pods (inbound). Egress controls where the selected pods can send traffic TO (outbound). Think: "In-gress = IN-coming" and "E-gress = EX-it."

Q5
What's the difference between L4 and L7 policy rules?
Show Answer
Answer

L4 (Layer 4): Filters by port number and protocol (TCP/UDP) — "Allow port 8000." Fast, enforced in eBPF. L7 (Layer 7): Reads the application protocol — "Allow HTTP GET to /api/v1." Requires Envoy proxy, smarter but slightly more overhead. L7 rules nest UNDER L4 rules (rules.http under toPorts).

Q6
A company needs to ensure all outbound traffic from backend pods goes through a single static IP for whitelisting. Which Cilium policy should they use?
Show Answer
Answer

CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy (B.7). It routes selected pods' egress traffic through a designated gateway node with a fixed IP. External services see only that single IP regardless of how many backend pods exist.

Q7
If two CiliumNetworkPolicies select the same pod, how are their rules combined?
Show Answer
Answer

Rules are UNIONED (added together). The pod gets the most permissive combination of all policies. If Policy-A allows port 80 and Policy-B allows port 443, the pod can receive traffic on both ports. Policies never cancel each other out.

Q8
What is the recommended order to apply policies for zero-trust security?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Default-deny-all CCNP (B.4) — lock everything. 2. DNS egress rule — allow pods to resolve names. 3. App-specific CNPs (B.1/B.2) — open specific needed ports. 4. L7 rules (B.2) — add HTTP-level restrictions. 5. Egress controls (B.3/B.7) — restrict external access. This is the "default-deny, explicit-allow" zero-trust pattern.

Appendix C: Common Errors and Solutions

Quick troubleshooting reference for the most common Cilium issues. CCA Exam Tip: Expect 2-3 troubleshooting questions. Know which command to run FIRST for each symptom!

🔧 CCA Troubleshooting Pattern — The "3-Question" Method

For ANY troubleshooting question on the exam, ask yourself:

  • 1. Is it a health issue? → cilium status
  • 2. Is it a policy issue? → hubble observe --verdict DROPPED
  • 3. Is it a connectivity issue? → cilium connectivity test
🔀 Cilium Troubleshooting Decision Tree
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  POD CAN'T COMMUNICATE                       │
  └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                         │
            ┌────────────▼────────────┐
            │ cilium status           │
            │ Are all components OK?  │
            └──────┬──────────┬───────┘
                   │ NO       │ YES
                   ▼          ▼
            Fix component  ┌────────────────────┐
            health first   │ hubble observe      │
                           │ --verdict DROPPED   │
                           │ --from-pod ns/pod   │
                           └────┬──────────┬─────┘
                                │ DROPPED  │ NO DROPS
                                ▼          ▼
                           ┌─────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
                           │ Policy  │  │ Network issue │
                           │ issue!  │  │ or DNS!       │
                           │ Fix CNP │  │ Check DNS +   │
                           └─────────┘  │ routing       │
                                        └──────────────┘

C.1 "Cilium Agent Not Ready" Errors

Error / SymptomRoot CauseSolution
"Cilium agent not ready"eBPF not available, kernel too old (<5.10), or wrong CNI configCheck kernel: uname -r. Verify eBPF: ls /sys/kernel/btf/. Check agent logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/cilium
Pods stuck in ContainerCreatingCNI plugin not installed or IPAM exhaustedCheck Cilium status. Verify IPAM mode. Check node CIDR: kubectl get ciliumnodes. If cluster-pool, ensure enough IPs in pool.
🆕 Novice: "Agent not ready" = The Cilium brain on a node isn't working

Every node runs a Cilium Agent (DaemonSet). If it's "not ready," that node can't manage any pods' networking. Common causes: kernel too old (need 5.10+), BTF not available (check /sys/kernel/btf/), or another CNI still running. Quick fix: cilium status --wait to see exactly what's failing.

C.2 "Policy Not Working" Troubleshooting

Error / SymptomRoot CauseSolution
"Policy not working" — traffic still flows after applying denyWrong selectors, DNS not allowed in egress, or CCNP overridden by CNPCheck policy: cilium policy get. Verify endpoints: kubectl get cep -n ns. Look for drops: hubble observe --verdict DROPPED
"Policy too restrictive" — legitimate traffic blockedMissing DNS egress rule (most common!), or too narrow selectorsAlways add DNS (UDP 53) egress first. Check with hubble observe --verdict DROPPED. Test with cilium policy validate before applying.
L7 policy rules not enforcedMissing L7 proxy (Envoy) or policy syntax errorVerify policy YAML with cilium policy validate. Check that rules.http is nested under toPorts correctly. Ensure proxy is running: cilium status | grep Proxy
⚠️ Novice: "My policy doesn't work" = The #1 support ticket

90% of "policy not working" issues are one of: (1) DNS not allowed in egress, (2) Wrong label selectors (policy selects different pods than you think), (3) Another policy is overriding yours (CNP beats CCNP). Always verify selectors with cilium policy selectors app=backend to see WHICH pods your policy actually targets.

C.3 Hubble Connectivity Issues

Error / SymptomRoot CauseSolution
Hubble UI blank / no flowsHubble Relay not running or Hubble not enabledCheck: cilium status (look for Hubble Relay). Enable: cilium hubble enable. Restart Relay if needed.
Hubble observe returns "connection refused"Hubble Relay service not exposed or port-forward not activecilium hubble port-forward & then retry. Or kubectl port-forward -n kube-system svc/hubble-relay 4245:80
🔭 Novice: "Hubble shows nothing" = The observability layer is disconnected

Hubble is like a security camera system. If it shows nothing, either: (1) The cameras (Hubble on each node) aren't recording, (2) The central monitor (Hubble Relay) isn't collecting from all cameras, or (3) You're not connected to the monitor. Always run cilium status first to see which Hubble components are green/red.

C.4 Cluster Mesh Connection Failures

Error / SymptomRoot CauseSolution
Cluster Mesh connection failsNetwork connectivity, different Cilium versions, or TLS cert issuesVerify pod CIDRs don't overlap. Check version parity. Validate TLS: cilium clustermesh status --verbose. Ensure ports 4240/4244 open between clusters.
Service ClusterIP not reachablekube-proxy replacement not working or wrong modeCheck: cilium status | grep KubeProxyReplacement. Verify with cilium service list. Test with cilium connectivity test.
🌍 Novice: "Cluster Mesh failed" = Two clusters can't talk to each other

Cluster Mesh lets pods in Cluster-A talk to pods in Cluster-B directly. If it fails: (1) Check that pod CIDR ranges don't overlap (both clusters can't use 10.0.0.0/16), (2) Verify the clusters can reach each other on ports 4240 (health) and 4244 (data), (3) Make sure both clusters run the same Cilium major.minor version.

C.5 Encryption Configuration Errors

Error / SymptomRoot CauseSolution
Encryption not activeWireGuard/IPSec not enabled or kernel module missingCheck: cilium encrypt status. Enable: --set encryption.enabled=true --set encryption.type=wireguard. Verify kernel: modprobe wireguard
🔒 Novice: "Encryption not active" = Your data is going over the wire in plain text!

Without encryption, ANYONE on the same network can read your pod-to-pod traffic. WireGuard is the easiest fix — it's a modern VPN built into Linux (kernel 5.6+). Enable it with one flag: --set encryption.type=wireguard. Verify with cilium encrypt status — all nodes should show "OK."

🐍 Real-World: Troubleshooting anihpj — Step-by-Step
1️⃣
Symptom: "My anihpj frontend can't reach the backend!"
→ Check: hubble observe --from-pod anihpj/frontend-xxx --to-pod anihpj/backend-yyy
2️⃣
Diagnosis: Hubble shows VERDICT: DROPPED with policy allow-backend
→ The policy EXISTS but is blocking our traffic!
3️⃣
Root Cause: cilium policy get allow-backend -n anihpj reveals typo: app: backend vs actual label app: back-end (hyphen!)
→ Label mismatch! Policy selects nothing → denies everything.
4️⃣
Fix: Update policy: matchLabels: {app: back-end} → cilium policy import fixed-policy.yaml
→ Verify: hubble observe --verdict FORWARDED shows traffic flowing again!
💡 Lesson: Always verify your label selectors with cilium policy selectors before applying!

📝 Appendix C — CCA Practice Questions (8 Questions)

Q1
What is the FIRST command you should run when troubleshooting any Cilium issue?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium status — it shows the health of ALL Cilium components (Agent, Operator, Hubble Relay, Encryption). If any component is "not ready," fix that first before investigating further.

Q2
You applied a CiliumNetworkPolicy to deny traffic, but traffic still flows. What are 3 possible causes?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Wrong label selector — policy doesn't actually select the target pods. (2) A more specific CNP is overriding your policy (CNP beats CCNP). (3) Another policy is unioning with yours (policies ADD, not replace). Verify with cilium policy get and hubble observe --verdict DROPPED.

Q3
Hubble UI shows no flows. What are the most common causes?
Show Answer
Answer

Hubble Relay is not running or Hubble is not enabled. Check with cilium status and look for Hubble components. Enable with cilium hubble enable and restart Relay if needed.

Q4
Cluster Mesh fails to connect. What should you check first?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Pod CIDRs don't overlap between clusters. (2) Both clusters run the same Cilium version. (3) Ports 4240 (health) and 4244 (data) are open between clusters. (4) TLS certificates are valid. Use cilium clustermesh status --verbose.

Q5
What does it mean when "encryption is not active" in cilium status?
Show Answer
Answer

Pod-to-pod traffic is being sent in plain text — anyone on the same network can potentially read it. Enable WireGuard with --set encryption.type=wireguard and verify with cilium encrypt status.

Q6
Pods are stuck in "ContainerCreating" status. How do you diagnose?
Show Answer
Answer

This usually means the CNI plugin can't assign networking. Check: (1) cilium status — is the agent running? (2) kubectl get ciliumnodes — is IPAM exhausted? (3) kubectl describe pod — look for CNI errors in events.

Q7
What is the difference between cilium monitor and hubble observe for troubleshooting?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium monitor shows raw eBPF events from a SINGLE node — use for packet-level debugging on one node. hubble observe shows cluster-wide flow data through Hubble Relay — better for policy-level troubleshooting. Use monitor for deep debugging, hubble for operational visibility.

Q8
Your anihpj backend pod can't connect to an external API. Walk through the troubleshooting steps.
Show Answer
Answer

Step 1: hubble observe --from-pod anihpj/backend-xxx --verdict DROPPED to check if a policy blocks it. Step 2: cilium policy get -n anihpj to review policies. Step 3: Check DNS: hubble observe --from-pod anihpj/backend-xxx --to-port 53 — is DNS working? Step 4: Check egress gateway and toFQDNs policies. Step 5: cilium connectivity test for full validation.

Appendix D: Glossary — Cilium & eBPF Terminology

50+ essential terms grouped by category. CCA Exam Tip: Read this glossary the night before your exam — it covers the key terminology that appears in every domain.

D.1 eBPF & Kernel Concepts

TermDefinition
eBPFExtended Berkeley Packet Filter — technology that runs sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel without changing kernel source code. Cilium's core engine.
XDPeXpress Data Path — earliest packet processing hook, before SKB allocation. Fastest eBPF attach point.
TCTraffic Control — Linux subsystem. eBPF programs attach to TC ingress/egress hooks for packet processing.
VerifierIn-kernel static analyzer that proves eBPF programs are safe: always terminate, no out-of-bounds memory access, max 1M instructions.
JIT CompilerJust-In-Time compiler that converts verified eBPF bytecode to native CPU instructions (x86, ARM) for maximum performance.
eBPF MapsKey-value data structures shared between eBPF programs and userspace. Cilium uses them for policy tables, connection tracking, load balancer state.
BTFBPF Type Format — enables eBPF programs to be portable across kernel versions by describing data structures. Required for CO-RE.
CO-RECompile Once, Run Everywhere — BTF-based approach allowing a single eBPF binary to run on different kernel versions.
Hook PointsSpecific locations in the kernel where eBPF programs attach: XDP, TC, cgroup, socket, kprobe, tracepoint.

D.2 Cilium Core Concepts

TermDefinition
Cilium AgentDaemonSet pod running on every node. Manages eBPF programs, endpoints, and policies for that node.
Cilium OperatorDeployment handling cluster-wide tasks: IPAM, identity GC, node heartbeats, KVStore sync.
DatapathThe code path packets take through Cilium's eBPF programs — from network device ingress to egress.
Cilium CLIcilium binary for install, status, policy management, connectivity testing, and debugging.
IdentityNumeric label (1, 2, 3...) assigned by Cilium to a set of pod labels. Identity 1 = reserved for "world". Basis of identity-aware policy.
EndpointCilium's representation of a network-connected entity (usually a pod). Has identity, IP, and policy enforcement state.
KVStoreKey-Value Store — etcd used by Cilium for cluster state synchronization (optional; CRDs are preferred now).

D.3 Cilium CRDs

TermDefinition
CNPCiliumNetworkPolicy — namespace-scoped policy CRD. Supports L3/L4/L7, DNS, identity-based rules.
CCNPCiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy — cluster-wide policy CRD. Applies across all namespaces. Lower priority than CNP.
CEPCiliumEndpoint — per-pod CRD showing networking state, identity, policy enforcement status, and eBPF map references.
CIDCiliumIdentity — CRD mapping label sets to numeric identities. One identity shared by all pods with same labels.
CiliumNodeCRD representing each node's Cilium state: IPAM allocations, addresses, health status.
CiliumBGPPeeringPolicyCRD (v2alpha1) configuring BGP peering with external routers for Service LoadBalancer advertisement.
CiliumEgressGatewayPolicyCRD routing specific pods' egress traffic through designated gateway nodes with static IPs.

D.4 Networking & Service Mesh

TermDefinition
CNIContainer Network Interface — standard for configuring container networking. Cilium implements the CNI spec.
VXLANVirtual Extensible LAN — tunneling protocol. Default Cilium encapsulation mode. Adds 50-byte overhead.
GeneveGeneric Network Virtualization Encapsulation — alternative to VXLAN. More extensible metadata support.
Direct RoutingCilium mode where pod traffic is routed directly (no encapsulation). Higher performance, requires L3-capable network.
KPRKube-Proxy Replacement — Cilium replaces kube-proxy's iptables rules with eBPF programs for Service load balancing.
MaglevConsistent hashing algorithm used by Cilium for Service load balancing. Minimizes disruption when backends change.
DSRDirect Server Return — backend responds directly to client, bypassing load balancer on return path. Faster but requires specific setup.
SNATSource Network Address Translation — load balancer rewrites source IP. Simpler than DSR but adds bottleneck.
EnvoyL7 proxy embedded in Cilium for HTTP/gRPC processing. Runs per-node (not per-pod) — sidecar-less.
Service MeshControls service-to-service communication. Cilium provides sidecar-less service mesh via eBPF + Envoy.
IngressK8s resource for HTTP routing. Cilium has built-in Envoy-based Ingress controller (no separate deployment needed).
Gateway APINext-gen K8s networking API (replaces Ingress). Cilium supports Gateway API for advanced routing.

D.5 Observability & Security

TermDefinition
HubbleCilium's observability layer — provides flow logs, service maps, and Prometheus metrics for all cluster traffic.
Hubble RelayCluster-wide aggregation service. CLI and UI connect through Relay for a unified view across all nodes.
Hubble UIWeb-based dashboard showing service dependency map, flow browser, and network topology.
Service MapReal-time dependency graph in Hubble UI. Green edges = allowed, red edges = dropped, thickness = volume.
WireGuardModern VPN protocol (kernel 5.6+). Cilium uses it for transparent node-to-node encryption with minimal overhead.
mTLSMutual TLS — both client and server authenticate using certificates. Cilium can enforce mTLS without sidecars.
toFQDNsCNP rule type allowing egress to specific domain names. Cilium dynamically tracks DNS resolutions and updates eBPF maps.
L7 PolicyApplication-layer rules filtering by HTTP method, path, headers, gRPC method, Kafka topic, DNS name.
Egress GatewayRoutes pod egress traffic through specific nodes with static IPs — useful for IP whitelisting with external services.
Bandwidth ManagereBPF-based bandwidth enforcement using Fair Queue (FQ) pacing at the egress device.

D.6 Multi-Cluster & Advanced

TermDefinition
Cluster MeshCilium feature connecting multiple K8s clusters. Pods communicate directly across clusters with full policy enforcement.
BGPBorder Gateway Protocol — Cilium can peer with routers via BGP to advertise Service LoadBalancer IPs.
IPAMIP Address Management — modes: cluster-pool, Kubernetes, AWS ENI, Azure, GKE. Controls how pod IPs are allocated.
BBRBottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip — TCP congestion control algorithm. Cilium supports BBR for improved throughput.
SRv6Segment Routing over IPv6 — advanced routing where the source specifies the packet's path through the network.

D.7 Additional Essential Terms

TermDefinition
Pod CIDRIP address range allocated to a node for its pods. Must not overlap between nodes or clusters (Cluster Mesh).
Service CIDRIP range reserved for Kubernetes Service ClusterIPs. Cilium's KPR handles Service IP translation in eBPF.
NodePortService type that exposes a port on every node's IP. Cilium's eBPF handles NodePort without kube-proxy.
LoadBalancerService type that provisions an external load balancer (cloud or BGP). Cilium supports both modes.
ExternalTrafficPolicyControls whether NodePort/LB preserves client source IP (Local) or load balances cluster-wide (Cluster).
Session AffinitySticky sessions — routes requests from the same client to the same backend. Maglev provides connection affinity.
NetworkPolicy (K8s)Standard K8s resource for L3/L4 ingress/egress rules. No L7, no DNS, no identity. Cilium fully supports it.
Default DenySecurity baseline: deny all traffic, then explicitly allow what's needed. Cilium enforces via eBPF — no iptables.
Audit ModePolicy mode (enableAudit: true) that LOGS violations without blocking. Used to test policies before enforcement.
Policy TraceCilium tool (cilium policy trace) that simulates traffic between endpoints to verify policy decisions.
Mutating WebhookK8s admission controller. Cilium can use webhooks to inject policy defaults or modify pod specs.
Helm ChartPackaged Cilium installation via Helm. cilium install uses Helm under the hood.
Tunnel ModeCilium encapsulation: VXLAN or Geneve. Pod traffic is encapsulated in UDP. Works on any network.
Native RoutingAlternative to tunneling: pods route directly via host network. Faster but requires L3-aware network.
MTUMaximum Transmission Unit — VXLAN/Geneve adds overhead (50 bytes). Cilium auto-detects or can be set manually.
CNI ChainingRunning Cilium alongside another CNI (e.g., for multi-network). Cilium handles policy; other CNI handles IPAM.
Health EndpointSpecial endpoint Cilium creates per-node for health checks. Used by cilium status to verify node readiness.
Endpoint RegenerationProcess of rebuilding all eBPF programs for an endpoint after policy changes. Triggered automatically or via cilium endpoint regenerate.
PreflightCilium pre-upgrade validation: cilium preflight checks cluster compatibility before upgrading to a new version.
Host FirewallCilium feature that applies eBPF-based firewall rules to the host itself (not just pods). Protects node-level services.
IPSecAlternative to WireGuard for encryption. Older protocol, wider kernel support, but higher overhead than WireGuard.
FQDN ProxyCilium component that intercepts DNS and dynamically programs eBPF maps with resolved IPs for toFQDNs rules.
Socket LBeBPF-level load balancing that intercepts connect() syscalls at the socket layer. Eliminates DNAT hop for lower latency.
Hubble TimescapeHubble feature for historical flow data — record and replay traffic patterns for forensic analysis and compliance.

D.8 CCA Exam-Specific Terms

TermDefinition
Open BookCCA exam allows docs.cilium.io during the test. No other websites, notes, or resources permitted.
Proctored ExamOnline exam with live proctor monitoring via webcam. Requires quiet room, cleared desk, valid ID.
Multiple ChoiceCCA question format: select the BEST answer from options. No penalty for wrong answers — always answer every question.
Domain Weighting5 domains weighted: Architecture 30%, Network Policy 20%, Service Mesh 20%, Observability 18%, Installation 12%.
Time Management90 minutes / ~60 questions = ~1.5 min per question. Flag hard ones, answer easy ones first, return at the end.

📝 Appendix D — CCA Practice Questions (8 Questions)

Q1
What is eBPF and why is it important for Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) runs sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel without changing kernel source code. It's Cilium's core engine — replacing iptables, kube-proxy, and sidecar proxies with fast, safe kernel-level programs (up to 587x faster than iptables).

Q2
What is the difference between CNP and CCNP?
Show Answer
Answer

CNP (CiliumNetworkPolicy) is namespace-scoped. CCNP (CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy) applies cluster-wide across ALL namespaces. CNP has higher priority and can override CCNP rules.

Q3
What is Cilium Identity and how does it differ from IP-based security?
Show Answer
Answer

Identity is a numeric label assigned to all pods sharing the same label set. Unlike IP-based security, identity-based policies survive pod restarts and IP changes — the identity stays the same while the IP changes.

Q4
What is KPR (Kube-Proxy Replacement)?
Show Answer
Answer

KPR replaces kube-proxy's iptables-based Service load balancing with eBPF programs. Benefits: O(1) hash table lookups instead of O(n) iptables chains, Maglev consistent hashing, socket-level redirection (no DNAT hop).

Q5
What is the eBPF verifier and why does it matter?
Show Answer
Answer

The verifier is the kernel's safety gate for eBPF. It mathematically proves every program: (1) always terminates, (2) never accesses out-of-bounds memory, (3) executes at most 1M instructions. Unsafe programs are rejected — this is why eBPF is safe for production.

Q6
What is Maglev hashing used for in Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

Maglev is a consistent hashing algorithm for Service load balancing. It ensures even backend distribution with minimal disruption when backends change. Provides connection affinity (same client → same backend).

Q7
What does "sidecar-less service mesh" mean in Cilium?
Show Answer
Answer

Traditional service meshes (Istio) inject a sidecar proxy container into every pod — consuming memory and adding latency. Cilium's mesh uses eBPF in the kernel + per-node Envoy — zero sidecar containers, zero per-pod memory overhead, lower latency.

Q8
What are the 5 CCA exam domains and their weights?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Architecture & Concepts (30%), 2. Network Policy (20%), 3. Service Mesh & Load Balancing (20%), 4. Observability & Hubble (18%), 5. Installation & Operations (12%). Total: 100%, 90 minutes, ~60 questions.

Appendix E: Complete anihpj Cilium Configuration

Ready-to-apply Cilium configuration for the anihpj/jobpost Django project used throughout this guide. All values tested and verified.

E.1 Cilium Install with anihpj Values

Production-ready install command enabling KPR, Hubble (Relay + UI + Metrics), WireGuard encryption, and cluster-pool IPAM.

Bash
cilium install \
  --set kubeProxyReplacement=true \
  --set hubble.enabled=true \
  --set hubble.relay.enabled=true \
  --set hubble.ui.enabled=true \
  --set hubble.metrics.enabled="{dns,drop,tcp,flow,http}" \
  --set encryption.enabled=true \
  --set encryption.type=wireguard \
  --set ipam.mode=cluster-pool \
  --set ipam.operator.clusterPoolIPv4PodCIDRList="10.0.0.0/16"

E.2 Complete NetworkPolicy Set for anihpj

🔒 Three-Layer Zero-Trust Architecture

Frontend (port 80/443, public) → Backend (port 8000, internal) → Database (port 5432, restricted). Each layer only accepts traffic from the layer above it. Default deny everywhere.

Policy NameSelected PodsAllows FromPorts
allow-frontendapp: frontendworld (0.0.0.0/0)80, 443
allow-backendapp: backendapp: frontend8000
allow-databaseapp: postgresapp: backend5432
egress-dnsall podsCoreDNS (kube-system)53/UDP

Complete anihpj Backend CNP — Production-Ready Example

This is the actual CiliumNetworkPolicy you would apply to secure the anihpj backend. It combines ingress rules (allow frontend) and egress rules (DNS + database).

YAML
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: secure-backend
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend        # Protects ALL backend pods
  ingress:                # WHO can reach the backend?
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        app: frontend     # Only frontend pods
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "8000"      # Django runs on port 8000
        protocol: TCP
  egress:                 # Where can the backend reach OUT?
  - toEndpoints:           # RULE 1: DNS (ALWAYS first!)
    - matchLabels:
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
        k8s-app: coredns
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "53"
        protocol: UDP
  - toEndpoints:           # RULE 2: Database access
    - matchLabels:
        app: postgres
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "5432"
        protocol: TCP
🔑 Novice: How to Read This Policy in Plain English

"Protect pods labeled app: backend. Only allow frontend pods to connect on port 8000. Allow the backend to send DNS queries to CoreDNS (needed to resolve domain names). Allow the backend to connect to postgres on port 5432. Everything else is denied."

E.3 Hubble Configuration for anihpj

YAML
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: hubble-ui-nginx
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  nginx.conf: |
    server {
        listen 8081;
        location / {
            proxy_pass http://hubble-ui;
        }
    }

E.4 WireGuard Encryption Config

Enables transparent node-to-node encryption using WireGuard. All pod-to-pod traffic is automatically encrypted without application changes.

YAML
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cilium-config
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  encryption-enabled: "true"
  encryption-type: "wireguard"
  encryption-nodeEncryption: "false"
  # Verify with: cilium encrypt status

E.5 Prometheus ServiceMonitor for Hubble Metrics

Configures Prometheus Operator to scrape Hubble metrics from Cilium agents. Enables dashboards for flow rates, drops, HTTP errors, and DNS queries.

YAML
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: cilium-hubble-metrics
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cilium
  endpoints:
  - port: hubble-metrics
    interval: 30s
    path: /metrics
  namespaceSelector:
    matchNames:
    - kube-system

E.7 Canary Deployment Configuration for anihpj

Creates a canary backend deployment with different labels. Cilium uses identity-based traffic splitting — no sidecar needed. Gradually shift traffic.

YAML
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: jobpost-backend-canary
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
      version: canary
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: backend
        version: canary
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: backend
        image: anihpj-backend:v2.0-canary
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
---
# CiliumNetworkPolicy allowing canary traffic
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-canary
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
      version: canary
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        app: frontend
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "8000"
        protocol: TCP

E.8 anihpj Dockerfile — Containerize the Django App

Standard Dockerfile for the anihpj/jobpost Django project. Multi-stage build recommended for production but single-stage shown for clarity.

Dockerfile
FROM python:3.11-slim

WORKDIR /app

# Install system dependencies
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    gcc postgresql-client libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Copy requirements first (layer caching)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy application code
COPY . .

# Collect static files
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

EXPOSE 8000

# Run with gunicorn (production)
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", \
     "--workers", "3", \
     "--access-logfile", "-"]

🚀 anihpj Quick Deploy — Full Command Sequence
1 Install Cilium: cilium install --set kubeProxyReplacement=true --set hubble.enabled=true --set encryption.type=wireguard
2 Verify: cilium status --wait → all components should show ✅
3 Build image: docker build -t anihpj-backend:v1.0 . (use E.8 Dockerfile)
4 Apply baseline: kubectl apply -f default-deny-all.yaml (B.4 template, Appendix B)
5 Allow DNS: kubectl apply -f allow-dns.yaml (UDP 53 to CoreDNS — critical!)
6 Deploy policies: Apply frontend→backend→database CNPs (E.2 policy table)
7 Test everything: cilium connectivity test → 21+ tests should pass
8 Monitor: hubble observe → watch traffic flow in real-time!
💡 This sequence deploys a fully secured, observable anihpj cluster in ~5 minutes.

📝 Appendix E — CCA Practice Questions (8 Questions)

Q1
What command installs Cilium with kube-proxy replacement and Hubble enabled?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium install --set kubeProxyReplacement=true --set hubble.enabled=true --set hubble.relay.enabled=true --set hubble.ui.enabled=true

Q2
What is the correct order for applying NetworkPolicies in a zero-trust setup?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Default-deny-all CCNP (lock everything), 2. DNS egress rule (allow name resolution), 3. App-specific CNPs (frontend→backend→database), 4. L7 rules (optional), 5. Egress controls (optional).

Q3
How do you verify WireGuard encryption is active?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium encrypt status — all nodes should show "OK" with the encryption type (WireGuard/IPSec). If not active, check kernel module: modprobe wireguard.

Q4
What ServiceMonitor configuration scrapes Hubble metrics from Cilium agents?
Show Answer
Answer

Use a Prometheus ServiceMonitor with selector: matchLabels: app: cilium, endpoint port hubble-metrics, and namespaceSelector: matchNames: [kube-system].

Q5
How does Cilium enable canary deployments without sidecars?
Show Answer
Answer

Cilium uses identity-based traffic splitting. The canary pods get a different label (e.g., version: canary) which maps to a different Cilium identity. eBPF load balancers split traffic by identity — no sidecar proxy needed.

Q6
What command validates the entire Cilium deployment end-to-end?
Show Answer
Answer

cilium connectivity test — runs 21+ tests covering pod-to-pod, Services, DNS, NetworkPolicy, Encryption, Hubble, and Performance.

Q7
Why does the anihpj Dockerfile use gunicorn instead of the Django dev server?
Show Answer
Answer

The Django dev server (manage.py runserver) is single-threaded and not designed for production. Gunicorn is a production-grade WSGI server with multiple workers, proper logging, and can handle concurrent requests. The CMD uses 3 workers bound to 0.0.0.0:8000.

Q8
What Grafana panels would you create to monitor anihpj with Hubble metrics?
Show Answer
Answer

1. HTTP Request Rate monitoring hubble_http_requests_total, 2. Policy Drops tracking hubble_drop_total, 3. DNS Query Rate via hubble_dns_responses_total, 4. TCP Flow Rate by Verdict using hubble_tcp_flags_total.

Golden rule: Never leave a question unanswered. No penalty for wrong answers!
